content: Simon Cox is the international bestselling author of Cracking the Da Vinci Code, Illuminating Angels & Demons, The Dan Brown Companion and his A to Z series. He is a well-known speaker on the lecture circuit and splits his time between the UK and Los Angeles, where he has set up the media production company Henu Productions. The BBC has dubbed him ‘an historian of the obscure’.
DECODING T H E L O S T S Y M B O L SIMON COX With additional research and material by Ed Davies, Susan Davies, Mark Foster, Jacqueline Harvey, Ian Robertson and Ace Trump

Jacqueline Harvey for once again producing wonders. Ed Davies, of Ancient World Research, for the extra research and material. Thank you, MJ Miller, Joel Schroeder and Steve Honig – the American connection – who have been supportive, kind and positive throughout everything. And MJ, it’s not all about me any more! To Jennifer Clymer, for going above and beyond, and for everything in between. To John Payne – musical genius, friend and a great guy. To Henu Productions, and all at www.intotheduat.com, for a great thrill ride. To my mum and dad on Gozo, you have been awesome. With everything you have gone through and for your amazing fighting spirit and support of me, I am in awe. To Mark Cox, for the words of encouragement. To Salah Tawfik and Ahmed Ali in Cairo, great friends – here’s to a great future together in friendship and business. To Mark Oxbrow, for your unwavering optimism and friendship. To Edgar and Dave at Casa Hayworth, and Judith at Casa Hayworth for the insights. To Gemma Smith – good luck in Oz, Gemms! And to the guys in Agalloch, for letting me use the music. In the publishing world, I would like to thank Bill, Fiona, Deborah, Sharon and all at Mainstream in Edinburgh for the chance to make this a reality. In the US, Trish Todd at Touchstone Fireside/ Simon & Schuster has been a dream to work with, along with all her colleagues. The Pan Macmillan team in Oz have been great, too.

The guys at Generate – Jared, Chris, Michael, Matthew, my new management team in LA – are real superstars and I’m looking forward to working with them on all my future projects. To Laurie Petok, for the Upper Class euphoria and the amazing introduction and friendship. To Betty and Chip Clymer and family in NJ. To all my Facebook friends and Twitter followers (@FindSimonCox), many of you have been wonderfully supportive, even though we have never met. A second mention goes out to Mark Foster – this time in his guise as graphic designer and artist. A brilliant cover, matey! To Sushi Dan on Sunset – the best white tuna sashimi in the world! To Aaron and Emily at Greenblatt’s in LA – I told you it was a stone! To Yolanda in Northern Ireland and Viv in Edinburgh for the amazing hospitality. To David Ritchie up on Skye, for the insights and education. To Beth Andrews – it’s only the beginning! To Sue McGregor for the interview; Robert John at Robert John Photography for the incredible headshots; Robert and Olivia Temple for the friendship, great conversations and for writing the best book on the Sphinx ever! Oh, yes – to Dan Brown. You keep the Langdon novels coming, I’ll keep doing the guides! Finally, to Claire Cox, Mark and Tina Finnel, Lynn Schroeder, Dennis on Gozo, William Henry, Richard Ranken, Richard Belfield, Gordon Rutter and all the Edinburgh crew, the Marina Court mob, Jane and Alexander, Neil and Alison (and Joe and Imogen) Roberts, Tricia Legan, Jon Rappoport, Michael Cremo, John Major Jenkins, Kay Davies, Marcus and Hayley, Tracy Boniface, for the financial wizardry, Mark, Jill and Lily Oxbrow, and Mandy Brown. It’s at this point in my books that I usually give a rundown of my musical listening pleasure whilst writing. Normally, it’s a heavy mix, with lots of dark, gothic, heavy material, but this time around it’s slightly different: female jazz/blues singers have graced the CD player as much as rock bands. Melody Gardot, Sophie Milman and Madeleine Peyroux have all whispered softly in my ear. On the other side of the coin, Epica, Kamelot, Amorphis, Agalloch and Wuthering Heights, to name a few, have let me know I am still alive. I will have missed people, I’m sure, and for that I am sorry. I hope that you will forgive me. It’s been a long, hard road to get to this point and I am indebted to you all. Thank you.

INTRODUCTION It was April 2009, and I had just arrived at the London Book Fair at the Earls Court Exhibition Centre. I was intending to catch up with friends and my UK publishers and have a general look at what was new in the publishing world. However, I knew that something remarkable had happened the minute I arrived. An air of excitement and expectation filled the packed halls and smiles were emanating from all around. I instantly knew what had happened. The new Dan Brown book had been announced. This was to be the start of nearly five months of manic preparation and debate. Clues and hints would be given out, opinions bandied about and crazed speculation would fill thousands of web pages. However, let’s back-pedal a little bit and wind the clock back to the publication of Brown’s previous Robert Langdon thriller, The Da Vinci Code, in 2003. At the time, Dan Brown was the semi-successful author of several thrillers, one of which was the first Robert Langdon novel, Angels & Demons. Sales had been average to poor and Brown’s publisher decided to take a gamble with The Da Vinci Code. They sent 10,000 free copies of the book out to book shops, book buyers, reviewers and trade professionals. The policy worked, and soon sales were really beginning to take off. Back then, I was the editor in chief of a US-based newsstand magazine called Phenomena. (We even ran a fantasy Da Vinci Code movie-casting feature in one edition of the magazine, though none of the actors we suggested was cast in the end.) The Da Vinci Code caused quite a stir in the alternative-history genre that I inhabited, with several of the authors I had worked for being credited as source material for the book. Eventually, I was approached by a small London publisher and asked if I would quickly write a guide to The Da Vinci Code. So Cracking the Da Vinci Code was born and became an international bestseller in its own right. I went on to write Illuminating Angels & Demons. What was intriguing, however, was that on the US dust jacket of the hardcover edition of The Da Vinci Code there seemed to be clues that hinted at the next novel in the series. This was fascinating to me, and I found out all I could about these clues and the secrets that they held.

Time passed and rumours began circulating that a title had been chosen. The new book was to be called The Solomon Key. This was an interesting title, hinting at a medieval book on magic, The Key of Solomon, supposedly written around the fourteenth or fifteenth century in Renaissance Italy. Impatiently, I began researching all that I could about this manuscript, which was claimed to have a lineage that went all the way back to the legendary King Solomon himself. Perfect material for a Dan Brown thriller, I thought. A website for the new title was registered by Brown’s publishing team and all seemed set for the new book to arrive soon. More time passed, and yet more, and still no word about the book. Researchers and commentators began claiming that Brown had scrapped the book, that there would be no follow-up. It was claimed that the high-profile court case with which he had been involved in London had taken its toll and that he had decided to take an extended break from writing. It was even claimed that the movie National Treasure had stolen so much of the new book’s thunder that a complete rewrite had been called for. All of these rumours were unsubstantiated and completely fanciful, of course, but they had free rein on the ever conspiratorial Internet sites that monitored the story and the rumour mill went into overdrive. Then came the London Book Fair. I had accurately predicted to my UK publishers only a couple of months before that the announcement would be made at the London event. I’d said it more in hope than expectation, it has to be said, but it was accurate nonetheless. A press release was handed out by Brown’s publishers and suddenly a new title presented itself: The Lost Symbol, to be published on 15 September 2009. I held my breath. What could this enigmatic title mean? What was the lost symbol? I exhaled. The race was on, the game was afoot, and I rushed headlong into research and reading mode. What you hold in your hands before you is the outcome of that labour. Before long, a new website appeared at thelostsymbol.com, though nothing but a holding page was evident for quite some while. Then, out of the blue, links to a Dan Brown Facebook page and Twitter feed were placed on the site. Excitement grew to fever pitch as overnight thousands of people became Facebook and Twitter followers of Brown. Steadily and surely, clues, hints and little titbits of storyline

began to be revealed through these new media outlets. I started to furiously take notes and begin to research everything I could find as each new clue and hint was revealed. Suddenly a whole new world was opening up. Where previously researchers had had to rely on the scant few clues on the dust jacket of The Da Vinci Code and the odd hint given in interviews, now we were inundated with substantial clues from Twitter and Facebook. It was a cornucopia of material and I started to order new books for my library to cover some of the subjects mentioned in the emerging hints. Some of the clues actually gave coordinates to places. The so- called Bimini Road was one such place. This unusual underwater structure off the island of Bimini in the Bahamas is believed by some to be a man-made edifice and a remnant of Atlantis. I had actually spent two summers on Bimini a number of years back, researching the site for a book on Atlantis I was preparing. Great, I thought, now I have a head start. Other places we were given coordinates to included the Great Pyramid of Giza, the last standing wonder of the ancient world and a place with which I was also intimately familiar. Then there were the coordinates to Newgrange in Ireland, a monumental passage tomb famous for its alignment to the rising sun on the winter solstice, when a narrow beam of light illuminates the floor of the chamber for a brief period of time. I had just visited Newgrange with the author and Freemason Chris McClintock. Possible adversaries and secret societies were hinted at. Ciphers, codes and cryptograms were revealed. Historical figures were mentioned. It was all adding up to a furious game of who could be first to reveal the answers to the clues being given out. Websites sprang up examining, some in great detail, the background and history of some of the people, places and groups being mentioned. It was an Internet feeding frenzy. And then I remembered something. Aringarosa. A character from The Da Vinci Code whose name had a hidden meaning. Aringa is the Italian for ‘herring’ and rossa the Italian for ‘red’. Dan Brown liked to throw multiple red herrings into the mix. I began to look at the Twitter and Facebook clues in a new light. What if many of these were indeed red herrings? Blind panic overtook me. What if I was thoroughly researching subjects that would not be included in the published book? That was when I stopped looking at the Facebook and Twitter pages. After all, everything would be revealed on 15

September 2009. Even the publication date, we were told, was part of the game. I began to check almanacs, history books, websites, conspiracy theorists’ blogs – nothing. Then it hit me. 15/09/09 – three numbers that added up to 33. So it was true. The Freemasons, and specifically Scottish Rite Freemasons, would be a central theme of the book – something that had been hinted at on the dust jacket of The Da Vinci Code all those years ago. Then, before I knew it, publication day arrived. Clutching The Lost Symbol in my sweaty palms, I began to read furiously. Some 12 hours later, it was all over. And then the realisation. A huge number of the hints and clues given out over the previous few months on the Dan Brown Twitter and Facebook pages were indeed ‘Aringarosas’. There was no Morgan affair, no Aaron Burr, no William Wirt (and the strange story of his skull), no Knights of the Golden Circle, no substantial mentions of Albert Pike, no Benedict Arnold, no Confederate gold, no Babington Plot, no Alexander Hamilton and the origins of the New York Stock Exchange, no Sons of Liberty, no Roanoke and the first settlers, no Robert Hanssen, no Checkpoint Charlie in Berlin. All of these people, places and groups had been mentioned in the clues. None of them are in the book. Cleverly, there was no Key of Solomon either. Instead we have a family with the name Solomon, who hold the keys to the eventual outcome. Needless to say, there was no Bimini or Newgrange; there was, however, the Great Pyramid – though not in the context many had anticipated. So Dan Brown and his publishers had managed to pull off something of a coup. They had successfully kept the plot of The Lost Symbol pretty well hidden until the day of publication (though a couple of US newspapers did print reviews a day before publication in defiance of an embargo). This was an amazing feat. In excess of five million books had been printed up and yet there were no reported leaks or rogue books appearing on Internet auction sites. Dan Brown had managed to deflect attention away from the real storyline, keeping people occupied with subjects that at best were only on the fringes of the novel. It was an incredible undertaking that guaranteed a huge amount of media and public attention on launch day. So what did we end up with? Is The Lost Symbol a worthy successor to Angels & Demons and The Da Vinci Code? The Lost Symbol is, in the end, a pretty good thriller, with a plot

that keeps Robert Langdon on his toes and involves some big themes and historical enigmas. However, it’s the deeper, more hidden elements to the book that I believe will have the most impact over time. What Dan Brown has attempted to do is to write something akin to a hidden hermetic text between the lines of the novel. It’s a bold and ambitious undertaking and one that I applaud him for. Indeed, the last ten chapters of the book and the epilogue are more or less an extended treatise on deism, hermetic thought and religious tolerance. The Freemasons are the secret society of choice this time round. There are those who see in Freemasonry a secretive, covert and sinister movement, blasphemous and intent on power. I see it in a rather different way. I personally am not a Freemason. Nor will I ever be one, as I prefer to write about and observe things from an outsider’s perspective, but I do know many Freemasons. Indeed, Ian Robertson, one of the chief researchers for this very book is a Freemason, as is my friend Chris McClintock, author of the soon to be published Sun of God series of books on the origins of the craft and its symbolism. Neither of these two people are in any way sinister and nor are the countless other Freemasons whom I know and respect. I like the stance that Dan Brown has taken on Freemasonry in The Lost Symbol. Many commentators thought that the Masons would in effect be the ‘bad guys’; this is not the case, and Brown makes a good case for Freemasonry being a tolerant and enlightened movement with some interesting and forward-thinking ideas. Whilst it must be admitted that Freemasonry is a secretive society, it is not a secret society. Membership is easy to research, and most members are not shy about letting you know that they are within the craft. Since its heyday in the mid to late 1700s, Freemasonry has attracted men of a certain social standing, but it has become a more welcoming group to join of late and I hope that this trend continues. One of the things I wanted to get across in some of the entries in this book is that maybe it’s not Freemasonry we should be wary of; maybe it’s the secret groups and societies that we actually know very little about that should be feared. Then again, maybe we are simply chasing shadows, wisps of rumour and supposition that have tormented us for millennia. Perhaps we have a fear of secret and hidden things that in the end are not so very secret or hidden after

all. Another thing worth noting is that many of the people mentioned in this book, although they were not Freemasons (Pierre L’Enfant springs to mind), or at least we have no evidence that they were, would nonetheless have been intimately familiar with the society and its workings. Their contemporaries and peers would have been members and the craft would have been all around. It seems likely, for instance, that Thomas Jefferson, though we have no direct evidence of his membership of a Masonic lodge, did have sympathies with the Masonic ideals of brotherhood, enlightenment and religious tolerance. Like my previous guides to Dan Brown’s books, Decoding the Lost Symbol is laid out in an easy to read A to Z format. There are some 60 entries in all, which is less than in previous guides, and this was a deliberate decision. Here I wanted to be able to give you a much more in-depth look at some of the themes, places, people and groups that are featured in the novel. I hope I have succeeded in this task. The BBC once called me ‘an historian of the obscure’, a title that I like very much indeed. I have aimed to bring you some of the history of obscure and hidden subjects in the pages of this book. If you feel the urge to look deeper and delve further into some of the subjects highlighted here, then take a look at the bibliography and start to build your own library on esoteric and arcane subjects, though just be careful to actually sleep and eat while you become familiar with the ancient mystery traditions. It’s an addictive pursuit but also a very rewarding one – and one I hope many of you will undertake. If you want to talk about, debate, argue or expound upon any of the subjects in this book or the novel itself, then head over to my website at www.decodingthelostsymbol.com, where you will find a forum for debate and articles and blogs about many of the subjects discussed within these pages. If you want to contact me directly to talk about any of the issues raised, I have my very own Facebook page and can be found on Twitter too (@FindSimonCox). Writing this book was a lot of fun, and it has given me a newfound respect and admiration for the men who founded the nation of America at the end of the eighteenth century. It’s a period of history that I was not particularly familiar with and I have really enjoyed researching and subsequent writing about this tumultuous time. The Founding Fathers really were incredibly enlightened and

forward-thinking men, and they guided the formation of the republic with steady hands and an unwavering resolve. I now look at them and that period of time in a new light. I hope you enjoy Decoding the Lost Symbol, and find its contents enlightening and interesting. I pass it on to you in the hope that you will find it as fun to read as it was to write. Simon Cox September 2009

2012 The world is going to end in 2012. To be precise, it will end on 22 December 2012. Or so say the burgeoning number of believers who are convinced that when this fateful day arrives it will be our last. In The Lost Symbol, the character Peter Solomon discusses the prophecy of the enlightenment of mankind with a group of students, one of whom shouts out that this date is predicted as 2012 and this is revealed to be a prediction from Mayan mathematics. The roots of this prophecy lie in antiquity and in particular hinge upon an ancient Mayan calendar known as the Meso-American Long Count calendar. Put simply, the current cycle of this calendar comes to an end after some 5,125 years in December 2012. The Long Count calendar is divided into various cycles: a uinal is comprised of 20 days; a tun is 18 uinals, or 360 days; a katun is 20 tuns, or 7,200 days; and, finally, 20 katuns are known as a baktun, 144,000 days. We know that the Long Count was begun in August 3114 bc and, so far, we have progressed through well over 12 baktuns. More precisely, in the Long Count as of 17 September 2009, we stand at 12.19.16.12.9. Some scholars believe that the arrival of 13 baktuns, or a date of 13.0.0.0.0 – the very date that will occur on 22 December 2012 – is a significant event and in fact marks the end of the Long Count itself. The number 13 was indeed very sacred to the ancient Mayans, not least because it represented the 13 major joints in the body. It is also the number of times the moon orbits the earth during one of our years. One of the sacred Mayan calendars is the Tzolkin, a ritual calendar consisting of 260 days, which matches exactly the duration of a human pregnancy, and was used to track Earth–Venus conjunctions. In the Tzolkin calendar, the number 13 features again, the 260 days being broken down into 13 ‘months’, each of 20 days. People set such great store by the Mayan calendars – especially the Long Count calendar, with its ominous indication towards the year 2012 – because the culture that created them was obsessed with marking time and was able to do so with remarkable accuracy. Lawrence E. Joseph highlights this in his book Apocalypse 2012:

The Maya love their calendars, see them as visual depictions of the passage of time, which is how life unfolds. They charted the unfolding with not one but twenty calendars, only fifteen of which have been released to the modern world; the remaining five are still kept secret by Mayan Elders. Mayan calendars are pegged to the movements of the Sun, the Moon, and the visible planets, to harvest and insect cycles. This compulsive attitude towards time led them to make some incredible measurements. For example, they were able to calculate the orbit of Venus to within one day every 1,000 years. Thirteen of the cycles known as a baktun, or 5,125 of our years, comprise an ‘age’ and were known to the Mayans as a Sun. According to their detailed beliefs, we are currently in the fourth Sun, having progressed through three Suns in the past. The fifth Sun – if there is to be a fifth – will start on 22 December 2012, which in the Long Count will be 13.0.0.0.0. Literally, year zero. According to Mayan legends, our current age, the fourth Sun, actually began with the birth of Venus, in the year 3114 BC. In The Mayan Prophecies, Adrian Gilbert and Maurice Cotterell explain why this is significant in relation to 2012: As we approach the doomsday year of 2012, which the ancient Mayans prophesised would be the end of the last age, one can only feel apprehension for the future of our Earth. The start of the last Mayan age was the Birth of Venus, the Quetzalcoatl star, on 12 August 3114 BC. On the last day of the age, 22 December 2012, the cosmic connections between Venus, the sun and the Pleiades, and Orion are once more in evidence. For just as Venus was indeed ‘born’ on the earlier date, its rising just before the dawn being heralded by the Pleiades at the meridian, so it now symbolically ‘dies’. While this makes for dramatic reading, what is not conclusive is what Venus ‘dying’ actually means for us and the planet Earth. There are many who would assume that the ending of one age

simply leads to the beginning of another. That we are moving out of one Mayan age into another is indisputable; the only unknown is how much blood and agony, if any, will be associated with this ‘birth’. A number of academics believe that they have found within Mayan inscriptions dates that exist beyond 13.0.0.0.0; in fact, dates are mentioned that are thousands of years in our future. For example, an event in the year 4772 is highlighted amongst the inscriptions found at Palenque in southern Mexico. So, are these academics correct? Is the turning of the calendar and the arrival of 13.0.0.0.0 nothing more than a magnificent event to be celebrated, just another notch on the great calendar? If you side with the doomsayers who believe the world really will end in 2012, then there are currently a lot of world-destroying scenarios to choose from. Aside from the usual round of nuclear wars, threats from climate change or mankind-killing plagues, there are also a number of other contenders. Some theories suggest that what will destroy us all in 2012 is a polar shift. This, it is purported, would lead to a crustal displacement, as theorised by Charles Hapgood in his 1958 book Earth’s Shifting Crust. The idea is terrifying. Hapgood even grabbed the attention of Albert Einstein, who not only corresponded with Hapgood and agreed with his research but also endorsed it by writing a foreword to Hapgood’s book. In brief, the theory suggests that every few thousand years the Earth’s poles literally ‘shift’, often suddenly moving large distances. When this happens, it can be accompanied by a crustal displacement, a scenario where the crust of the earth moves across the inner core of the planet, shifting the poles over a vast distance and ultimately moving them nearer to the equator. It goes without saying that such a movement would result in not only the destruction of most of the civilised world that exists on this thin crust, but also massive flooding, which would wipe out anyone and anything that had managed to survive the initial displacement. Another popular theory is that the sun will flex her muscles and demonstrate her true power come 2012. Quite simply, the sun is not a stable celestial object; it is in constant flux, and the surface is not an even temperature. Over time her power waxes and wanes, subject to cycles that are so complex we are still trying to map them all. The surface is said to be an average temperature of 5,800

degrees Celsius; however, areas that are much cooler, some 1,500 degrees cooler, develop due to strong concentrations of magnetic flux on the surface and appear as large black dots on the sun. These are the areas that we call sunspots. This sunspot activity is closely linked to the sun’s cycles and we progress from a solar maximum (the maximum number of sunspots) to a solar minimum, when sunspot activity is at its lowest. A group of scientists, including S.K. Solanski from the Max-Planck Institute for Solar System Research, published a report in Nature in 2004 explaining that, according to their data, the sun has been unusually active since 1940: Here we report a reconstruction of the sunspot number covering the past 11,400 years . . . According to our reconstruction, the level of solar activity during the past 70 years is exceptional, and the previous period of equally high activity occurred more than 8,000 years ago. We find that during the past 11,400 years the Sun spent only of the order of 10% of the time at a similarly high level of magnetic activity and almost all of the earlier high activity periods were shorter than the present episode. This is indeed a strange coincidence; the sun just happens to be demonstrating much higher than usual activity in the run-up to the Long Count end date of 2012. Will the sun play a pivotal role, and has it got a surprise in store for us on 22 December that year? While there is no conclusive evidence that the sun will play a role in events of 22 December 2012, we have to remember that the civilisation that devised the Long Count calendar spent a vast amount of time viewing the heavens and many of their calendars are tied closely to the sun. The sun isn’t the only force of nature capable of wiping us out in 2012, mind you. There are also large asteroids to consider. An impact similar to the one that occurred roughly 65.5 million years ago on the coast of the Yucatán land mass, coincidentally the same land mass that was home to the Mayans, would certainly wipe out civilised life as we know it. Then there is the idea that our entire solar system is moving as a

single unit through the inner space of our galaxy, the Milky Way. Some scientists hypothesise that our system could be moving into a much more active and unstable region of space. Our sun and her planets, including Earth, could be at risk from these dangerous regions and it goes without saying that we would be totally exposed and utterly defenceless against such natural phenomena. Like gears in some vast and ancient machine, we have no control over where our planet – indeed, our solar system – is headed. That we have passed through such regions in the past is without doubt; the question is, did the Mayans possess knowledge of these celestial regions, and did they know the precise date when we would return through possibly deadly environs? There have been mass extinctions throughout Earth’s long history. The undeniable truth is that one will happen again at some point in our future; however, is it likely that such an event is just a few years away? Having scared the living daylights out of everyone, it is now time to come back down to earth and try to look logically at where we are now. All of this began because of a date contained in one ancient calendar. While it is without doubt a significant milestone, we cannot be certain that it marks an end time. In fact, many New Age writers suggest that, rather than the end of the world, what this date actually marks is in fact a rebirth. Authors such as John Major Jenkins propose that the Mayans anticipated a great change in humanity’s spiritual potential at the end of the current baktun, or age, and many have seized on this idea, predicting that human consciousness will develop further in the light of 2012 and usher in a new era – a golden age for mankind, if you will. Many other people believe that the calendar will tick over with absolutely no drama at all. It will be just a day like any other. The truth is that if we are basing our beliefs about the destruction of the world solely on the complex calendars of Meso-America, then we have a problem. So many ancient texts were destroyed following the Spanish conquest of Mexico in 1521, led by Hernán Cortés, that we simply no longer have the full story available to us. While fragments of the Mayan beliefs remain, we are missing a great deal. Therefore all we can really do is wait until 22 December 2012. If we do wake up that morning, we should make sure that we all celebrate, no matter what our beliefs.

Subjects such as 2012 make us realise how fragile the very existence of humanity is, and the truth is it is a miracle that we are here at all. That our entire civilisation exists on the surface of one tiny rock that is subject to all the dangers of the galaxy is cause for wonderment.

ABADDON One of the character pseudonyms used by Mal’akh in The Lost Symbol is that of Dr Christopher Abaddon. The name is an interesting choice, as it encompasses both the name of Christ and the name of the demon Abaddon. In ancient Hebrew legend, Abaddon is said to mean ‘to perish’, ‘a place of destruction’ and ‘destroyer’. In the New Testament, the Revelation of St John 9:11, Abaddon is the king of tormenting locusts and the angel of the bottomless pit. In Revelation, he is said to have sent out his locusts at the sounding of the fifth trumpet. Upon the sounding of this trumpet, a star is said to fall from heaven to earth and this star is then given the keys to the abyss. When the abyss is opened, thick smoke issues forth, followed by the locusts, led by Abaddon. These locusts are of an extraordinary type, resembling some strange hybrid animal, with a woman’s hair, lion’s teeth and scorpion’s tail, amongst other weird attributes. In Greek, Abaddon is known as Apollyon, which means ‘destroyer’. Abaddon is also associated with death and hell in ancient rabinnical writings, and in the Old Testament Abaddon is seen as a poetic name for the realm of the dead, Hades or hell (see Job 26:6). Within these ancient texts, it’s clear that Abaddon can either be an individual, as we see in the Book of Revelation, or a place of the dead and of destruction. In the Dead Sea Scrolls, Abaddon is mentioned in the context of a place called ‘the Sheol of Abaddon’. In other words, the name is synonymous with the underworld realm of the dead. The Coptic Christian Church translates his name as Abbaton, and under this guise he is the angel of death. In certain Coptic writings, it becomes clear that Abaddon/Abbaton is, in effect, a kind of mirror image of the Christ figure. Indeed, in the text known as The Apocalypse of Bartholomew, Abbaton is mentioned as having been present in the tomb at the moment of Christ’s resurrection. Interestingly, we see echoes of the nature of the character of Christopher Abaddon/Mal’akh when we look more closely at the Coptic legends associated with this demon. It is said that any man who venerated him stood a chance of being saved at the End of Days, and the figure of Abbaton plays an important role in the scenario of the Last Judgement. In this guise, Abbadon can almost

be seen as an Antichrist type of figure and this fits perfectly with the character in the book. In contrast to those seeking knowledge and enlightenment, Mal’akh/Christopher Abaddon is hell-bent on preventing the discoveries of Noetic science from being distributed to the wider world, as well as hoping that Freemasonry will be discredited and seen as sinister. He is the antithesis of his father. The name Abaddon has been used extensively in modern popular culture. Even author J.K. Rowling, in her Harry Potter books, introduced a character using the Greek version of the name, Apollyon, who was a previous caretaker of Hogwarts School and someone who would punish the students.

AKEDAH In The Lost Symbol, Mal’akh wields an ancient weapon with a notorious past called the Akedah knife. Not content to furnish the villain of the novel with just any old ancient knife of power, Dan Brown tells us that this is the most famous knife in existence. In the novel, we hear that Mal’akh spent a large part of his fortune obtaining this legendary weapon. It had been crafted from meteoritic iron 3,000 years earlier and was said to be the exact same knife that Abraham had wielded in the Book of Genesis when he was prepared to sacrifice his son Isaac to obey God’s command. We are also told that the knife has a long and chequered history, having been owned by Nazis, Popes and European alchemists, amongst others. At the end of The Lost Symbol, Mal’akh places the Akedah knife in the hand of his father, Peter Solomon, and attempts to coerce him into killing his estranged son. Something interesting to note here is that Mal’akh places the Akedah knife in the left hand of Peter Solomon, his one remaining hand. We are told ‘the left hand serves the darkness’ and also that the removal of Peter Solomon’s right hand had been designed with this very moment in mind – quite simply, he has no choice but to use his left hand to grasp the knife. If Peter Solomon was to carry out this sacrificial killing with his left hand, then, according to Mal’akh’s twisted beliefs at least, the sacrifice would be perfect and Mal’akh would secure his place as a demon in the afterlife. Furthermore, the scene takes place on a granite altar in the House of the Temple so we are left in no doubt that this is a re-creation of the fabled attempted sacrifice of Isaac by his father Abraham. It is in the Old Testament, in the Book of Genesis 22:2, that we find the story that is itself called the Akedah, or the Binding of Isaac. We are told from the outset that God is testing Abraham and so says to him, ‘Take your son, your only son, Isaac, your beloved, and go to the land of Moriah, where you are to offer him as a burnt offering on one of the mountains which I shall point out to you.’ Abraham left early in the morning, following God’s instructions. He took two young men, together with his son Isaac, and headed for Mount Moriah. He arrived at the sacred spot three days later and Abraham bound his son to an altar and was about to take Isaac’s life

with his knife when an angel appeared and implored Abraham to stop, telling him that he had passed God’s test. So it was that Isaac was spared and a ram was sacrificed on the altar instead. The story fits neatly into The Lost Symbol because we are told that Mal’akh took his name and identity from Moloch, a fearsome fallen angel who appears in John Milton’s Paradise Lost, the epic poem that describes the Fall of Man. We begin to see the relationship between Moloch and sacrifice in these lines from the poem: First, Moloch, horrid king, besmear’d with blood Of human sacrifice, and parents’ tears. There are also references to Moloch (or Molech) in the biblical texts that link the deity with sacrifice and this is in accordance with the story of the Akedah and God’s command that Isaac be offered up by Abraham. In Leviticus 18:21, we find the following passage: ‘You will not allow any of your children to be sacrificed to Molech, thus profaning the name of your God.’ Dan Brown has brought all of these elements together in The Lost Symbol and the climactic scene in the House of the Temple is loaded with historical references and symbolism relating to sacrifice. Not only do we have Mal’akh, who is modelled on Moloch, a deity to whom the Canaanites would often sacrifice their children, but we also have him wielding the very knife of Abraham. In addition, he is asking his father to slay him and, furthermore, this occurs beside the altar in a sacred temple. When Dan Brown writes that once again this blade would be used in a ritual of sacrifice for which it had been forged, we see how he has cleverly brought together all of these powerful symbols and references of sacrifice and set up this pivotal moment for maximum impact. Another intriguing point here is that Mal’akh is offering himself as a willing sacrificial victim, a theme that we often see in the ancient world. There is growing evidence that many cultures practised sacrifice and that often the victims gave themselves not only willingly but also gladly: to offer oneself as a sacrifice seems to have been a matter of great honour and reverence. Today, we can see how this conception of sacrifice still influences the behaviour of idealists who offer themselves without reservation as suicide bombers. Many scholars believe that at the time of the Akedah, when Isaac

was bound to the altar, he was no longer a child. Rather, various sources state that he was somewhere between the ages of 25 and 37, so he would have been perfectly capable of resisting his father if he had wanted to. Josephus, the Jewish historian from the first century ad, refers to this concept, and in his Antiquities of the Jews he states that Isaac responded to the news that he was to be sacrificed with equanimity: Now Isaac was of such a generous disposition as became the son of such a father, and was pleased with his discourse; and said, ‘That he was not worthy to be born at first, if he should reject the determination of God and of his father, and should resign himself up readily to both their pleasures; since it would have been unjust if he had not obeyed, even if his father alone had so resolved.’ So, he went immediately to the altar to be sacrificed. The Akedah is without doubt one of the most controversial sections of the Book of Genesis and debate still rages about not just God’s motives but also those of Abraham and Isaac. By ordering Abraham to kill his firstborn and beloved son – a son who came to Abraham’s wife, Sarah, only after much suffering – we see God testing the absolute limits of someone’s faith. This test continues to be taught as a moral lesson in several faiths today, the parable being found within the Jewish sacred writings and also in the Islamic Qur’an, for example. The setting of the Akedah also has a special significance in The Lost Symbol. It was said to have taken place on Mount Moriah, and this sacred mountain – the mount of the Lord, according to the Book of Genesis – just happens to be exactly the same spot where Solomon’s Temple was later constructed. Mount Moriah is, to many scholars, the Temple Mount. I cover Solomon’s Temple in further detail elsewhere in this book. However, it is worth mentioning here that not only is Solomon’s Temple fundamentally important within Freemasonry, but it also served as a model for the Capitol Building in Washington DC. So Mount Moriah, the place of the Akedah, was not just the location of the attempted sacrifice of Isaac, it was also set to become the home of the holiest of ancient temples, upon

which the Capitol itself was modelled. In The Lost Symbol, one final intriguing attribute Dan Brown gives the knife of Akedah is the manner of its construction. We are told that it was forged of iron from a meteorite that crashed into the desert of Canaan long ago. Although this information is not in the original version of the Akedah story in the Book of Genesis, the invention is not a complete fabrication for the novel. It is well known that the ancient peoples of the Middle East would construct sacred knives and powerful weapons from iron that had fallen in the form of meteors. This material was highly prized, not only because it was a source of iron which could be forged, but also because meteorites were often described in the ancient world as thunderbolts, probably because of the observed phenomena when a meteor descends from the skies and impacts the earth. A weapon shaped from a thunderbolt was a potent symbol indeed. G.A. Wainwright, in a seminal paper entitled ‘Iron in Egypt’, states that many ancient peoples came to call this form of iron from the skies ‘lightning-iron’. He also gives one example of the use of such weapons, citing the story of Antar, the pre-Islamic Arabian warrior and poet, who came to possess a powerful sword he called Dhami: On discovering the stone to be a thunderbolt the man gave it to a blacksmith to have a sword made of it. On two separate occasions a single stroke of this supernatural weapon clove through the armour and split horse and horseman asunder, ‘so that they fell apart in four pieces’. On another occasion it clove a warrior ‘to his girdle’. These magic weapons have naturally been in great demand throughout the East. The Egyptian god Horus himself wielded a blade of meteoritic iron in his legendary clash with the god Seth, in which Horus defeated Seth in revenge for the death of his father, Osiris. As well as the potency of such meteoritic iron, the material also had profound religious significance. There was a sacred ritual in Ancient Egypt known as the Opening of the Mouth. It was performed on the dead Pharaoh and a sacred knife known as a ntrwj-blade was used to prise open the mouth of the king. These

sacred knives, or adzes, had blades formed from meteoritic iron, also known to the Egyptians as bja. To complement the celestial origins of the blades, the handles of these knives were formed in the shape of the constellation Ursus Major, otherwise known as ‘the big dipper’ and ‘the plough’. It is clear why in the eyes of the ancient priests these blades made from meteoritic iron were such powerful objects. They were perfect for opening the mouth of the deceased in a religious ritual because they were made from thunderbolts.. What better way to physically and metaphorically prise open the lips of the dead? The Ancient Egyptians also believed that the vault of heaven itself was constructed from bja and upon death the limbs of the deceased were themselves turned into bja. The word bja was also used to mean ‘a miracle’ and ‘to depart from’. From this, we come to understand that iron that fell to earth was not just iron from the heavens, it was actually seen as being heaven itself, nothing less than the very same material from which heaven was constructed. Since it could also mean ‘to depart from’, it is clear that the Ancient Egyptians believed that these meteors had left heaven to fall to earth. The Muslims later held a belief that Allah’s angels used meteors to drive away Satan and to fight djinns, who were seen as supernatural beings. With such powerful concepts in play, it is no wonder that knives and weapons forged from this material were considered weapons of the gods themselves, thunderbolts that could be brandished by mortal hands. Putting all of this together, we see why a character such as Mal’akh in The Lost Symbol would use a knife that was crafted from meteoric iron; there is no more potent weapon than one shaped from such material. Abraham, too, would have been aware of the significance of such a knife, though whether he truly did wield a knife of meteoritic iron during the events that came to be known as the Akedah we will probably never know. ALCHEMY In The Lost Symbol, Dan Brown has pulled together various traditions that fall under the banner of the Western Mystery or Esoteric Tradition. The Great Library at Alexandria is mentioned in the novel, as are the ancient cultures of Egypt, Rome and Greece. Mystery schools feature, as do the Hebrew Kabbalah, hermeticism, the mystical Rosicrucians, Tarot cards and Freemasonry. Arguably the most important, having influenced all of the above, is alchemy, referred to as the ‘perennial philosophy’. Alchemy is at the heart of the Western Mysteries and pervades all traditions in some way, shape or form through its exquisite language of symbols. Its origins are lost in the mists of time but are extremely ancient, and there are many stories concerning its beginnings. It was known to and practised by the Egyptians and Chinese in antiquity. Its name means ‘the Land of Khem’, or ‘the black land’, from the Arabic name for Egypt, Al-Khemia or Kemet. The reference to black relates to the fertile soil of the Nile Delta that spreads across the Nile Valley with the annual flooding of the river. It is from this etymology that alchemy is often called ‘the Black Art’, and it is from alchemy that the modern science of chemistry arose, although this name did not appear until the seventeenth century. Robert Boyle, an alchemist and a friend of Isaac Newton, wrote The Sceptical Chymist in 1661. It is widely regarded as the first book about chemistry. Professor Robert Langdon, in The Lost Symbol, states that in Newton’s letters to Boyle he warned him that the mystical knowledge they were studying could not be communicated without dangerous consequences for the world. There exists a range of legendary accounts of alchemy’s origins. The Egyptian god Thoth is often said to be its founder. He is described as the ‘god man’ who brought religion and learning to Egypt and was credited with being the inventor of writing, mathematics, music, astronomy, architecture and medicine. The similarities between Thoth, Hermes and Mercury, being custodians of all knowledge as well as intermediaries between heaven and earth within their respective cultures (Egyptian, Greek and Roman), have collectively shaped the character known as ‘Hermes Trismegistus’, the father of alchemy. It is Hermes Trismegistus who gives his name to the term

hermeticism, primarily through a collection of Hellenistic texts known as the Corpus Hermeticum. These texts were first popular during the peak of Alexandrian culture and came to the fore again during the European Renaissance, when they became essential reading during a revival of interest in the esoteric and the occult. According to legend, Hermes Trismegistus created a fabulous emerald tablet said to contain the secrets of creation for those who could penetrate their meaning. Sir Isaac Newton made an English translation around 1680 of the alleged content of the tablet, which had been passed down through ancient texts. Newton’s translation read: Tis true without lying, certain and most true. That which is below is like that which is above and that which is above is like that which is below to do the miracles of One only Thing. And as all things have been and arose from One by the mediation of One: so all things have their birth from this One Thing by adaptation. The Sun is its father, the Moon its mother, the Wind hath carried it in its belly, the Earth its nurse. The father of all perfection in the whole world is here. Its force or power is entire if it be converted into earth. Separate thou the Earth from the Fire, the subtle from the gross, sweetly with great industry. It ascends from the Earth to Heaven and again it descends to the Earth and receives the force of things superior and inferior. By this means you shall have the glory of the whole world and thereby all obscurity shall fly from you. Its force is above all force for it vanquishes every subtle thing and penetrates every solid thing. So was the world created. From this are and do come admirable adaptations whereof the means (or process) is here in this. Hence I am called Hermes Trismegistus, having the three parts of the philosophy of the whole world. That which I have said of the operation of the Sun is accomplished and ended. ‘The Emerald Tablet’ is the key text used in alchemy, as it maps out

the seven steps of transformation required to create the elusive Philosopher’s Stone. According to other legends, the father of alchemy is Seth, the son of Adam, who apparently created the emerald tablet in the hope that those who followed its teachings would correct the Fall of Adam from the Garden of Eden, because it would allow them to discover the key to perfection. In some Gnostic legends, Seth is also given the secrets of the Kabbalah by Adam. Other variants say that the tablet was saved from the Flood by Noah, who took it aboard the Ark and afterwards hid it in a cave near Hebron. Sarah, the wife of Abraham, later discovered the tablet, and it informed the Hebrew faith. Yet another tale is that Miriam, the daughter of Moses, was entrusted with its safekeeping, and she placed it in the Ark of the Covenant along with the sacred relics. ‘The Emerald Tablet’ is also said to be one of the tablets brought down from Mount Sinai by Moses. In esoteric circles, the Ten Commandments were said to have been the exoteric teachings for the masses, while ‘the Emerald Tablet’ was reserved for initiates of the mysteries. In Islamic tradition, Hermes Trismegistus is identified with the wise man Idris, who revealed divine laws to the faithful. Some Muslim scholars have also associated Idris with Enoch. The apocryphal Book of Enoch describes the angelic wisdom that was shared with Enoch. In some Kabbalistic traditions, Enoch is transformed into the archangel Metatron to become the Chancellor of Heaven. The variety of characters mentioned have one thing in common: each personifies the qualities, values and characteristics that seekers of true perfection, alchemists, strive for. Another legend concerning the origin of ‘the Emerald Tablet’ claims that it was discovered by Alexander the Great and later exhibited at the Great Library at Alexandria in Egypt. This library was reportedly a massive repository for alchemical texts that were later destroyed by a great fire. Fortunately, Arab scholars had copied many of the works, thus preserving the knowledge for the following centuries. Alchemy then found its way to Europe via the Islamic invasion of Spain and the south of France in ad 711. Latin translations began to appear as early as the twelfth and thirteenth centuries and became widespread from the Renaissance onwards. The influence of alchemy was expressed in the legends of the Holy Grail as they developed in Europe. The Sacro Catino, a sacred hexagonal bowl to be found in Genoa, has been identified by some

as the Holy Grail. Legend says that it was fashioned from a solid piece of emerald and was the dish used at the Last Supper. In Parzival, his epic poem, Wolfram von Eschenbach describes the Grail as a green stone not as the familiar cup we now think of. Possession of the stone offered the individual eternal life in the same way that the Philosopher’s Stone of the alchemists is said to. ‘The Emerald Tablet’, according to a final legendary account, was said to have been last seen in the tomb of Christian Rosenkreutz, the legendary founder of the Rosicrucians. Alchemy can seem a complex subject, given its strange language and symbolism. The purpose of alchemy is transmutation, and although many alchemists of the Middle Ages claimed to have turned lead into gold, Robert Langdon is correct when he states that spiritual alchemy is about enlightenment. It is an investigation into hermetic philosophy to discover the interconnectedness of everything, the macrocosm and the microcosm, the above and the below, in order to utilise this knowledge in both spiritual and practical ways. This explains why the members of the Royal Society, or ‘Invisible College’ – men steeped in the arcane – were fascinated by its teachings. With the rise of the various modern sciences in the eighteenth century and beyond, alchemy was viewed as outdated and superstitious by the masses. Today, however, alchemy is experiencing a renaissance and is viewed in a completely new way, with psychologists and quantum physicists seeing parallels with their work. The famous analyst Carl Gustav Jung spent the latter part of his life studying the rich symbolism of alchemy and this inspired his groundbreaking work on archetypes, which helped his patients bring about inner transformation. Today there are a range of websites and groups dedicated to the study of alchemy and alchemical texts and drawings, possibly making the Black Art more accessible than it has ever been. The figurative process of change can be characterised in a number of ways that correspond to the seven steps. For example, with metals, the process of turning lead to gold goes through stages: first, the lead turns to tin, then iron, copper, mercury, silver and finally gold. The metals appear in this order because each is considered to be superior to the one before, with gold being the most perfect. Each step has a range of other correspondences, such as to astronomical bodies: Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, Mercury,

the Moon and the Sun. In terms of alchemical elements (not to be confused with the chemical elements contained on the periodic table), they are, in order: fire, water, air, earth, sulphur, mercury and salt. The old expression ‘salt of the earth’ possibly begins to make more sense when it is seen in this context. In alchemy, these elements are used to describe the characteristics or nature of things. For example, acid is a mixture of the elements fire and water: water because it is liquid and fire because it burns; together they produce the characteristics of acid. The names for the steps are calcination, dissolution, separation, conjunction, fermentation, distillation and coagulation. Using the language of symbols, alchemical diagrams are filled with strange images. For those who understand what the images represent, however, a diagram will map out one of the stages of the alchemical process as described on ‘the Emerald Tablet’. The diagrams need to be studied carefully by looking at what is on the top and bottom of the picture or on the left or right. This is because alchemy works to bring together opposites, to create a union of all things. The Philosopher’s Stone, often depicted as having androgynous characteristics, is sometimes described as ‘the Chemical Wedding’. In the symbolism of Freemasonry, the steps to enlightenment are illustrated by the rough ashlar (or stone) and the polished ashlar. The new Masonry candidate is the base material, lead or the rough ashlar, and is transformed into an enlightened Master Mason, gold or the polished ashlar. Freemasonry describes this in the 3rd degree as the point within a circle from which no Master Mason can err. This process is by way of entering the porch or entrance to King Solomon’s Temple, past the great pillars of Boaz and Jachin, and journeying up the winding staircase in order to reach the Holy of Holies or the sanctum sanctorum. Other Masonic allegories discuss the Lost Word and the all-seeing eye of God, which are more metaphors for the Philosopher’s Stone. In Scottish Rite Freemasonry, the double-headed eagle of the 33rd degree serves a similar purpose. In The Lost Symbol, Robert Langdon gives a lecture describing ‘the most hidden of all hidden things’. He explains that the circle with a round dot in the middle is called the circumpunct. This is the alchemical symbol for gold; it was also the symbol of the Egyptian sun god, Ra. He offers more examples, but finishes by saying that

what it really stands for is the mind and soul being at one. Langdon also focuses on the imagery of the pyramid and the symbolism of stones when he discusses the alchemical motto VITRIOL: visita interiora terrae rectificando invenies occultum lapidem. Dennis William Hauck’s book The Complete Idiot’s Guide to Alchemy offers the following explanation: Vista Interiora Terra Rectificando Invenies Occultum Lapidem (Visit the innermost parts of the earth; and by setting things right [rectifying], you will find the hidden Stone). The first letters of these seven Latin words spell out ‘VITRIOL’ which is a natural form of sulfuric acid. This liquid fire is the fundamental agent of change in most alchemical experiments and also symbolic of the Secret Fire that drives the spiritual perfection of the alchemist. Using the phrase to describe the seven steps as set out in ‘the Emerald Tablet’, we find that ‘Vista’ represents what is called the ‘black phase’ of the work and that the word means ‘to visit or start a journey’. The alchemical process is called calcination, its element is Fire and the corresponding verse from ‘the Emerald Tablet’ is ‘the Sun is its father’. ‘Interiora’ refers to our own interior work, whereby we dissolve away our old self. This step is called dissolution and its element is water. The corresponding verse from the tablet is ‘its Moon its mother’. ‘Terra’, meaning ‘of the earth’, alludes to a person’s essences being separated from the dregs of matter in preparation for a more spiritual life. This phase of the work is called separation, its element is air and the verse from the tablet is ‘the Wind hath carried it in its belly’. ‘Rectificando’ means ‘setting things right’ and is the fourth phase of the work. Its element is earth and the operation represents the soul and the spirit leaving the earth together towards the above. This represents the quintessence, or fifth element, recovered from the previous operations. This alchemical operation is called conjunction, described by ‘the Emerald Tablet’ as ‘the Earth its nurse’. ‘Invenies’ means ‘you will discover’. This is the ‘red phase’ of the

alchemist’s work where the soul and spirit of the alchemist nurture the alchemical egg. This step is called fermentation, its element is sulphur and its verse is ‘Separate thou the Earth from the Fire, the subtle from the gross, sweetly with great industry’. ‘Occultum’ means ‘secret’ or ‘hidden’ and applies to the stage of distillation. Its element is alchemical mercury and the verse is ‘It ascends from the Earth to Heaven and again it descends to the Earth and receives the force of things superior and inferior’. ‘Lapidem’ means ‘stone’ – the Philosopher’s Stone, the ultimate aim of the alchemist. This phase is called coagulation and brings together the purest essences from our body, soul and spirit. Its element is salt and ‘the Emerald Tablet’ describes this final transmutation as ‘By this means you shall have the glory of the whole world and thereby all obscurity shall fly from you. Its force is above all force for it vanquishes every subtle thing and penetrates every solid thing. So was the world created.’ The quest to find God, the ‘One Mind’ in the language of ‘the Emerald Tablet’, or our own higher self, is the ultimate goal. Alchemists explain that this is achieved by means of discovering the One Thing, or First Matter. This then gives the alchemist the ability to create the Philosopher’s Stone and the Elixir of Life. ‘The Emerald Tablet’ states ‘And as all things have been and arose from One by the mediation of One: so all things have their birth from this One Thing by adaptation.’ Therefore the quest of the alchemists and mystics of all ages is this: to change the world into a better place, the work starts and finishes with you! SEE ALSO: Freemasonry, Hermetica, Sir Isaac Newton, Philosopher’s Stone, Rosicrucians

ALL-SEEING EYE The all-seeing eye is a part of the Great Seal of the United States, the mysterious symbol that is depicted on the One Dollar Bill. The symbol of an eye radiating light has been used as a visual metaphor for God for many centuries. It suggests divine watchfulness over everything, no matter how small or how far away, and is a potent image of an omniscient deity. To Freemasons, this eye surrounded by rays of light is known as the Eye of Providence. It is usually not connected with a pyramid when used in Masonic regalia and either floats on its own or among clouds. An eye within a triangle can be found at least as far back as medieval times, but here the triangle represents the holy trinity of Christian faith, rather than a pyramid. Going back much further in history, we find the powerful symbol known as the Eye of Horus in Ancient Egypt. The symbol was often used as a protective amulet, and pharaohs would go to their tombs with Eye of Horus amulets placed within the many wrappings that enclosed the mummified body. The first occasion when the Eye of Providence was placed in conjunction with a pyramid seems to have been when the Great Seal was conceived. There are no known examples of both being used together; if it had been done before, then it was not publicly. It was Pierre Eugene du Simitiere, a Swiss-born artist and philosopher, who placed the Eye of Providence in the Great Seal of the United States after he was asked to design an emblem that might be used as the seal of the nation. Accompanying the original sketch, we find the following description: ‘The Eye of Providence in a radiant Triangle whose Glory extends over the Shield and beyond the Figures.’ A number of committees were formed to design the seal, and versions that included the Eye of Providence were twice rejected. However, in 1782, some six years after the first committee had been formed, it was suggested that the eye could be used on the reverse of the seal, and that is how it came to be placed above the unfinished pyramid. Whatever the precise reasons for combining these very powerful symbols, the Eye of Providence and the unfinished pyramid below,

the resulting image is a very potent one. The two are combined in such a way on the Great Seal that the eye above does indeed look as if it completes the pyramid below. This is a very clever allegory, one that suggests that only by the Providence of God will the nation of man be made perfect. Of course, as Dan Brown suggests in The Lost Symbol, it could also be a metaphor for a more personal transformation: the apotheosis of the human mind into that of the divine, the shaping of the rough block of stone that is the human spirit into a more perfect form. Another interesting point to note is that the character Katherine Solomon explains in the final chapter of the book, Chapter 133, that the pineal gland of the human brain can be compared to the all- seeing eye. This gland, according to the Western Mystery Tradition, is the very part of the human body that is often considered to be the mythical ‘third eye’. This leads us to Buddhism and Hinduism, in which the concept of the third eye and the sixth chakra (located behind the brow) are widely accepted. According to the Indian tradition, this third eye is the ‘eye of knowledge’, and it is considered so powerful that it acts rather like an internal guru, teaching us all we need to know if only we listen. This, of course, dovetails neatly with ideas put forward in The Lost Symbol, which states quite clearly that ‘god is within’. Finally, we shouldn’t leave the discussion of the all-seeing eye without mentioning that Manly P. Hall, the occult mystic and philosopher whom Dan Brown quotes in The Lost Symbol, published his own monthly magazine called The All Seeing Eye, which covered various esoteric subjects, including articles on Atlantis, the Tarot, the I Ching, Freemasonry, Ancient Egypt and Meso-American mysteries amongst many other topics. SEE ALSO: Great Seal of the United States, Manly P. Hall, Pineal Gland

THE ANCIENT MYSTERIES In The Lost Symbol, Robert Langdon tells us that the Ancient Mysteries are the combined wisdom of the ages, a collection of the greatest mysteries known to man gathered in one place and kept secret. We learn that the Hand of the Mysteries is an invitation to an initiate to access and discover the Ancient Mysteries. In effect, the Ancient Mysteries are the key to the whole novel. They are ultimately what Robert Langdon is searching for: the final reward of the whole quest. The clues on the granite pyramid, the search for the Lost Word . . . they are said to lead to the uncovering of the Ancient Mysteries, which it is assumed are hidden somewhere in Washington DC. The way they are presented in Dan Brown’s book suggests that the Ancient Mysteries are the collected knowledge of many disciplines, something that could be thought of as an encyclopedia of the teachings of all the mystery schools. In fact, there is no evidence that such a collection of writings exists. Instead, we have disparate works of ancient wisdom from the various strands of the Mysteries. While these are all of inestimable value to mankind, there is not one all-encompassing work that could be said to contain the whole truth. Some of the earliest mystery schools were established in Ancient Greece. Many were well known, so their existence was not a secret; however, the actual knowledge held within the schools was fiercely protected and initiates were expected to guard the secrets and rites of the fraternities with their lives. Just as in Freemasonry today, the initiates of the ancient mystery schools took sacred oaths: they vowed that death should seal their lips before they would reveal any secret knowledge. The mystery schools of Ancient Greece were born from the disciplines of philosophy and mysticism, and the exploration of both subjects naturally led to the Mysteries. Sacred dramas were performed that were connected with the Mysteries, the most prominent of them being those concerning Isis, a goddess whose cult began in Ancient Egypt; Cybele, the great oracle of the ancient Asiatic world; and Demeter and Persephone, the Greek goddesses who gave birth to the Eleusinian Mysteries, probably the most important of the mystery schools in Ancient Greece.

The Eleusinian Mysteries are thought to have begun in 1600 bc and were concerned with the recurring theme of the immortality of the human soul, known as Psyche, whose true home is in the spirit world, free of the cage, or tomb, of the human form. As far as the Eleusinians were concerned, birth in human form was death itself for the soul and only through death could the soul be finally reborn. Later, in Rome, there were mystery schools such as the cult of Mithras, which had imported much of the knowledge of the Persians, and so it was that the ancient knowledge was passed down through the generations. The mystery schools themselves might have evolved and changed, but the secrets that were passed on were the same. The mystery schools of the Western world were forced underground between the fifth and sixth centuries, when paganism was banned in the Roman Empire. It is said that the final, decisive act in the destruction of the Ancient Mysteries was the closure of Plato’s Academy in Athens in ad 529 by the Byzantine Emperor Justinian I. However, the Ancient Mysteries did not die. They were kept safe and simply lay dormant, waiting to flourish again. Gnostics safeguarded many of the mysteries that had become embedded in the new religion of Christianity. In the Middle Ages, the Knights Templar certainly kept alive some of the Ancient Mysteries, as did the hermeticists and the alchemists, while the founding of the Rosicrucians and other secret orders during the Renaissance led to a resurgence in the knowledge of the ancients. Something that The Lost Symbol tells us quite clearly is that Freemasonry not only has access to the Ancient Mysteries but also acts as their guardian, keeping safe a huge body of ancient knowledge and passing it down through the various degrees of the craft. The question of whether the secrets that Freemasonry clings to are understood in the modern era is open to debate, but there is no doubt that Freemasonry is a modern mystery school that serves to keep alive the Ancient Mysteries. In The Secret Teaching of All Ages, Manly P. Hall quotes Robert Macoy, a 33rd-degree Freemason, to relay how important the Ancient Mysteries have been in shaping human society: It appears that all the perfection of civilization, and all the advancement made in philosophy, science, and art among the ancients are due to those

institutions which, under the veil of mystery, sought to illustrate the sublimest truths of religion, morality, and virtue, and impress them on the hearts of their disciples. Their chief object was to teach the doctrine of one God, the resurrection of man to eternal life, the dignity of the human soul, and to lead the people to see the shadow of the deity, in the beauty, magnificence, and splendor of the universe. We glimpse in this the idea that many of the world’s religions could also be classed as guardians of the Ancient Mysteries. Christianity, Islam, Judaism, Zoroastrianism, Buddhism and countless others all contain a germ of the Ancient Mysteries, passing down sacred and ancient traditions concerning the rebirth of the human soul. The conclusion of The Lost Symbol certainly alludes to this idea. In describing the Bible as possibly a collection of the Ancient Mysteries, the realisation dawns that ancient knowledge could have been encoded within the chapters of this religious book. The Lost Symbol begins with a quote from Manly P. Hall and his writings have influenced the novel, beyond any shadow of a doubt. In The Secret Teachings of All Ages, he sums up the hidden wisdom of the ancients, then suggests that it will rise again one day, as irrepressible as a mountain spring. SEE ALSO: Manly P. Hall, Hermetica

THE APOTHEOSIS OF WASHINGTON Apotheosis is an Ancient Greek word that translates as ‘to change into a God’ – apo meaning ‘change’ and theos meaning ‘god’. Many ancient cultures embraced this idea: man being raised to divinity is a common motif throughout history. Though we don’t come across the term until after the rule of Alexander the Great, there is no doubt that the concept was in existence long before him. The Ancient Greek religion of Orphism, based on the writings of the mythical poet Orpheus, went so far as to state that the human soul did not become divine at the moment of death; rather, it was divine already. Even before the Ancient Greeks, kings in Ancient Egypt were thought to be transformed into gods after death, with some of the earliest texts detailing the sacred process that lay at the heart of the Ancient Egyptian religion, dating back to 2400 bc in the form of the Pyramid Texts. The concept of apotheosis was also popular in ancient Rome and the deification of the Roman emperor eventually became a standard religious practice. An illustration of this can be seen today in Rome on the Arch of Titus, a monument that was raised shortly after the death of the Emperor Titus in ad 81. Here we find scenes of the apotheosised Titus being borne on the wings of eagles as he ascends to heaven. The practice of depicting famous leaders from history ascending to heaven continued into modern times. One example is Jean Auguste Dominique Ingres’s Apotheosis of Napoleon I. And so it was that George Washington came to receive the same treatment. The Apotheosis of Washington is the crowning glory of the Capitol Building. It is a vast fresco that decorates the inside of the dome itself. Painted in 1865 by Constantino Brumidi, it covers 4,664 square feet and is suspended some 180 feet above the floor of the Rotunda directly below. The original wood and copper dome of the Capitol was replaced after Congress ordered Thomas Walter, Architect of the Capitol for the extension, to construct a new dome in 1855, much grander than the previous structure and this time made of iron. One very interesting point to note about the fresco is that it sits between the high outer shell of the dome and a lower, inner shell.

There is a circular opening more than 60 feet across, and in this space a plaster canopy is suspended by the aid of iron supports. This was to be the blank canvas that was afforded the artist Brumidi. Due to this peculiar construction, the oculus of the inner dome is actually smaller than the fresco itself, so it is impossible to see the entire fresco from any one vantage point inside the Rotunda. The commission for the fresco was finally given in August 1862. George Washington, the first president of the United States, and commander-in-chief of the American Continental Army in the American Revolutionary War, had been dead some 131 years and over the course of those years his reputation had continued to grow. The fresco was to be painted in his honour. Washington was seen as the father of the nation and, as early as 1802, the idea of the apotheosis of George Washington was in circulation, John James Barralet having completed an engraving that year depicting the very moment when Washington ascended to heaven. Barralet chose to depict Washington ascending to Mount Olympus, echoing some of the earliest accounts of apotheosis in Ancient Greece. He also chose symbolic figures to surround Washington, such as Liberty, Father Time, Faith, Hope and Charity, and even included a figure to represent the indigenous Indian. In 1860, another coloured engraving illustrating the apotheosis of Washington was completed, this time by German artist H. Weishaupt. All of these works of art reinforced the idea of the divinity of George Washington and paved the way for Brumidi’s commission. So it was that in 1862 Brumidi received a letter from Thomas Walter, stating: It is intended to have a picture 65 feet in diameter, painted in fresco, on the concave canopy over the eye of the New Dome of the U.S. Capitol. I would thank you to furnish me with a design for the said picture, at your earliest convenience. After Brumidi provided preliminary sketches, the two parties agreed terms and, from April 1863, it was agreed to pay Brumidi monthly instalments of $2,000, the total amount not to exceed $40,000. Brumidi began the fresco itself in 1865 and the scaffolding finally came down in 1866. When the public were at last allowed in to

view the incredible painting, the response was very favourable. Brumidi had created what is still considered to be one of the best examples of academic painting in America. What we see when we look up at that vast fresco is George Washington sitting in the heavens in glory, with Liberty to his left, Victory/Fame to his right. He is surrounded by 13 maidens, representing the 13 original colonies that formed the United States. Also shown is the United States prospering under the guidance of the gods. The following lend their protection: Mercury, passing a bag of gold to Robert Morris to assist with the financing of the Revolutionary War; Minerva, the goddess of wisdom, offering instruction to Benjamin Franklin; Ceres, Flora and Pomona, all Roman goddesses linked to agriculture and fertile crops, offering assistance to Young America, who is seen wearing a red liberty cap as together they gather a rich harvest; Neptune, clearing a path through the ocean in preparation for the laying of a cable along the sea floor; Vulcan, at the forge, producing a cannon and steam engine; and finally Freedom routing the enemies of America, her sword raised and a bald eagle to her left. Brumidi’s masterpiece drew upon many classical paintings and frescoes, yet he also blended these influences with images of the modern world, creating a fresh vision of George Washington as god of the new, progressive United States. In The Lost Symbol, The Apotheosis of Washington sits at the heart of the story. One of the underlying themes of the novel is that god is within us all, that we are ourselves god. Dan Brown tells us that this concept of man transforming into god is central to the artworks decorating the Rotunda of the Capitol. We learn that it is not just a question of George Washington becoming a god; the symbolism on display in the Capitol has one aim: to help us realise that in order to access God all we really need to do is look inside ourselves. A recent book by William Henry and Dr Mark Gray has shed new light on The Apotheosis of Washington. Entitled Freedom’s Gate: The Lost Symbols in the U.S. Capitol, one of the many curious details it reveals concerns the circle of 72 stars that surrounds the work of art: The fresco depicts the first President of the United States rising into the clouds in glory. Floating in the center of the painting, the deified Washington sits

enthroned on a rainbow – the judgment seat of Heaven – in a circle or ‘gate’ of 72 stars. It is intriguing to discover that this ring of 72 stars actually sits at the outer rim of the oculus that opens at the very apex of the interior of the dome, allowing the fresco beyond to be seen. Upon closer inspection, we find that they are five-pointed stars. This seems significant because five-pointed stars in Ancient Egypt signified the Duat – quite simply heaven, literally a celestial underworld, the place where the soul of the deceased pharaoh travelled to become a god amongst the stars. The five-pointed star in a circle is often seen painted onto the ceilings of the tombs of the Ancient Egyptians. Since the earliest accounts of apotheosis originate in Ancient Egypt, it seems fitting that this ring of stars is found surrounding The Apotheosis of Washington. Also, if we look carefully at the arrangement of the stars, we notice that they are enclosed by a long chain of intertwined figure eights, or, as would seem more likely in this case, the symbol for infinity. George Washington sits in a ring of infinity, an appropriate visual metaphor. Another intriguing detail of The Apotheosis of Washington is the rainbow that runs through the cloud upon which George Washington is sitting. In Freedom’s Gate, Henry and Gray highlight the significance of this, telling us that rainbows have often been used to signify the idea of apotheosis: In Last Judgment scenes, Jesus is frequently seen on or in a rainbow. Hence, the rainbow is associated with glory. This makes sense. Symbolically, rainbows are intermediaries between heaven and earth. They are bridges the gods use to toggle between the worlds . . . In the Great Perfection or Rainbow Body teaching, the human body is considered an intermediate phase, a bridge. Our next phase, putting on the Light Body, is referred to as putting on the whole armor of God in Ephesians 6:10–20. This Light Body (or Star Body, Rainbow Body) is our hidden inner ‘spiritual’ body referenced in numerous traditions. In Sufism it is called ‘the most sacred body’ and ‘supracelestial

body.’ Taoists call it ‘the diamond body,’ and those who have attained it are called ‘the immortals’ and ‘the cloudwalkers.’ The ancient Egyptians called it ‘the luminous body or being.’ From this perspective, the meaning behind the symbolism of George Washington sitting on the rainbow is clear.
