Washington is a perfected human, not only an enlightened Grand Master, but also an ‘American Christ,’ in tune with his divine nature. He is now somewhere over the rainbow, and his image is a bridge between Heaven and Earth. It seems that Brumidi was well versed in the symbolism of transformation and he went to great lengths to encode many of these elements within The Apotheosis of Washington. What at first glance appears to be nothing more than a very well-executed fresco venerating the first US president turns out to be a painting that is literally bursting with symbolism for those with eyes to see it. Considering the links between the Capitol Building and Freemasonry, this is not at all surprising. Towards the end of The Lost Symbol, Dan Brown has Robert Langdon – while viewing The Apotheosis of Washington – quote the words of Manly P. Hall, taken from the incredibly revealing The Secret Teachings of All Ages, written in 1928: ‘If the Infinite had not desired man to become wise, He would not have bestowed upon him the faculty of knowing.’ This seems a fitting quote to use at this point in the book because many ancient secret teachings are embedded in The Apotheosis of Washington. It takes some specialist knowledge to read the signs, but when we study the fresco in detail we start to realise that Brumidi was fully conversant with the heady and intoxicating language of symbolism. SEE ALSO: Constantino Brumidi, Capitol Building, George Washington

BACON, SIR FRANCIS Sir Francis Bacon was a man who cast a long shadow over the philosophical thinking of the western world. He was a member of what Dan Brown describes as ‘a brain trust of the world’s most enlightened minds’, along with Sir Isaac Newton, Robert Boyle and Benjamin Franklin. He appears again as the author of The New Atlantis, a book describing a utopian vision of a society, said to have influenced the Founding Fathers of America in establishing their new world. The Bacon Society of America, founded in 1922, paid tribute to Sir Francis Bacon by stating that: It should be of particular concern to Americans to become better acquainted with Bacon’s part in the planting and promotion of the earliest British colonies in North America, because, though not generally known, he assisted in preparing the 1609 and 1612 charters of the Virginia company. This contribution is perhaps one of the reasons he is acknowledged in the Main Reading Room of the Library of Congress, where above a statue representing Philosophy is an abbreviated quote from Bacon’s essay ‘Of Truth’: ‘The inquiry, knowledge, and belief of truth is the sovereign good of human nature.’ Bacon (1561–1626) was the author of The Wisdom of the Ancients, in which he explained the hidden meanings he thought were revealed in ancient myths. Some have argued that Bacon may have been chosen by King James I of England and VI of Scotland to edit the new translation of the Bible known as the Authorised Version. In Sir Francis Bacon: Poet, Philosopher, Statesman, Lawyer, Wit, Parker Woodward says: It has been suggested that the Authorized Version of the Bible printed 1610/11, was submitted for final editing to Francis, but that could only have been for rounding off its English, the translation having been made by a special commission of scholarly clergymen.

American occultist and philosopher Manly P. Hall was more convinced of Bacon’s role in the production of the King James Bible. In a lecture called ‘Rosicrucian and Masonic Origins’, he claimed: ‘The first edition of the King James Bible, which was edited by Francis Bacon and prepared under Masonic supervision, bears more Mason’s marks than the Cathedral of Strasbourg.’ Francis Bacon studied at Trinity College, Cambridge, and then spent three years in France in the service of the English ambassador. He worked as a barrister, eventually becoming solicitor general and attorney general. His own claim was that his interests lay in gaining knowledge of everything and his written work displays a wonderful command of the English language. Bacon became a Member of Parliament in 1584 and a few years later the Earl of Essex, an ambitious favourite of Elizabeth I, recognised his talents and became his patron. Essex’s rebellious behaviour led to his trial and subsequent execution following an attempt to seize power, and Bacon, distanced now from this traitorous undertaking, produced the official report on the matter. He was successful in gaining the favour of King James after he succeeded to the English throne and was knighted by him in 1603. Now Sir Francis, after serving in various legal positions, became Lord Chancellor in 1618 and was created first Baron Verulam and then two years later Viscount St Albans. Soon afterwards he was accused of corruption and fell from grace. His conviction ended his political career. Bacon’s last years were occupied mainly with his literary work. The manner of Bacon’s death is indicative of his inquisitive nature. He had clearly been giving thought to the idea of preserving meat by freezing it. One snowy day, he took a trip to Highgate, London, along with the King’s physician and they bought a fowl and stuffed it with snow to test the theory out. Sadly, the exposure to the cold affected Bacon’s health dramatically and led to his death two or three days later, of pneumonia. He did have time to write a letter before he died, explaining cheerfully, ‘As for the experiment itself, it succeeded excellently well.’ Katherine Solomon and Robert Langdon pass the Folger Shakespeare Library in Washington DC, where the original Latin copy of Bacon’s New Atlantis is housed. Even though Langdon is embroiled in an escape from the CIA, he manages to recognise the significance of the book. The library is a repository for many

valuable and rare manuscripts, including copies of Shakespeare’s First Folio, dating from the time of Shakespeare and Bacon. It may be possible that these two contemporaries have a closer relationship than meets the eye. Many experts cannot believe that William Shakespeare, a small- town boy from Stratford-upon-Avon, England could possibly have acquired the knowledge to enable him to write the famous plays that bear his name. If he did not, then of course the question arises, who did? There are a number of possible candidates for the actual author of the plays published in Shakespeare’s name, including Sir Francis Bacon, Christopher Marlowe and the earls of Oxford and Derby. Sir Francis Bacon is a strong contender according to some. His extensive travel on the Continent exposed him to the political intrigues and courtly ritual present in Shakespeare’s plays. Some have theorised from the legal detail and procedure included in some of the plays that the author had trained as a lawyer, as, of course, Bacon had. He possessed the diplomatic, philosophical and linguistic skills evident in the playwright’s work. One of the most enthusiastic supporters of the theory that Sir Francis Bacon was the author of Shakespeare’s works was Ignatius Donnelly. Donnelly was a senator for Minnesota between 1874 and ‘78, during which time he made use of the facilities at the Library of Congress to advance his studies. After leaving political office, he had time to pursue his literary interests. He became convinced that the answer to the puzzle lay in the words of the plays themselves and set out to decipher Shakespeare’s work. The key that Donnelly tried to apply was the Bacon cipher, a method of concealing a message within a text that Bacon had described and illustrated in his book The Advancement of Learning. That Sir Francis Bacon was the inventor of a cipher was perhaps not surprising, given that his role in government presumably required messages to be sent securely. As a result of exhaustive study, Ignatius Donnelly published The Great Cryptogram in 1888, more than 1,000 pages long, in which he claimed to have found number patterns that provided the decoded message: ‘Seas ill said that More low or Shak’st spur never writ a word of them.’ The convoluted method he used to come up with this supposed admission that Shakespeare was not the author of the plays detracted from some of the other, more cogent evidence he included. Ignatius Donnelly is more famous today for his work Atlantis: The

Antediluvian World, a favourite amongst historical revisionists, conspiracy theorists and alternative historians. Like Sir Francis Bacon, his admirer Donnelly was convinced that Plato had been recording historical fact when he wrote about the land of Atlantis. For those who enjoy number symbolism, and this would of course include Robert Langdon, there is a much remarked upon ‘coincidence’ to be found in the Authorised Version of the Bible. It was completed in 1611, when William Shakespeare was 46 years of age. Turning to Psalm 46, we find that the 46th word from the beginning is ‘shake’ and the 46th word from the end is ‘spear’. It is delightful to think that Shakespeare’s ‘ghostwriter’ could have inserted this little joke. In The Lost Symbol the dean of the Washington National Cathedral, Reverend Colin Galloway, credits Sir Francis with being able to ‘write in clear language’ in the context of anticipating human enlightenment, while Robert Langdon knows Bacon to have been a Rosicrucian. The Rosicrucian symbol was a flowering rose on a cross. Galloway suggests that Bacon may even have been the legendary Christian Rosenkreutz, founder of the Rosicrucian movement. In The Occult Philosophy in the Elizabethan Age, the renowned scholar Frances Yates, referring to one of her earlier works, presents the argument for Bacon’s involvement with the Rosicrucians: I have argued in The Rosicrucian Enlightenment that Francis Bacon’s movement for the advancement of learning was closely connected with the German Rosicrucian movement, having a similar mystical and millennial outlook . . . I emphasised that Bacon’s New Atlantis, published in 1627, a year after his death, is full of echoes of the Rosicrucian manifestos. Bacon described a movement or group with Rosicrucian ideals in his The Advancement of Learning, writing: ‘so in like manner there cannot but be a fraternity in learning and illumination, relating to that paternity which is attributed to God, who is called the Father of illuminations or lights’. Sir Francis was well aware that merely to conduct and observe scientific experiments was not enough. To be worthwhile, these

observations require careful analysis. In The New Atlantis, he tells a story that enhanced his reputation among the men who went on to form the Royal Society. They took inspiration from Bacon’s vision of ‘Salomon’s House’ on the ‘Island of Bensalem’. This was a kind of research college, its name derived from the biblical King Solomon, where scientific inquiries into the creations of God were pursued. The New Atlantis is set on a Utopian island, Bensalem, in the South Pacific. Bensalem is, particularly considering that the book was written in the early seventeenth century, probably around 1623, a paradise of enlightenment. It is in sharp contrast with the Europe of the time, where various forms of Protestantism and Roman Catholicism were in constant and sometimes deadly conflict. The name Atlantis is taken from a mysterious civilisation that, according to legend, was created by advanced people in very ancient times. Its disappearance and its original whereabouts have been argued about for millennia. Bacon’s influence in the development of science does not lie in his having made great discoveries or set up elaborate experiments. What he achieved was to outline a major principle of modern scientific investigation, that we should be open-minded about the conclusions of an experiment until proof is obtained. In The Advancement of Learning, he stated, ‘If we begin with certainties, we shall end in doubts, but if we begin with doubts, and are patient in them, we shall end in certainties.’ Sir Francis Bacon was the author of many books and the propagator of many ideas. He was undoubtedly a multifaceted genius. Alexander Pope, the poet and literary scholar, said of him, ‘Lord Bacon was the greatest genius that England, or perhaps any country, ever produced.’ SEE ALSO: Manly P. Hall, Rosicrucianism, Royal Society and the Invisible College

BOAZ AND JACHIN In The Lost Symbol, the character Mal’akh is revealed to have numerous tattoos all over his body. The two tattoos that adorn his legs are said to be representations of Boaz and Jachin, the mysterious pillars associated with the legendary site of Solomon’s Temple in Jerusalem. These pillars have two distinct sets of mythologies associated with them, a biblical one and a Masonic one. Etymologically, it would seem that Jachin means ‘establish’ and Boaz, though somewhat disputed, may mean ‘strength’. Some scholars see a relationship, metaphorically, between King Solomon, as represented by Jachin, and King David, as represented by Boaz. Others see Boaz as representing the grandfather of King David and Jachin a certain high priest. These two pillars then seem to have become symbolically representative the priesthood, Jachin, and the royal line, Boaz. What is certain, though, is that these two pillars were thought to stand in the porch of Solomon’s Temple, with Jachin on the right and Boaz on the left of the eastern entrance. Some editions of the Bible say that the pillars were made of copper, other versions say bronze or brass. The building of these pillars may well have been influenced by their use in Egypt, guarding the entrances to temples, or their use in the Roman temples of the Levant. In II Chronicles 3:15–17, it is said of the pillars: In front of the Hall he made two pillars thirty-five cubits high, and on the top of each a capital measuring five cubits. He made festoons, in the Debir, to go at the tops of the pillars, and made a hundred pomegranates to go on the festoons. He erected the pillars in front of the Temple, one on the right, the other on the left; the one on the right he called Jachin and the one on the left Boaz. In II Chronicles 4:13–17, the pillars are described as being decorated by: The four hundred pomegranates for the two sets of

filigree – two rows of pomegranates for each set of filigree; the ten stands and the ten basins on the stands; the one Sea and the twelve oxen under it; the ash containers, scoops and forks. All these utensils made by Huram-Abi for King Solomon for the Temple of Yahweh were of burnished bronze. The King made them by the process of sand casting in the plain of the Jordan between Succoth and Zeredah. However, in II Kings 25:17, a discrepancy in the size of the pillars creeps into the description: The height of one pillar was eighteen cubits, and on it stood a capital of bronze, the height of the capital being five cubits; round the capital were filigree and pomegranates, all in bronze. So also for the second pillar. The last we hear of the pillars in the Bible is when they are broken up and carried off to Babylon, in Jeremiah 52:17. Boaz and Jachin have become the pillars upon which Freemasonry is built. The role they play in the ceremonies, mystery and rituals of Masonic lodges cannot be overstated and the symbolism attached to them is seen as very important. The two pillars are to be found in every Masonic hall in the world, though their placement is not standardised or uniform within the Masonic craft. In The Lost Symbol, the tattoos of Boaz and Jachin upon the legs of Mal’akh are described thus: ‘his left leg spiraled and his right vertically striated. Boaz and Jachin.’ What is meant by this? We seem to have here a nod to a location that Dan Brown has explored at length in his previous book The Da Vinci Code: Rosslyn Chapel. Mal’akh’s tattoos portray two pillars at Rossyln Chapel: the so-called Apprentice Pillar, with its beautifully spiralled carving, which is said to represent the pillar of Boaz; and the Mason’s Pillar, with its striated carvings, which is claimed to be an image of Jachin. These highly decorated pillars form the centrepiece of one of Rosslyn Chapel’s most enduring myths and are believed by many Masons to stand for Boaz and Jachin in a chapel that itself is
thought to symbolically represent Solomon’s Temple. In some Masonic imagery, the pillars are said to be the ‘pillar of fire’ and the ‘pillar of cloud’. SEE ALSO: Freemasonry, Solomon’s Temple

BRUMIDI, CONSTANTINO Constantino Brumidi is the Italian-born artist responsible for painting the pivotal artwork in the Capitol Building: The Apotheosis of Washington, the vast fresco that adorns the ceiling of the dome. It remains one of the best examples of the academic style of painting in America. Born in Rome in July 1805, his father was Greek, from the Peloponnese, and his mother was Italian. Brumidi studied at the illustrious Accademia di San Luca after showing a great aptitude for art as a youth. The academy was named after Saint Luke because he was supposed to have painted the Virgin Mary and so was adopted as the patron saint of painters’ guilds. Founded in 1593, the academy had a long history of training fine artists, including painters, sculptors and architects. After leaving the academy, Brumidi set about building a career for himself in Rome. His prodigious talent was recognised and he received the patronage of Pope Gregory XVI, being given the task of working on frescoes in the Vatican and restoring the loggia of Raphael. A conflict with the papal secretary of state over political matters saw an end to Brumidi’s work at the Vatican, and his next assignment was for Prince Torlonia. Later, in 1847, he worked for Pope Pius IX, painting a full-length portrait of the pontiff, again reinforcing Brumidi’s status as one of Rome’s finest painters. Brumidi’s course seemed set. He had carved a niche for himself and continued to attract the patronage of the city’s wealthy aristocracy, but suddenly revolutionary fever gripped Rome and his world was turned upside down. On 15 November 1848, Pellegrino Rossi, the Minister of Justice of the Papal States, was assassinated. His death was followed by rioting on the streets and demands for a democratic government. The Pope fled and a Roman Republic was established. Brumidi sided with the revolutionaries, and this was to be his downfall. The Pope, with the help of several European powers, wrested control back from the upstart republic. Brumidi was arrested in 1851 and – accused of taking part in the uprising – was sentenced to 18 years in prison. Soon afterwards Pope Pius IX, with whom Brumidi had become acquainted when he had painted his portrait just a few years earlier, granted Brumidi a pardon on the condition

that he leave Italy for good. So it was that Brumidi, his wife Anna and their two children left Italy for New York. Brumidi became a citizen of the United States in 1852 and began a new career for himself. He carried on where he had left off in Rome, completing a fresco behind the altar in St Stephen’s Church in New York before working in Baltimore and then Mexico. On his way home to New York from Mexico in 1854, Brumidi stopped off in Washington DC. Greatly impressed by the grand architecture of the city, and especially the Capitol, he arranged a meeting with Captain Montgomery C. Meigs, the supervising engineer of the United States Capitol, and suggested to him that he would be available to decorate the building’s many empty spaces. Meigs was a controversial figure at the time and many did not believe that this important position within the Capitol should be occupied by someone with an army background such as his. He succeeded in upsetting many of the artists of the day and petitions were submitted to Congress requesting his removal. However, Meigs had a strong vision of his own and he set out to ensure that the Capitol became the single greatest national monument of the Republic. He wanted it brimming with all the skill and invention that the greatest American artists could muster. At the time, the Washington volume of the American Guide Series listed Brumidi as ‘a decorative painter of mediocre talent [who] worked in what was left of the tradition of Raphael and Correggio’. This seems an amusing description in light of what we now know Brumidi would go on to create. Kent Ahrens, in Nineteenth Century History Painting and the United States Capitol, comments on how Brumidi established himself in Washington: However mediocre, Brumidi was a frescoist and as such possessed a skill which no contemporary American artist shared. Perhaps he also possessed already the beginnings of a dream, that as Michelangelo had dedicated his later life to the glorification of St Peter’s, so he, Brumidi, would dedicate himself to the new cathedral of human freedom, the Capitol of the United States. He asked Meigs for employment as an artist, and he suggested that the task suitable for him was to

adorn the walls and ceilings with frescoes. So it was that Brumidi was asked to contribute a series of frescoes in the House Committee Room on Agriculture in 1855. Meigs wrote: ‘This will enable Congress to see a specimen of this, the highest style of architectural decoration.’ The results attracted much attention and ensured that Brumidi would work in the Capitol for the next 25 years. In 1856, Brumidi began sketching designs for what are now known as the Brumidi Corridors. The Architect of the Capitol, Thomas Walter, had originally conceived the corridors to be decorated simply and then hung with oil paintings; Captain Meigs, however, had other ideas. Since Brumidi had experience restoring Raphael’s loggia at the Vatican, Meigs asked the Italian-American artist to attempt an elaborate design. Working with a team of artists and assistants, Brumidi made the corridors his own and the ornate decoration can still be appreciated today. Brumidi worked in the corridors during the 1850s, ‘60s and ‘70s. Brumidi seems always to have wanted to paint a grand fresco within the dome of the Capitol and there is evidence that he made an oil sketch for what became known as The Apotheosis of Washington as early as 1859, despite not officially being offered the commission until 1863. By finally completing what is now considered his crowning achievement, Brumidi ensured that his name would forever be remembered amongst those of the great American artists. Brumidi continued to work inside the Capitol long after The Apotheosis of Washington was complete, adding to the decoration of the corridors and many rooms of the Senate wing. The final project he would tackle was the frieze that surrounds the base of the dome, 58 feet above the Rotunda floor. However, the long years had taken their toll, and by 1879, at 74 years of age, his health was frail. He was often afflicted by bouts of asthma, as well as severe diarrhoea. On top of this, his working conditions were strenuous, to say the least. Barbara A. Wolanin, author of Constantino Brumidi: Artist of the Capitol, offers this first- hand account of the working conditions that the ageing and frail Brumidi had to endure: . . . this wonderful old man has daily to climb up to

an elevation of fully eighty feet, enter a window and then descend a ladder at least twenty-five feet long to the little pent-up crib where he toils. He is so aged and feeble that he requires help to reach the place, and you can easily imagine the fatigue attendant upon the mere labor of getting to and away from his work. Besides, in stormy wet tempestuous weather he cannot get there at all. To give him some comfort, a chair was provided and set atop the precarious scaffold. In October 1879, Brumidi fell from this chair, with nearly fatal consequences. Again, from Constantino Brumidi: Artist of the Capitol: . . . while sitting upon a temporary scaffold, and near its edge the chair turned from under him and threw him over; he caught the round of a ladder and remained suspended by the strength of his arms for the space of fifteen minutes, till officer Lammon descended from the top of the Dome to the scaffold and called two men from the floor of the Rotunda to assist in the rescue of your petitioner. While Brumidi did recover from this dreadful experience – in fact, he worked the very next day on the same scaffold – his increasing ill health meant that he would never see the frieze finished. He became confined to his house at the outset of that season’s cold weather and he died in February 1880. Today, a bust of Brumidi sits in the Brumidi Corridors, a memorial to the long years he dedicated to the beautification of the numerous halls and spaces of the Capitol. He completed more works of art in the Capitol than any other artist and his name is stamped firmly across the building. Brumidi himself would proudly sign his name ‘C. Brumidi: Artist Citizen of the U.S.’ His adopted country is surely as proud of him and his achievements as he was to be an American. SEE ALSO: The Apotheosis of Washington, Capitol Building

CAPITOL BUILDING The United States is often represented around the world by the image of the Capitol: its pure white, perfect dome set against the sky. It is just as iconic an image of America as the famous red, white and blue flag. Yet most people have never seen past that glorious facade; they have no idea what wonders lie inside the dome, or just how large and complex a building the Capitol is. It is not only a museum filled with fine art and treasures but also a working building, where Congress sits daily and from which the federal government of the United States operates. It is hard to imagine the seat of government not being in Washington and the Capitol Building, but it took extraordinary efforts to create what would become the heart of the nation. While victory was achieved in the American Revolutionary War in 1781, it took until 1789 to form what is known today as the United States Congress. The newly formed Congress sat first in New York but moved to Philadelphia after just two sessions. An Act passed in 1790, known as the Residence Act, set out a detailed plan for establishing a new capital city in the United States and, after much debate, a compromise was struck and a site on the Potomac River, in the region known as the District of Columbia, was selected. Representatives of both New York and Philadelphia protested, desirous of securing the seat of government for themselves, and it was decided that Philadelphia be designated the temporary seat of government until the new Capitol was completed in Washington. The Residence Act stated that the president, George Washington, had to ensure that the new Capitol Building would be completed and ready for Congress by December 1800. Design of the new capital began in earnest, with George Washington taking an active role in its execution. Pierre L’Enfant, a French-born architect and veteran of the American Revolutionary War, was appointed to design the new city. The final layout and design of what would become Washington DC was presented and agreed on 19 August 1791, with the location of the Capitol and other federal buildings, including the White House, marked out. Just as a fine painting sits in a frame befitting its artistry, so the Capitol was set within a grand arrangement of vistas and avenues that sweep towards what was at the time Jenkin’s Hill. In a letter to

George Washington, L’Enfant wrote that the virgin Jenkin’s Hill was like ‘a pedestal waiting for a monument’. Despite the location of the Capitol having been agreed upon, there was still no design for the building itself, although the name of the new seat of government had been decided, with ‘Capitol’ chosen over ‘Congress House’, and Jenkin’s Hill in Washington renamed Capitol Hill, after the famous hill in ancient Rome known as the Capitoline Hill. By 1792, L’Enfant had fallen out with George Washington and his tenure as chief designer was over, so the search was on to finalise a design for what would be the most important building in the United States. It is hard conceive that the design for what would end up as one of the world’s most recognisable buildings began life as part of a $500 competition. Looking back at some of the possible contenders, one wonders what might have happened if any of the other designs had been chosen instead. We could very well have been looking up today at a curious giant stone eagle perched on a pedestal. The design that won the day was that of Dr William Thornton, a physician as well as a keen, though amateur, architect. Thornton was handed $500 and a plot of land in the city as his prize. Although his design was modified and adjusted considerably over the years, the building we see today was born from the plans he submitted. The famous dome was not part of this original design, however. The first incarnation of the Capitol had a much less grand wood-and-copper dome, designed by Charles Bullfinch, which was only half the height of the structure that exists today. But the Capitol was to be without a dome for a long time yet. With the site on Jenkin’s Hill laid out and the foundations constructed, the cornerstone of the Capitol was laid on 18 September 1793. It was accompanied by a grand ceremony, the first in the new federal city, and conducted by none other than the president of the United States, George Washington. He presided over affairs not only as president but also in his capacity as a Masonic leader, dressed in his Masonic regalia. After the pomp and ceremony, a silver plate was placed in a trench over which the cornerstone would be laid. The plaque read: This South East corner stone, of the Capitol of the United States of America in the City of Washington,

was laid on the 18th day of September, in the thirteenth year of American Independence, in the first year of the second term of the Presidency of George Washington, whose virtues in the civil administration of his country have been as conspicuous and beneficial as his Military valor and prudence have been useful in establishing her liberties, and in the year of Masonry 5793, by the Grand Lodge of Maryland, several lodges under its jurisdiction, and Lodge 22, from Alexandria, Virginia. Despite ongoing problems with sourcing sufficient labour for the construction of the Capitol, as well as continuing difficulties with funding, the Senate wing was completed in 1800 and, though the building was still incomplete, the United States Congress held its first session in the Capitol in November of that year. There were now 16 states in the Union. George Washington didn’t live to see Congress in its new home in the Capitol, having died almost a year before, so it was left to President Adams to make the first speech in the still unfinished building: It would be unbecoming the representatives of this nation to assemble, for the first time, in this solemn temple, without looking up to the Supreme Ruler of the universe, and imploring his blessing. May this territory be the residence of virtue and happiness! In this city may that piety and virtue, that wisdom and magnanimity, that constancy and self- government, which adorned the great character whose name it bears, be forever held in veneration! Here, and throughout our country, may simple manners, pure morals, and true religion, flourish for ever! It was a speech full of the promise of what the Capitol, and the nation itself, might become, but in truth the Capitol wasn’t anywhere near finished. In fact it wasn’t until 1811 that the wing intended for the House of Representatives was completed. The

central section that would be crowned by the dome had not been touched since the foundations had been laid almost 20 years earlier. By the fateful year of 1812, Benjamin Latrobe was in charge of construction, having taken over as Surveyor of the Public Buildings of the United States in 1803, in the process becoming the fourth architect in charge of the construction of the Capitol. His designs were proceeding favourably, but the outbreak of the Anglo- American War threatened to destroy all the progress made over the previous 20 years. The British Army took control of Washington in August 1814, with disastrous consequences for the United States. In what was known as the Burning of Washington, the British Admiral, George Cockburn, ordered many federal buildings in the city to be burned down. Although the interiors of the Capitol were almost completely destroyed, the outer construction remained. Still, much of the work of the preceding two decades was undone. One wonders what George Washington would have thought had he been alive. Latrobe returned to Washington in 1815 after the war, with a new mandate to rebuild the Capitol. This time he was given more freedom and was able to introduce his own ideas into the design. He came up with a new design for the dome, replacing that envisaged originally by Thornton, although he was destined not to see it built. By 1817, he had resigned, deeply frustrated at reports that he was responsible for the slow progress at the Capitol and provoked into a serious outburst in front of President James Monroe. So it was that Charles Bullfinch took over as Architect of the Capitol. Under his stewardship, the Capitol was finally finished in 1829 – some 36 years after George Washington had laid the cornerstone. The Capitol even had its dome now, a wood-andcopper construction designed by Bullfinch. Inside the dome, there was a Rotunda, designed to replicate the dimensions and grandeur of the Pantheon in Rome, complete with its own oculus. For the next 20 years, between 1830 and 1850, work continued inside the Capitol. Externally, the building remained as Bullfinch had left it. Construction had begun on a tomb below the lower rotunda, or crypt, for George Washington in anticipation of the centennial of his birth in 1832. However, at the last minute Washington’s heir refused permission to move the remains to the Capitol, not wishing

to contradict Washington’s own instructions regarding his burial. So it was that the proposed tomb in the Capitol became a storeroom. Disappointed by this turn of events, Congress discussed other ways to honour Washington and decided on a marble statue, which would be given pride of place in the Rotunda itself. Sculptor Horatio Greenough was appointed to the task and the result depicted George Washington as Zeus, seated, bare-chested, pointing at the heavens and handing a sheathed sword to the viewer. The completed statue – a truly epic piece of sculpture, weighing some twenty tons – was placed in the Rotunda in 1841, though it only remained in the Capitol for two years. Public outrage at the depiction of Washington meant that it was quickly removed to the Capitol grounds and today it resides in the Smithsonian National Museum of American History. While people were happy to consider the deceased Washington divine, it seems they did not want to see their first president literally as a god, at least not close up. In History of the United States Capitol, William C. Allen states that Charles Bullfinch summed up the public mood at the time – a strange mix of outrage and amusement – in a letter to his son: I fear that it will cause much disappointment – it may be an exquisite piece of work, but our people will hardly be satisfied with looking on well developed muscles, when they wish to see the great man as their imagination has painted him . . . [I] am not convinced the sculpture is suited for modern subjects; the dress presents insuperable difficulties . . . And now I fear that this will only give the idea of entering or leaving a bath. In The Lost Symbol, Robert Langdon refers to the statue when he says that Peter Solomon’s severed hand, pointing upwards, was not the first such vision to have graced the Rotunda. When the statue of Washington was installed in the Rotunda, however, the famous fresco The Apotheosis of Washington, towards which Peter Solomon’s hand is directed, had not even been conceived of. So it was that the first chapter of the Capitol’s history came to an end. Rapid growth within the United States during the 1850s meant the Capitol was expanded and enlarged. Not having learned any

lessons from the original birth pangs of the design phase of the Capitol, the Senate proposed another competition and placed an advertisement in local Washington newspapers. This read: It is required that these plans and estimates shall provide for the extension of the Capitol, either by additional wings, to be placed on the north and south of the present building, or by the erection of a separate and distinct building within the enclosure to the east of the building. After an extensive review period, in May 1851 Thomas U. Walter became the new Architect of the Capitol. His designs would change the Capitol for ever, making it one of the modern world’s most recognisable buildings. During Walter’s reign at the Capitol, the building would triple in size. He added the dome that we see today, replacing Bullfinch’s wood-and-copper construction with a new, grandiose structure made of iron and stone – one that would tower above the original, at more than twice the height. The earliest date that Walter mentions for work on the design of the new dome is May 1854. We know that he was inspired by the dome of St Paul’s Cathedral in London, along with St Peter’s in Rome and the Panthéon in Paris. While he designed the current dome, he was not in charge of the construction and did not work alone on the project. Captain M.C. Meigs had been brought in as engineer in charge of the whole Capitol refurbishment in 1853 and, despite many differences and quarrels, and much bitterness, the two men worked together to construct the dome. Meigs had a tremendous flair for administration and an eye for fine detail, and he drove the project forward, often with the sheer force of his will alone. Under Meigs’s watchful direction, the Capitol was transformed into a work of incredible beauty, both inside and out. The interiors received as much lavish attention to detail as the exterior. He supervised the most fantastic iron-and-glass ceilings, installed exquisite marble carvings and hired the most talented artists to create breathtaking rooms and corridors. One of those was Constantino Brumidi, who went on to complete The Apotheosis of Washington. It would take many volumes to describe accurately all of the

Capitol’s myriad features and rooms, every inch of which is covered in wondrous decoration and the most exquisite craftsmanship. Yet still the Capitol is evolving. In order to provide a much-needed separate entrance for tourists, with the modern facilities required of a building attracting a huge number of visitors, a new visitor centre was added in 2000. This features in The Lost Symbol, when Langdon arrives at the Capitol expecting to present his lecture. Dan Brown writes in his novel that there was once an eternal flame in the crypt; however, while it is true that the floor of the Rotunda was for a time open to allow a view into the crypt, this feature was created to allow visitors to peer down to the tomb of Washington. Vivien Green Fryd describes the closing of this feature in her book Art and Empire: The Politics of Ethnicity in the U.S. Capitol: In preparation for the eventual transfer of Washington’s remains to the basement of the Capitol, however, the builders left a circular opening about ten feet in diameter in the center of the Rotunda floor, enabling visitors to view in the crypt a statue of Washington that was eventually to be placed above his tomb. In 1828, Congress ordered the closing of the aperture, because dampness emanating from it adversely affected John Trumbull’s paintings on the walls of the Rotunda. There is no evidence of the eternal flame mentioned in The Lost Symbol; the star on the floor of the crypt below the Rotunda actually marks the point from which the city of Washington’s streets are laid out. At the end of The Lost Symbol, we see Robert Langdon and Katherine Solomon lying on their backs meditating on the meaning of The Apotheosis of Washington and the phrase painted on the curved surface: E pluribus unum. We start to wonder, not for the first time, what exactly was in the minds of the great men who raised this stone edifice on the hill. In Freedom’s Gate, William Henry and Dr Mark Gray put forward the idea that the Capitol, as well as being the seat of government of

the United States, is actually a temple of the people, a place of enlightenment that anyone can experience and everyone can access: Is the U.S. Capitol actually a temple? In our quest to answer this question, we discovered that indeed it is. At the core of this living and continually evolving civic temple is Jefferson’s Enlightened vision of Liberty as the new secular religion of Light. The mighty Capitol Hill is a great High Hill, in the tradition of all holy hills. The temple atop this mount emerges as a Temple of Enlightenment and Transformation that uses sacred architectural principles and spiritual symbolism to create a magnificent space or place where Heaven and Earth unite. By definition it is a gateway, a stargate, to use a 21st century term. There is little doubt that the Capitol was constructed with as much purpose and vision as the finest cathedrals of the Middle Ages. Many find it a truly spiritual place and are greatly moved by the experience of being in the Rotunda. Some might say it is a response to the weight of history pressing down on the visitor, but it is surely more than this. The Capitol has been carefully sculpted into a solemn place of transcendence. Henry and Gray highlight what the Capitol really represents and the long lineage of holy buildings, such as Jerusalem’s Solomon’s Temple and Rome’s Pantheon, in whose shadow the Capitol truly lies: America was the place where religious and political refugees from Ireland, France, Germany, Italy and other parts of Europe came for safety and better lives free of tyranny, religious and civil, and persecution. They came seeking religious freedom and liberty. Many enthusiastically supported their leaders who sought to create a ‘city on a hill’ or a ‘holy experiment,’ the fulfilment of the New Jerusalem. When we look up at the imposing structure of the Capitol, we are not looking at a modern building, we are looking at the past, the present and the future melded into one – a monument to mankind’s
enduring love of the mysteries of the universe and the unknown. SEE ALSO: The Apotheosis of Washington, Constantino Brumidi, Pierre L’Enfant

CERNEAU RITE In the opening prologue to The Lost Symbol, Dan Brown writes about a Masonic ritual during which Mal’akh receives the 33rd degree. This evocative scene plays out much like a layperson would imagine and includes stereotypical ideas about what such a ritual entails. However, it is not an accurate depiction of modern-day Masonic practice and is one of the only places in the novel where the author seems to embellish and has introduced sinister undertones to the rituals and symbolism of Freemasonry. What we are witnessing in Dan Brown’s prologue is indeed a real and well-documented ritual of initiation, but not that of the regular Scottish Rite order, which it is supposed to depict. The ritual in fact dates back to the nineteenth century, when a renegade group of alternative Scottish Rite Masons formed what was to become the Cerneau Rite. The Cerneau Supreme Council was never properly chartered by either the Northern or Southern Jurisdictions of Scottish Rite Freemasonry and remained outside mainstream Masonry, establishing early power bases in New York and New Jersey. Albert Pike, head of the Southern Jurisdiction of the Scottish Rite, was especially vocal in his opposition to the group and refused to have a charter issued to them. In the ritual, Mal’akh is seen to raise a human skull to his lips and drink the blood-like red wine from it. This is certainly part of the Cerneau ritual for the 33rd degree, where both a human skull and a whole skeleton were used. The invocation that is uttered in the book by Mal’akh is also accurate for the Cerneau ritual. The member who is receiving the 33rd degree utters the words: I furthermore solemnly swear that I will hold true allegiance to the Supreme Council of the United States of America, its territories and dependencies. And that I will never acknowledge any body or bodies of men as belonging to the Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite, claiming to be such, except such as hold allegiance to this Supreme Council, or those who recognise this Council. To all these, I do most solemnly swear, calling upon the Most High God to ratify my oath.

And should I knowingly or wilfully violate the same, may this wine I now drink become a deadly poison to me, as the hemlock juice drunk by Socrates. [Initiate drinks wine out of the skull.] And may these cold arms forever encircle me. [Skeleton’s arms enfold the initiate.] Amen. Some of the above words are spoken by Mal’akh in the rite as described in the book. In 1807, Joseph Cerneau established a Grand Consistory of the Rite of Heredom in New York City, claiming a right to organise and charter bodies as the ‘Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite’. By 1813, he had established a Supreme Council in New York and, by 1816, had established branches in Maryland and Baltimore. In 1889, however, an edict was issued by the Grand Master of Masons of the District of Columbia against the Cerneau Rite followers, stating that alleged members of the Cerneau Rite had entered into fraternal relations with members of the Grand Orient of France. A second edict was also issued, as reported in the New York Times of 23 April 1890 thus: A second edict on the subject has just been issued by the present Grand Master, annulling the former edict and declaring it no longer in force. It directs that Masters of lodges under its jurisdiction cease to include in the recognized and imperative test to be administered to visitors to their lodges the statement by such visitors that they are not members of any body acknowledging allegiance to the said Gorgas-Cerneau rite. However, their rehabilitation within the craft was short-lived and by the early twentieth century the Cerneau Rite was all but snuffed out. Aleister Crowley was said to have been initiated into the 33rd degree of Scottish Rite Freemasonry in Mexico, within the Cerneau Rite and using its rituals. SEE ALSO: Aleister Crowley, Freemasonry, House of the Temple, Scottish Rite Freemasonry

CIA – OFFICE OF SECURITY In The Lost Symbol, from the moment Robert Langdon leaves the basement of the Capitol Building after an assault on the director of the Office of Security, he becomes a fugitive. Dan Brown’s hero is thereafter involved in a chase around Washington DC in which he tries to remain one step ahead of the CIA, while all their manpower and technological resources are devoted to locating him and the mysterious pyramid he is carrying. The Central Intelligence Agency is an independent agency created by the United States government responsible for providing national security intelligence to the senior levels of government. Within the CIA, there is a division of the Directorate of Support that is labelled the Office of Security, which is responsible for the internal security of all personnel, operations and facilities that are part of the CIA. In addition, the Office of Security also runs the CIA’s security clearance program and is responsible for investigating breaches in procedure by any person or agency affiliated to the CIA. It also handles protection for those persons who have defected from other countries to the United States. In a nutshell, the Office of Security is made up of the spies who spy on the spies. One other role of the Office of Security is to carry out investigations within the United States in response to specific allegations of jeopardy to intelligence sources and methods. In a small number of these cases, it has been alleged that several intrusive methods of investigation were employed, for example surveillance, unauthorised entry, mail interception and review of tax returns. There has been much debate over the questionable nature of these methods and whether or not it is proper for the CIA to use these techniques, regardless of the dangers at hand. There is no evidence so far that these techniques have been used in the last 30 years. A subdivision of the Office of Security is the Technical Security Division, which is responsible for making sure that all of the security systems used by the CIA are state of the art. Their remit includes everything from debugging CIA facilities and maintaining white-noise machines to installing locks, safes and alarms in CIA facilities. It has been alleged that the Technical Security Division even play ‘bug-planting’ games, where two teams working

independently test their methods. One team hides the bugs and the other tries to find them. There is no evidence of a non-CIA bug ever having been found in CIA headquarters. The CIA’s activities in a more controversial area of security are also mentioned within the pages of The Lost Symbol – remote viewing, which offers the possibility of using paranormal means to gather intelligence on secret installations or other hidden locations. From the early 1970s to the mid-1990s, the CIA was involved with a project known as Stargate, using psychics and intuitives to ascertain the validity and effectiveness of remote viewing as a military and political advantage. This programme has been written about extensively and speculated upon by serious authors and conspiracy theorists alike, while many of the remote viewers involved have been named. Some of the more famous ‘viewers’ include Ingo Swann, Pat Price, Lyn Buchanan and Joseph McMoneagle. In an article on remote viewing in the January/February 2004 issue of Phenomena magazine, author and researcher Richard Dolan had this to say: Are remote viewers accurate all the time, is their information complete? Of course not, but there is compelling evidence that, in many cases, something is going on that, by the standards of current science, should not be going on. In other words, there is good reason to believe that remote viewing is for real. Officially, the CIA stopped the Stargate project and other remote- viewing programmes in the mid-1990s, but speculation is rife that other schemes looking at not only remote viewing but also myriad other psychic and occult phenomena may still be in operation and funded by the CIA. Leon E. Panetta became the 19th director of the CIA on 13 February 2009 at the nomination of President Barack Obama. Panetta had previously served as Congressman for California’s 16th District (1977 to 1993) and as Bill Clinton’s Chief of Staff ( July 1994 to January 1997). Before he took over the running of the CIA, the director was Porter Johnston Goss. There is some evidence that while attending Yale University Goss was a member of the secret society known as Book and Snake

(B&S). Notable members of this society include Washington Post journalist Bob Woodward, former Secretary of the US Treasury Nicholas Brady and former Secretary of Defense Les Aspin Jr. It is thought that Book and Snake had connections to another famous secret society, Skull and Bones (S&B). Both George H.W. Bush and his son George W. Bush are know to have belonged to S&B. George H.W. Bush served as director of the CIA under President Gerald Ford. Many members of S&B are known to have been Freemasons and conspiracy theorists have speculated that George H.W. Bush is a Freemason; however, he has never publicly confirmed this. The Office of Security has its headquarters in the main CIA offices located in McLean, Virginia. The 225-acre facility sits on the west bank of the Potomac River and is approximately seven miles from downtown Washington DC. Since April 1999, the complex has been officially called the George Bush Center for Intelligence, but it is more popularly known as Langley, which was the name of the estate that formerly occupied the location. There are more than 22,000 employees working at this facility, making it large enough to warrant its own postcode – 20505. Kryptos, a sculpture by the artist Jim Sanborn, was installed at CIA headquarters in 1990. The work of art is covered in ciphered messages and a considerable amount of energy has been put into efforts to decode them. At present, as The Lost Symbol tells us, the mystery of the sculpture remains intact. A biblical quote is etched into a wall in the lobby of the main building, reading, ‘And ye shall know the truth and the truth shall make you free’ ( John 8:32). Also within the facility are a museum, a 7,000-seat auditorium and of course the CIA library. The museum, called the National Historical Collection, houses the CIA’s collection of spy gadgets and other material amassed over the years. Much of the data is still classified and therefore the collection is not available for viewing by the public. The CIA library is the world’s best collection of material on the subject of intelligence. It is reported to contain more than 125,000 books and receives over 1,500 periodicals. It is also home to the historical intelligence collection, reported to include more than 25,000 volumes of work. Inoue Sato, one of the main characters in The Lost Symbol, is the director of the Office of Security. She seems to embody the CIA, being knowledgeable, authoritative, intelligent, suspicious and
strong. SEE ALSO: Kryptos

CIRCUMPUNCT The circumpunct is one of the oldest symbols known to mankind, a circle with a dot in the centre. Its name is derived from the Latin circum, meaning around on all sides, i.e. a circle, and punctum, a point. It is so easy to fashion that even the least artistic person can draw it. Certainly our ancient ancestors liked its pleasing simplicity and often took it to symbolise something of significance to them. Importantly, it was probably the most symmetrical shape they could create with basic materials. With just a piece of vine, a strand of cloth, a woven cord or some such string it would have been possible to map out a circumpunct. First, mark a spot, then hold one end of the cord firmly onto the spot. Stretching out the cord, mark the outside of the circle to be drawn around the centre spot, perhaps employing a pointed flint or a sharp stick tightly bound to the free end of the cord. It can be inscribed onto flat rock, ice or the ground, sand or earth. A circumpunct: literally a circle around a point. In The Lost Symbol, Robert Langdon discovers a circumpunct impressed on his fingertip after withdrawing his hand from the box that housed the pyramid. The Cathedral dean connects its appearance with alchemy. Alchemists used the circumpunct as a symbol for gold since the sun is, of course, similarly coloured to the precious metal some of them claimed to have the power to create. The universality of the image is illustrated by some of the cultures that left images of the circumpunct in their inscriptions. The Native American Chippewa or Ojibwe people of the United States and Canada, whose rich cultural heritage is being passed on to new generations of the tribe, use it. The circle circumscribing a point was used to represent our word ‘spirit’ in their pictorial recording of their religious practices on birch bark rolls. In Mexico, the Huichol tribe, remnants of the Aztecs, think of the circumpunct as symbolising the Eye of God, as did some early Christians.

Perhaps unsurprisingly, to two of the world’s oldest civilisations it represented the sun. An ancient Chinese script used it to symbolise the solar disc, or a day. To the Ancient Egyptians, it stood for their great god Ra, and for the sun itself. The Egyptians sometimes referred to themselves as ‘the cattle of Ra’ since a legend described how the tears and sweat of the god were formed into the first people. It might be thought strange that Egyptians would consider that a god’s sweat might be a suitable ingredient with which to create humankind; however, the blue lotus (nymphaea caerulea) was greatly loved in Egypt, for its beauty and its scent, which was equated with the divine essence and thought to have the perfume of Ra’s sweat. There are many examples still in existence of Egyptian art showing people sniffing the lotus. The ancient word for Ra’s tears, remyt, and mankind, remeth, also reveal an interesting link by sounding so similar. Egyptian obelisks were seen by those who built them as metaphorical connections between heaven and earth, with their top-most pyramidions symbolising the rays of the sun as they fall to earth. The Washington Monument, the obelisk structure that holds the key to the lost word in The Lost Symbol, is revealed to be itself a the centre of circumpunct. The plaza surrounding the monument provides the outer circle of the design. Astrologers and astronomers also recognise the circumpunct as representing the sun, while medieval astrologers, who included astronomers, used the sign for the Earth, since they believed that it was God’s special creation and therefore the centre of the universe. The space circling the earth was equivalent to a great ocean surrounding an island. On Salisbury Plain, Wiltshire, southern England, lies a massive and mysterious circumpunct: the ancient monument called Stonehenge. It is believed to be around 4,500 years old, although some of its huge stones may have been erected hundreds of years before that time. Outside its stone structures runs an earth bank and ditch (the henge), which archaeological investigation suggests can be dated to around 3,100 BC. Thus the henge forms the outer circle and the stone inner ring forms the remainder of the design. The countryside for miles around had been a cemetery for a long period of prehistory, and is covered with burial mounds. While it is clear that this part of England was regarded by ancient people as very special, it is by no means agreed why this should be so. The debate

about the function and purpose of Stonehenge itself has theorists touting it as an ancient calendar, an astro-laboratory, a temple or a place of sacrifice. For those who follow the mystical precepts of the Kabbalah, which has its own interpretation of Hebrew scriptures, the circumpunct symbolises Kether in the Sephiroth. Kether (Keter) is the crown at the top of the Sephiroth of the Tree of Life. The Tree of Life is a diagram to illustrate the creation of the universe. In Freemasonry, it is a symbol for the control of emotions. Freemasonry is absolutely full of symbolism. One of the objects most closely linked with the Brotherhood is the compass, which would be the most useful instrument, of course, for producing a circumpunct. Pythagorean philosophers called God, or the Primary Being, Monad, from whom all else ultimately sprang. Monad was represented by the circle with a point at its centre. When the word monad is used for a single, indivisible unit, it takes on the meaning of an atom. To Taoists, it symbolises the divine creative spark. Dan Brown’s last mention of the circumpunct in The Lost Symbol is when Robert Langdon realises that the painting The Apotheosis of Washington on the ceiling of the Capitol Building has the characters arranged in two concentric rings. What is most fascinating, perhaps, is that for so many centuries and across so many beliefs and philosophies the symbol of a point within a circle has been regarded as having a special significance, often representing aspects of God. Could it be something more than its simple design that holds the circumpunct’s appeal? SEE ALSO: Alchemy, The Apotheosis of Washington, Freemasonry

CROWLEY, ALEISTER Aleister Crowley is described in The Lost Symbol as an individual who greatly inspired Mal’akh at the time when he was still calling himself Andros Dareios and living in New York. We are told that it was through the writings of Crowley that Mal’akh learned about ritual magic and incantation. So who was Aleister Crowley? Some may know him by his popular title of ‘the Wickedest Man in the World’. Sections of the popular press labelled him ‘the most evil man who ever lived’. Rather than reject these titles, Crowley seemed to rejoice in the air of notoriety that followed him and he did nothing to try to change people’s opinions of him; in fact, one of the titles he gave himself was ‘the Beast whose number is 666’. Should we still be in any doubt over the public perception of this man, we need only look at a transcript of a London libel case from 1934 that involved Crowley. While summing up, the judge said: I thought that I knew of every conceivable form of wickedness, I thought that everything which was vicious and bad had been produced at one time or another before me. I have learned in this case that we can always learn something more . . . I have never heard such dreadful, horrible, blasphemous and abominable stuff as that which has been produced by the man who describes himself to you as the greatest living poet. So, what exactly did he do to deserve such palpable outrage? What is the story of Aleister Crowley? He was born in 1875 in Royal Leamington Spa, Warwickshire, the son of a successful retired brewer. Both of his parents were very strict Christians, being of the Plymouth Brethren sect. But in studying his upbringing we discover signs revealing that all was not as well as it might have been. His father died when he was still young. Afterwards, Crowley could not accept what he saw as the religious dogma of his parents’ faith, which led to a rift within the family. His mother, in particular, was distraught at his rebellious ways and began calling

him ‘the Beast’, in reference to the figure of the Antichrist found in the Bible’s Book of Revelation. Rather than be offended by this label, Crowley took it as his own and it was a title that he used until his death. Things did not improve for Crowley until he turned 21 and inherited his father’s fortune. Finally free of the religious background that he loathed, Crowley went to Cambridge, where he took the first steps towards what would become a lifetime devoted to the occult. He devoured books on magic and alchemy, and by 1898 he had been initiated into the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn, an esoteric society that had such luminaries as W.B. Yeats and Dion Fortune amongst its members. However, political infighting would see him leave the Order within just a couple of years, after which Crowley set up his own temple at Boleskine House on the shores of Loch Ness in Scotland. Over the course of the next few years, he would attempt to make sense of magical ritual. Crowley describes the ultimate aim of his great work in Magick in Theory and Practice, in which, strangely enough, we even see an echo of the Noetic sciences mentioned in The Lost Symbol: There is a single main definition of the object of all magical Ritual. It is the uniting of the Microcosm with the Macrocosm. The Supreme and Complete Ritual is therefore the Invocation of the Holy Guardian Angel; or, in the language of Mysticism, Union with God. Despite the reputation that Crowley has left behind, there is no firm evidence to suggest that he was a practitioner of the dark arts. He seems to have been strongly opposed to the notion that he was somehow a black magician and he went on public record to make his opposition to black magic clear, saying in a newspaper article of 1933: To practise black magic you have to violate every principle of science, decency and intelligence. You must be obsessed with an insane idea of the importance of the petty object of your wretched

and selfish desires. I have been accused of being a ‘black magician’. No more foolish statement was ever made about me. I despise the thing to such an extent that I can hardly believe in the existence of people so debased and idiotic as to practise it. Crowley’s most enduring work is his study of Thelema. This body of work could be said to be a treatise against black magic; in fact, the laws that Crowley penned and by which he lived his life forbade the practice of black magic. The result of his research was The Book of the Law, or Liber Al vel Legis. Crowley came to discover the Law of Thelema while he was in Cairo on honeymoon, where he claims he received what would become the final text from a spirit guide in the form of Aiwass, a messenger of the Egyptian god Horus. The famous quote from The Book of the Law, often used to paraphrase Crowley’s Law of Thelema, reads, in full: The word of the Law is Thelema. Who calls us Thelemites will do no wrong, if he look but close into the word. For there are therein Three Grades, the Hermit, and the Lover, and the man of Earth. Do what thou wilt shall be the whole of the Law. This message literally means that each of us is free to live our life in the way we choose; however, Crowley proposed that before we exercise this free will, we must first look within ourselves and through long study come to know ourselves and work out the true nature of our will before implementing it. This free will is, therefore, to be interpreted as the individual’s destiny or purpose in life and, in effect, with this freedom also comes great responsibility and self-discipline. Despite leaving behind a vast body of work, it was probably Crowley’s engagement in sex magic that earned him his reputation as the Wickedest Man in the World. He would routinely take part in magic rituals that involved sex with both male and female participants; it could be that history would have been kinder to him had he not outraged polite society of the early 1900s with some of his more salacious antics.

Returning to The Lost Symbol, it is relevant to note that amongst his many studies into the occult, Crowley also had encounters with Freemasonry. By his own accounts, he was initiated up to the third degree by 1904 at a lodge in Paris and continued to press for entry into lodge meetings in London, but he was refused. He also confessed in his autobiography that he had been initiated as a 33rd- degree Mason through the Ancient and Accepted Rite of Masonry at a lodge in Mexico. All of these facts are hard to verify outside of the claims he made himself. To further complicate matters, he later received entry into the 33rd degree, amongst other honours, via postal contact with a controversial British Mason known as John Yarker. Crowley was also associated with Freemasonry through the Ordo Templi Orientis, known as the OTO, which was itself modelled on the craft, becoming a member in 1912. After a bizarre series of events in 1923, Crowley went on to proclaim himself Outer Head of the Order, and after no one disputed his position he went on to lead the organisation for many years. Whether he was seriously interested in Freemasonry will never be known, but one thing is certain: with his many connections, he would have been privy to many of the secrets of the brotherhood. He seems to have been keen to assimilate the knowledge he had gained from Freemasonry with that from his occult studies. In his book The Confessions of Aleister Crowley: An Autohagiography, he offers the following: I proposed to define freemasonry as a system of communicating truth – religious, philosophical, magical and mystical; and indicating the proper means of developing human faculty by means of a peculiar language whose alphabet is the symbolism of ritual. Universal brotherhood and the great moral principles, independent of personal, racial, climatic and other prejudices, naturally formed a background which would assure individual security and social stability for each and all. The truth is that today Crowley is still an enigma; we are no closer to working out who he truly was than his peers were. One thing is certain, though: if he were here today, reading The Lost Symbol, he

would appreciate the persistent thread in the book that God is within us all. It would have been familiar territory to him. Furthermore, he would have warmly embraced the concept of Noetic science and practical applications such as the Intention Experiment. For what is magic ritual if it is not the application of human will to the physical environment around us? We may label them differently now, but to Crowley there would be no difference – the basis of the magic he practised and the basis of Noetic science are identical. Do what thou wilt shall be the whole of the Law. SEE ALSO: Freemasonry, Institute of Noetic Sciences

DOLLAR BILL SYMBOLISM The Dollar Bill is a magical thing. This everyday item of cloth, paper and ink is replete with sacred and mystical symbolism. For those who have the knowledge to see it, the Dollar Bill is a cornucopia of the mysterious and strange, chock-full of symbols and hints towards deeper meanings. It truly is a magical thing. When Katherine Solomon and Robert Langdon are trying to evade the CIA in the back of a cab in The Lost Symbol, Katherine suddenly takes out a Dollar Bill and proceeds to use a pen to draw on the reverse of the note, outlining a Star of David over the pyramid of the Great Seal and highlighting in each corner of the star the letters of the word Mason. This cameo appearance of the Dollar Bill in the book hints at its much greater – and to many unknown – role in the mysterious symbolism of the founding and creation of the fledgling United States. Strangely enough, it’s not necessary to go back through the mists of time to reveal the origins of the Dollar Bill as we see it today. The Dollar Bill was redesigned in 1935, during the administration of President Franklin Delaney Roosevelt, following the worst economic recession the world had ever seen. It is the cast of characters involved in its creation that proved to be the most mysterious aspect. One of these figures was a man called Nicholas Roerich. A striking-looking man, Roerich sported a shaven head and a long white beard. His piercing eyes were said to be able to look into your soul. Roerich was a Russian émigré to the United States and became renowned as a painter, peace activist and philosopher. He travelled extensively throughout the Far East and Europe and was nominated a number of times for the Nobel Peace Prize.

Roerich was also a great friend of another member of our cast of characters, Henry Agard Wallace, Secretary of Agriculture between 1933 and 1940 and a close confidant of Roosevelt. Wallace was also a 32nd-degree Freemason, as was Roosevelt himself. Wallace would go on to become the 33rd vice president of the United States under Roosevelt and came close to being nominated to run for office as the 33rd president. In the end, that honour went to Harry S. Truman, who was also a high-ranking Freemason. But there was another side to Henry Wallace. He was interested in the esoteric and associated himself with some notorious occult characters of the time. It was these friendships that would ultimately lead to Wallace being deemed untrustworthy as a politician and regarded by some as naive and impressionable. Wallace was a Theosophist, a follower of the writings and doctrine of Helena Blavatsky, and it was through this pursuit and a mutual interest in Rosicrucian ideas that he became acquainted with Nicholas Roerich. It is the connection between Roerich and Wallace that many researchers and conspiracy theorists see as pivotal in the decision to place both sides of the Great Seal of the United States on the Dollar Bill. Wallace was later to claim that he first saw the truncated pyramid motif of the Great Seal in a small government-published booklet, which he then showed to Roosevelt. Being Freemasons, both men instantly recognised its symbolic significance. However, it has been speculated that it was Roerich who influenced Wallace in the motif ‘s placement on the new Dollar Bill. The two men certainly met on occasion and corresponded frequently; indeed, it was their correspondence, known as the ‘Guru Letters’, that nearly brought Wallace’s career crashing down when the letters ended up in the hands of Republican politicians and journalists. The letters were headed ‘Dear Guru’ and signed with the letter ‘G’, supposedly standing for Galahad, the name Roerich used to refer to Wallace. They reveal that Wallace was a much more committed and devoted follower of Roerich than had been previously thought and make the connection between the two men even stronger. Roerich was undoubtedly familiar with the motif of the unfinished pyramid and the all-seeing eye above it, understanding it as a representation of, amongst other things, the Holy Grail and the

Stone of Destiny. Roerich’s influence should not be understated: he was seen by many of the Washington and New York elite of the time as a genuine enlightened guru and his reach ran far and wide. Apart from Roerich and Wallace, another interesting player was Manly P. Hall. A Freemason, writer and philosopher, Hall was also greatly influenced by the doctrines of Theosophy and the writings of Helena Blavatsky. He was a friend of the Roerich family and for a while attended meetings with Roerich in New York. Roosevelt was a fan of Hall, going so far as to have Hall’s extensive library of occult, philosophical, historical and archaic books transferred to microfiche in 1942. These, then, are the people and belief systems that gave birth to the One Dollar Bill. Roosevelt approved the new design of the Dollar Bill in 1935, and so the dollar that we see and love today came into being. But what are the symbolic elements of the One Dollar Bill? The eye above the pyramid can be seen in slightly different ways. The Masonic view would be that it is the Eye of Providence looking down with favour upon the new nation. Some see an echo of the Ancient Egyptian Eye of Horus, while others associate the eye with the star Sirius. What is clear is that the motif is both symbolic and occult in nature. The question of whether it was originally intended to be so is fiercely debated. Number symbolism also plays a role in the One Dollar Bill, the number 13 being prominent. We find that there are 13 stars on the back of the One Dollar Bill, above the head of the eagle. These 13 stars are arranged in such a way that if you were to draw lines between them, they would trace out the shape of the Seal of Solomon, also known as the Star of David. The eagle itself holds 13 arrows in one of its talons and 13 leaves of an olive branch in the other, signifying the United States’ ability to wage war and defend itself, and bring about peace and security in the world. On its chest, the eagle has a shield with 13 stripes, and in its beak it holds a banner with the Latin phrase E pluribus unum (one out of many); this phrase contains 13 letters. There are 13 feathers on each wing of the eagle. On the left side of the reverse of the One Dollar Bill, the unfinished pyramid has 13 courses of masonry. Incidentally, this is the same number of levels as the pyramid that stands on top of the

Washington Monument. Above the pyramid is the Latin motto Annuit coeptis (God has favoured our undertakings), which also has 13 letters. Commentators explain the recurring use of the number as representative of the original 13 founding colonies of the Republic, hence the 13 stripes on the flag of the United States. The original colonies were (from north to south): New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Connecticut, New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Delaware, Maryland, Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina and Georgia. However, the number 13 also has many mysterious and symbolic meanings. Many today see Friday the 13th as unlucky. This superstition, although relatively modern, arises from the date that commemorates the attack on the Knights Templar by King Philip of France that took place on Friday, 13 October 1307. The number 13 is also associated with Christ. There were 13 people in attendance at the Last Supper, for instance; there are also 13 Apostles. It is also the age that a child enters his or her teenage years. In Jewish tradition, 13 is the age a boy becomes a bar mitzvah. The number might then also symbolise the coming of age of the United States, the dawn of the new republic, standing alone. One interesting aside is that in the absolute centre of the front of the One Dollar Bill sits the right eye of George Washington, as seen in his portrait. This seems to mimic the Eye of Providence hovering above the pyramid on the reverse of the note. As David Ovason notes in The Secret Symbols of the Dollar Bill: The Symbolism is obvious: these associations are intended to suggest that Washington should be regarded symbolically as a kind of demigod. In spirit, he looks down over the destiny of the American nation, in much the same way as the eye of Providence overlooks the destiny of the world. The One Dollar Bill is teeming with esoteric meaning and symbolism, and this entry alone cannot cover the vast amount of material available. There is one small aspect of the Dollar Bill that often gets overlooked and it appears on the front, the side featuring the portrait of Washington. You may notice the numeral 1 placed in a

shield in the top right-hand corner. If you look at the top left of this shield and the indented corner, there – almost too small to notice – is a shape that almost seems to sit in the indentation. So what is this tiny speck? If you were to scan the One Dollar Bill and blow up this small section, you would find something that resembles a miniature owl (some have said it looks more like a spider). This image has caused much controversy and debate, especially amongst conspiracy theorists who see in the owl the semblance of the god Moloch, the Canaanite deity who has come to be represented by that bird. The owl is also the main mascot and motif of an elite gentleman’s club called Bohemian Grove located in Monte Rio, California. This exclusive male-only club has counted many US presidents among its members, as well as various heads of industry and finance. Once a year at Bohemian Grove, members take part in a ceremony called the Cremation of Care, in which offerings are made to a giant 40-foot owl shrine that stands at one end of the lake at the club. The ceremony culminates in the lighting of fires around the owl. All this was captured on video by conspiracy theorist and radio presenter Alex Jones in 2000. Jones claimed that the ceremony was satanic in nature and that the United States was run by a cabal of Satan worshippers and black magicians. In The Lost Symbol, Mal’akh’s name may echo that of Moloch. Perhaps Dan Brown is making a clever, oblique reference to this controversy. Of course, this small shape may just be a slip of the original engraver’s hand, which is the orthodox explanation commonly given for its mysterious appearance. The next time you come across a One Dollar Bill, take the time to really have a good look at this amazing piece of paper and ink. It contains hidden meanings, sacred symbolism and mysterious elements in equal measure. It truly is a thing of magic and wonder. SEE ALSO: Great Seal of the United States, Manly P. Hall, George Washington

DÜRER, ALBRECHT Following the theme established by Dan Brown in his previous Langdon novels, there is a world-renowned artist at the heart of the symbologist’s code-breaking in The Lost Symbol. After the chase around Rome via the breathtaking marble sculptures of Gian Lorenzo Bernini in Angels & Demons and the genius of Leonardo Da Vinci in The Da Vinci Code, we now have the formidable figure of Albrecht Dürer, greatest of the German Renaissance artists. Dürer was an artist and draughtsman who left a legacy of over 950 drawings, but he was also the author of books on measurement, the human body and fortifications. In this respect, he was an example of the true Renaissance man – a polymath, learned in many fields.
