The mountain, which has a conical summit and pyramid shape, has been seen as standing at the very centre of Scotland and was a place of spiritual pilgrimage in the past. Today, Heredom is the name given to the journal of the Scottish Rite Research Society, sent annually to members since 1992. SEE ALSO: House of the Temple

HERMETICA In The Lost Symbol, the term ‘As above, so it is below’ plays a pivotal role in Robert Langdon’s search for the location of the Ancient Mysteries; in fact, it is the lost key that allows all else to fall into place. This principle is also the central tenet that forms the basis of hermeticism, a mystical philosophical tradition developed in the cosmopolitan city of Alexandria in Egypt around the first century AD. It renounced codified dogma, priestly authority and the separation of God and Man, instead propounding belief in inner enlightenment, declaring that everyone should seek and aspire to a personal knowledge of the divine. Hermetic beliefs, a product of Alexandrian syncretism, were heavily influenced by Neoplatonism and Gnosticism, as well as Ptolemaic Egyptian, Judaic and Christian thought, and these beliefs were contained within the written works termed the Hermetica. The Hermetica cover topics such as philosophy, mysticism, magic, astrology, alchemy and medicine, and were supposedly written by Hermes Trismegistus (‘Hermes the Thrice-Great’), the central figure of the Hermetica and hermetic belief. Hermes Trismegistus was the product of fusing Thoth, the Egyptian god of learning, writing and magic, with Hermes, the Greek god of communication, inventions, language and travel. With both gods having many similar areas of responsibility, the two became combined in Ptolemaic Egypt to become the highly revered and important god Thoth-Hermes, who was believed to know all the secrets of heaven and earth, secrets that might be revealed to the worthy through the power of magic and dreams. By the time of the early Christian period, Hermes Trismegistus had developed into an ancient sage on a par with Moses, Pythagoras and Zoroaster, although having a more ancient existence. It is uncertain why Thoth-Hermes was given the title Thrice-Great. Some hermetic texts suggest that it was because of his three incarnations (his previous two being Enoch and Noah) or because he was the greatest philosopher, priest and king. However, ‘the Emerald Tablet’ (perhaps the most famous and concise work on hermetic philosophy, supposedly written by Hermes Trismegistus himself ) declares that the title was bestowed due to his knowledge

concerning the three wisdoms of the universe: alchemy, astrology and theurgy. The Egyptian god Thoth had been called Thrice-Great long before the Hermetica were written, so it would appear that Hermes Trismegistus was simply carrying on a long tradition associated with his Egyptian heritage. The philosophical works and teachings that have survived indicate that the Hermetica once formed a large body of literature pertaining to hermetic belief. The largest surviving collection is known as the Corpus Hermeticum, comprising 18 tracts originating from Alexandria but written in Greek. The Corpus Hermeticum is thought to date from the first to the third century ad and is purported to have been written or dictated by Hermes Trismegistus, a belief held until the seventeenth century, although today it is apparent that the Corpus was actually the work of a number of individuals over a considerable period of time. After the first book gives a general introduction, the second book of the Corpus, entitled ‘Poemander’ (‘Shepherd of Men’), concerns a revelation given to Hermes Trismegistus by a higher being called Poemander, while the other books relate the dialogues between Hermes and his pupil(s) on certain aspects of hermetic philosophy, hidden wisdom and secrets of the universe. While the Corpus is written in Greek, it has been suggested that the authors identified more with their Egyptian ancestry, bearing in mind the claims within the 16th book of the Corpus for the superiority of the Egyptian language over the Greek: ‘This discourse, expressed in our paternal language, keeps clear the meaning of its words. The very quality of the speech and the sound of Egyptian words have in themselves the energy of the objects they speak of.’ In contrast, they say that in translating the writings into Greek ‘the greatest distortion’ is produced. While it is not generally believed that the main source of these mystical texts goes as far back as Ancient Egypt, the style of the Corpus does echo a long Egyptian tradition of wisdom texts written in the style of a man teaching his son or a sage his pupil. In 1945 at Nag Hammadi, Egypt, a large number of papyrus texts were discovered, including some Coptic hermetic texts, some of which were already known as part of the Corpus Hermeticum, as well as a previously unknown hermetic text called The Ogdoad and the Ennead (or ‘The Eight Out of the Nine’), which describes the eight stages of hermetic initiation into gnosis (spiritual knowledge). Also

included within the body of hermetic writings are a text on astrology and magic titled Picatrix, believed to have been composed in Harran, Turkey, and dated to the eighth century ad, and the Liber Hermetis, a fifteenth-century work on alchemy and astrological writings that declares Hermes Trismegistus to be its author. However, in addition to the Corpus there are fragments, quotes and references that have come down to us through authors such as Iambichus, Porphyry and early Christian theologians including Clement of Alexandria (c. ad 150–212), whose writings indicate knowledge of hermetic works. John of Stobi’s Anthologium, from around ad 500, also contains some 40 passages and fragments of hermetic thought, highlighting the written information that had been lost to us. Yet ‘the Emerald Tablet’ remains perhaps the definitive text on hermetic philosophy. In The Western Way (1997), John Matthews states that ‘the Emerald Tablet’ ‘is one of the most profound and important documents to have come down to us. It has been said more than once that it contains the sum of all knowledge – for those able to understand it.’ ‘The Emerald Tablet’ is where the ‘As above, so it is below’ principle can be found. The earliest surviving copy of this work appears in the Book of Balinas the Wise on Causes, an Arabic book written around ad 650, which relates how, as a youth, Balinas supposedly discovered the tablet in a cave in Tyana, Turkey. The tablet’s origin, if it actually existed, is uncertain, but legend has it that it was written by the son of Adam, who inscribed it to atone for his father’s sins and thus enable Man to gain the knowledge he required to achieve redemption. Later apocryphal accounts record that Alexander the Great found the tablet in Hermes’s tomb near the Siwa Oasis, eventually taking it with him when he left Egypt and hiding it in an undisclosed location. It was Balinas who then found the tablet many years later and who spent his life writing, explaining and expounding upon the ideology it contained. ‘The Emerald Tablet’ states ‘that which is below corresponds to that which is above, and that which is above, corresponds to that which is below, to accomplish the miracles of the One Thing’. It also notes that the ‘structure of the microcosm is in accordance with the structure of the macrocosm’, indicating that the universe mirrors the earth and vice versa, the structure of the smallest atom contains within it the structure of the universe and vice versa, and

the world of matter reflects the divine, so that Man mirrors God and God ‘creates Man in His own image’. What happens in one realm has an effect on another, be it in the material or the spiritual world. Mankind, while existing in the lowest, material world, still contains within himself the divine spark, and therefore it is Man’s duty to try to reunite with the divine. Pleading with God is not considered necessary, for Mankind is not an evil, baseborn creature tainted by original sin, as Christianity purports; in fact, Man himself is a god. Hermetic thinking states: ‘Know ye not that ye are gods?’ It is this phrase that Dan Brown highlights when Robert Langdon is considering the teachings of the Ancient Mysteries. The idea is echoed in The Apotheosis of Washington, the painting on the ceiling of the Rotunda of the Capitol Building, in which America’s first president is becoming a god. Hermetic thought, as highlighted in the macrocosm/microcosm concept, taught that everything was one, with Michael Baigent and Richard Leigh in The Elixir and the Stone describing the hermeticist conception of the universe as a single all-persuasive, all-encompassing totality, a single whole in which all dichotomies, all distinctions between body and soul, spirit and matter, were accommodated and harmoniously integrated. Everything, in its own way, was valid. Everything was incorporated in the comprehensive design . . . For the hermeticist, gnosis entailed direct apprehension of, and integration with, the all-inclusive harmony. This harmony brought with it the interconnection of everything, allowing Man to play an active role and effectively change his lot in life. No longer would he be the helpless pawn dependent upon fate and the whims of the gods; he could be an active participant, manipulating the world around him to his own will in order to bring about significant change. Baigent and Leigh explain that according to the ‘As above, so it is below’ principle, ‘if everything were indeed interconnected, man himself . . . could make things happen to other spheres. If one pulled a particular string or thread in the tapestry of reality, something else, in some other quarter of the tapestry, would ensue.’

‘The Emerald Tablet’ explains that ‘all things have their birth from this One Thing by adaptation’, so that Man’s actions on earth mirror God’s actions in heaven and so on. Such concepts were conveyed by means of symbols, notably the Seal of Solomon hexagram with its two interlocking triangles representing ‘As above, so it is below’, male and female, Man and God. It was thought that these symbols could in turn be used to effect change, an idea that found expression in activities such as magic, alchemy and astrology and prompted a new examination of the world of God and Man. In The Egyptian Hermes, Garth Fowden states that the ‘procedures of conventional alchemy are strictly preparatory to the purification and perfection of the soul’. The hermetic idea of the macrocosm and microcosm thus became a powerful analogy, seen in alchemy as the transmutation of base metal into gold that likewise created a parallel transformation of the alchemist’s soul. In Harran, in modern-day Turkey, hermeticism played a major role in influencing Islamic science and mathematics, eliciting many Arab translations of old hermetic texts, as well as new Arabic ones. Indeed, one Arab writer notes that twenty-two hermetic works were available, with thirteen on alchemy alone. The later Crusades to the Holy Land brought many people into contact with these ideas for the first time. By the mid-thirteenth century, the Holy Roman Emperor, Friedrich of Germany, added his seal of approval to the study and promulgation of hermetic thought. One of the most famous thirteenth-century alchemists, and a hermetic philosopher, was Albertus Magnus, while in the fourteenth century, Nicolas Flamel was a famous proponent of alchemy and magic. It was Cosimo de Medici, however, who had a crucial role in collecting and promoting the Hermetica and hence had a direct effect on the enlightenment of Renaissance Europe. In the 1460s, he sent Fra Leonardo del Pistoja to Macedonia to find philosophical works. Pistoja brought back with him the Corpus Hermeticum, which caused Cosimo such excitement that he immediately ordered his academic translator, Marsilio Ficino, to translate it into Latin. The freshly translated Corpus ignited a new interest in hermeticism and alchemy that spread from Italy to the rest of Europe. Around this time some hermetic occult orders were founded, notably the Rosicrucians, whose emblems were the rose, symbolising the soul, and the cross, symbolising the material world.

Freemasonry also held hermetic beliefs in high regard, as noted in the Morals and Dogma of Freemasonry of the Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite of Freemasonry by Albert Pike, which advises: He who desires to attain the understanding of the Grand Word and the possession of the Great Secret, ought carefully to read the Hermetic philosophers, and will undoubtedly attain initiation, as others have done; but he must take, for the key of their allegories, the single dogma of Hermes, contained in his Table of Emerald. SEE ALSO: Alchemy, Freemasonry, Rosicrucianism, Seal of Solomon

HOUSE OF THE TEMPLE The House of the Temple is home to the headquarters of the Scottish Rite of Freemasonry in the Southern Jurisdiction of the United States. It is located in Washington DC at 1733 Sixteenth Street NW, between R and S streets, and is 13 blocks north of the White House. It has been the headquarters of the Supreme Council of Scottish Rite since 1915. The building is known to Scottish Rite Masons as Heredom. This amazing edifice plays a central role within the pages of The Lost Symbol, being the location of the showdown between Mal’akh and his father, Peter Solomon. This confrontation takes place in the innermost Temple Room of the building, beneath the large oculus in the ceiling. It is upon the central ‘altar’ of this room that Mal’akh attempts to make his father sacrifice him using the Akedah knife that he has purchased. The architect of the House of the Temple, John Russell Pope, was not in fact a Freemason, and had an assistant, Elliot Woods, assigned to help him with the Masonic symbolism that needed to be incorporated into the design. The structure is modelled on one of the ancient Seven Wonders, the Mausoleum of King Mausolus at Halicarnassus. The design of the building has been praised as an architectural wonder and Pope was much commended on the work. Indeed, in 1917 Pope was awarded a Gold Medal of the Architectural League of New York for his work on the House of the Temple. The building was Pope’s first major commission in Washington DC; he was only 36 at the time. He would go on to design and oversee the building of some of the most famous twentieth-century buildings in the city, such as the Jefferson Memorial, the National Archives and the National Gallery of Art. According to author David Ovason, the cornerstone of the House of the Temple was laid on the 18 October 1911, with hundreds of Masons attending. This ceremony was conducted by J. Claude Keiper, the Grand Master of the District of Columbia, using the same ceremonial gavel that George Washington had used at the Capitol Building cornerstone ceremony. Within the Temple itself is an alcove that holds the interred remains of Albert Pike, Confederate general and author of what has become the main source book for Scottish Rite Freemasonry, Morals

and Dogmas of the Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite of Freemasonry, written in 1871. In the library of the Temple is one of the largest collections of Masonry related books in the world; more than a quarter of a million titles are housed there. There is also a large banqueting room, several offices for high-ranking Masonic officials and an exhibition space. Tours are offered on weekdays and exhibitions of Masonic artefacts are often staged. Above the main door of the Temple is inscribed the maxim: ‘Freemasonry Builds its Temples in the Hearts of Men and Among Nations.’ Outside of the main doorway sit two huge sphinxes. One has its eyes open and signifies Power, the other has its eyes closed and symbolises Wisdom. Around the outside of the main structure are 33 columns, each 33 feet tall, representing the 33 degrees of Scottish Rite Freemasonry. The pyramidal structure that sits atop the Temple has 13 steps, seemingly mimicking the unfinished pyramid on the Great Seal of the United States. In the House of the Temple, the fast-paced plot of The Lost Symbol is driven forwards by a series of dramatic events that take place in the main Temple Room, where the ceremonies and rites of the Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite are conducted. The Temple has an enormous carved polished Belgian black marble altar sitting in the dead centre, dominating the room in a magnificently grand way. Visitors to the House of the Temple notice that around the walls is a frieze, also in black marble, inscribed in bronze letters: FROM THE OUTER DARKNESS OF IGNORANCE THROUGH THE SHADOWS OF OUR EARTH LIFE, WINDS THE BEAUTIFUL PATH OF INITIATION UNTO THE DIVINE LIGHT OF THE HOLY ALTAR. The altar itself is inlaid with Hebrew characters that offer initiates in particular the following message: GOD SAID, ‘LET THERE BE LIGHT,’ AND THERE WAS LIGHT. Dan Brown mentions on a few occasions throughout his novel that the only light that illuminates the altar at certain times is the ‘pale shaft of moonlight’ that streams in by way of the large oculus at the

top of the pyramid-shaped roof. Visitors to the House of the Temple are told that the oculus, which is 100 feet above the altar, is symbolic of the fact that light, as a metaphor for enlightenment and the light of learning, is something that is prized by the Scottish Rite. In British Masonic rituals, there is a reference to a similar light- giving window. The dormer window, as it is called, shines on the mosaic pavement, symbolic of opposites – darkness and light. Initiates are told that it gave light to the sanctum sanctorum or Holy of Holies in Solomon’s Temple. Interestingly, ‘oculus’ is the Latin for ‘eye’, as well as referring to a large window in a dome. In The Lost Symbol, oculus means both. The metaphor of the Temple representing the human links to the hermetic maxim ‘As above, so it is below’. In Mal’akh’s quest for knowledge, he realises that the fontanelle is the oculus to the brain. He notes that although the portal closes, it is a lost connection between our inner and outer worlds. Langdon also believed that the Lost Word was right before his eyes when he looked up to see an oculus to heaven, with the altar below it. SEE ALSO: Heredom, Scottish Rite Freemasonry

INSTITUTE OF NOETIC SCIENCES The Institute of Noetic Sciences (IONS) is a non-profit organisation that encourages and conducts research into human consciousness and its potential. It was founded in 1973 by astronaut Edgar Mitchell (one of the few to walk on the moon), together with Paul N. Temple, an industrialist with a background in the petroleum business. IONS now has more than 20,000 members and operates from a 200-acre location in the hills above San Francisco. It produces a quarterly magazine called Shift: At the Frontiers of Consciousness, a 48-page journal detailing research from the world of consciousness studies. In The Lost Symbol, Katherine Solomon is described as a Noetic scientist and there is considerable mention of various research projects that showcase this branch of study. The word ‘Noetic’ comes from the Ancient Greek word noesis, which roughly translates as ‘inner knowing’ or ‘intuition’. IONS has dedicated itself to exploring the nature of consciousness using rigorous scientific methods in an attempt to establish the connection between the microcosm and the macrocosm, as well as the inner and the outer worlds. Edgar Mitchell says that walking on the moon and seeing Earth from such a distance profoundly affected him. Before he went to the moon, he was a man who believed only in the strictly rational, but something within him changed for ever while gazing back at Earth. He explains the journey thus: Suddenly, from behind the rim of the moon, in long, slow-motion moments of immense majesty, there emerges a sparkling blue and white jewel, a light, delicate sky-blue sphere laced with slow swirling veils of white, rising gradually like a small pearl in a thick sea of black mystery. It takes more than a moment to fully realise this is Earth – home. On the return trip home, gazing through 240,000 miles of space toward the stars and the planet from which I had come, I suddenly experienced the universe as intelligent, loving, harmonious. We

went to the moon as technicians, we returned humanitarians. When I went to the moon, I was as pragmatic a test pilot, engineer and scientist as any of my colleagues. But when I saw the planet Earth floating in the vastness of space . . . the presence of divinity became almost palpable and I knew that life in the universe was not just an accident based on random processes. Just two years after returning home, he founded IONS. His work at the Institute could not have been more different from his work with NASA. As an astronaut, Mitchell had explored outer space; his work with IONS was all about exploring inner space, the world that exists only inside our heads, yet which, according to IONS, has the potential to have an impact on the world around us. Much of the work done at IONS sounds like science fiction, but it is all rooted in real science and the study of the human mind. The researchers study phenomena that a few hundred years ago would have been classified as magic or firmly in the realm of the occult: the Tarot (and divination in general), remote viewing, psychic healing (now known as distant healing), near-death experiences and meditation. One of the fields of Noetic science mentioned in The Lost Symbol is entanglement. As scientists understand more and more about how minute particles operate at the quantum level, so it has a bearing on consciousness studies. We are starting to learn that particles can seemingly ‘communicate’ with each other, even over vast distances. Einstein himself called this phenomena ‘spooky action at a distance’ and did not fully understand the process, believing it to be an error in our understanding of quantum mechanics, a flaw that could not possibly exist. However, we have since learned that it is possible that individual particles can communicate with each other using what is called quantum teleportation, a process whereby a unit of information can be transmitted from one particle to another, irrespective of location or distance. Some scientists hypothesise that these minute particles use equally infinitesimal wormholes to teleport the information from one particle to another, so that the data does not have to travel faster than the speed of light. While this goes far beyond the scope

of this book, it is evident that if we are starting to discover that particles can communicate in this way via tiny wormholes, then the possibility that our minds can potentially communicate with other particles outside our bodies, even other minds, opens up. The senior scientist at IONS, Dr Dean Radin, puts forward his belief that this new science of entanglement could go some way to explain psychic abilities in his book Entangled Minds. Dr Radin is probably the Institute’s most well-known face, after Edgar Mitchell. He is also the author of the bestselling The Conscious Universe, which serves as a great introduction to the world of consciousness studies. Along with his work for IONS, Dr Radin is known for his involvement with the Global Consciousness Project based at Princeton University. Its aim is to run a series of random event generators (REGs) around the clock in various locations around the globe to see if world events can ‘spike’ the REGs – that is, provoke them into recording periods when random numbers suddenly stop being produced and more ordered patterns are generated. The REGs are analogous to a simple coin flip, where the end result is either tails or heads. The REGs in the Global Consciousness Project produce 200 flips per second, but instead of heads or tails they produce either a one or a zero. Normally, there should be no discernible pattern to the strings of ones and zeros that are recorded. Roger D. Nelson, a scientist working at Princeton Engineering Anomalies Research, pioneered the work done at the Global Consciousness Project. He first discovered that group consciousness can have an effect on REGs, altering completely random sequences of data and shaping them into recognisable patterns in which the numbers are no longer random. Since the project’s inception in 1998, many major world events have caused dramatic changes in the patterns created by the REGs; the most controversial result of the Global Consciousness Project is mentioned in The Lost Symbol. On 11 September 2001, 37 REGs were running at the Global Consciousness Project and indeed seemed to spike, showing that they were affected by the mass outpouring of emotion emitted from the consciousness of humanity following the terrorist attack on the Twin Towers. However, while the data shows that there was a reaction in the REGs as the whole world came together to watch the

terrible events of that day unfold, there was a sting in the tail. The REGs also recorded anomalies in the hours running up to the attacks. The largest spike before the event occurred at 5.30 a.m. local time in New York and the anomaly lasted for half an hour. Debate still rages over the results and the data, but, if they are proved correct, then massed global consciousness on our planet has the ability to foretell major events. This could have profound consequences for our understanding of the powers of the human mind. The study of the effects the human mind can have on physical outcomes is explored in Lynne McTaggart’s book The Intention Experiment, which Dan Brown mentions in The Lost Symbol. When Edgar Mitchell started IONS, he had two aims: first, to study the phenomena of human consciousness and prove beyond doubt that the human mind was capable of far greater feats than science had attributed to it at the time; second, to ‘apply that knowledge to the enhancement of human well-being and the quality of life on the planet’. IONS believes it has accomplished the first of these aims, establishing beyond doubt that human minds really are interconnected with the world around them. While there is much work still to be done in exploring these fields, the Institute is now thinking long and hard about how it moves into its next phase, applying what it has learned for the betterment of mankind. For the last few years, IONS has been changing how it operates, gearing up for the new challenges that lie ahead. Noetic science will always struggle to convince sceptics that these phenomena are really happening, that the human mind really is as powerful as we are beginning to discover. But the more work IONS and other agencies complete, the better we will come to understand this fascinating field. Dr Radin is only too aware that it will be a long while before these sciences are accepted into the mainstream and made the following statement in an interview with Sub Rosa magazine: Keep in mind that the Wright brothers were actually flying their airplane in plain sight, in front of dozens of witnesses, while sceptics were still denying that flight was even possible. Old ideas die hard, even when pragmatic proof is obvious. Shortsightedness, stubbornness, inability to question fundamental assumptions, ignorance of

the philosophy, sociology and history of science, fear of disrupting the social order, fear of embarrassment, fear of losing one’s prestige by tackling a taboo, and so on. Most of the recalcitrance in science is driven by one form of fear or another. While the human mind is on the one hand capable of truly incredible feats, it is also capable of blindly ignoring what is in front of it. It will be a long road, but perhaps in a hundred years’ time we will look back at the Institute of Noetic Sciences and appreciate the trail they have blazed. SEE ALSO: Lynne McTaggart

JEFFERSON, THOMAS Thomas Jefferson, one of the men who helped to shape the United States of America, was born on 13 April 1743 in Virginia. A remarkable man who became the third president of America, he began his education learning Greek and Latin with a local schoolmaster. From 1760 he attended the College of William & Mary in Williamsburg, Virginia, where he read law. It was a college where deist beliefs were prevalent; in other words, many teachers and scholars there embraced the idea of a well-ordered world created by God, but they rejected certain traditional Christian beliefs, such as the existence of miracles. Jefferson included the writings of deist thinkers in his copybooks, and as a French speaker, he was also able to access works by French Enlightenment writers. While he was at college, he was a member of the Phi Beta Kappa fraternity, which is the oldest academic honour society in America. The society had all the hallmarks of a secret society: an elaborate initiation ceremony, a special handclasp, a secret oath and a set of rules. These are the same characteristics that mark out orders such as Freemasonry. In 1779, as governor of Virginia and a member of the Board of Visitors at William & Mary College, Jefferson was instrumental in making amendments to the structure of the college, now referred to as the ‘Jefferson Reorganization’. These amendments included the abolition of the divinity school and the creation of new professorships in medicine and modern languages, among others. These changes were consistent with Jefferson’s humanist beliefs. Thomas Jefferson married Martha Skelton, a widow, in 1772, and this increased his wealth and land. It also added to the number of slaves he owned, a problematic aspect of his life as viewed from more enlightened times. Over his lifetime he owned on average two hundred slaves at any one time, but he only freed a handful, all of them relatives of Sally Hemings. Sally was an African-American slave with whom Jefferson was reputed to have had a relationship and several children. Recent DNA analysis has proven this fact to many, although some still dispute the findings. In 1774, Jefferson’s nascent views on American independence were aired when he wrote A Summary View of the Rights of British America. The following year, he was appointed as a delegate for

Virginia to the Second Continental Congress in Philadelphia. He drafted resolutions and in June 1776 was appointed to a committee also including Benjamin Franklin to produce a formal statement justifying a breach with Britain. The document now known as the Declaration of Independence (which included these words written by Jefferson: ‘We hold these truths to be self-evident; that all men are created equal . . .’) was debated by Congress and adopted on 4 July 1776. Returning to Virginia, Jefferson applied the principle of fairness under the law to the state legal code, including the separation of the Church and secular functions. When the British launched a surprise attack on Virginia in 1780, Jefferson was forced into an undignified escape that his political enemies held against him for the rest of his life. Jefferson was appointed as American minister to France, and when he arrived there in 1784 the country was steeped in Enlightenment learning and political turmoil. Among his friends in France was the Marquis de Lafayette, a well-known and confirmed Freemason. Lafayette had fought for the cause of the American independence at the Battle of Brandywine in 1777 and was well acquainted with George Washington. After returning to France, Lafayette was active as an aristocratic liberal in the turmoil leading up to the French Revolution. As the French Revolution began the cycle of violence that was to become the Terror, Jefferson returned to America in 1789 to become the first Secretary of State under George Washington. His next high office was the position of vice president under John Adams, between 1797 and 1801. After a bruising and controversial election campaign in 1800, Thomas Jefferson became the third president of the United States, giving his inaugural address in March 1801 in the unfinished Capitol Building. Jefferson had worked closely with Washington on the plans and construction of the new capital city. In the early years of his presidency, Jefferson’s policies of dismantling federal government and reducing the national debt were successful. In 1803, he arranged to buy land from France for $15 million in the Louisiana Purchase. Although he had reservations about whether the purchase was constitutional, Jefferson doubled the size of America, gaining 828,000 square miles. Napoleon needed to sell the land to finance his European

wars, but the resumption of hostilities in Europe damaged American trade and the Embargo Act of 1807 wrecked the economy, backfiring on Jefferson, and he was beleaguered when he left office in 1809. Retiring to his estate at Monticello, Jefferson spent his retirement conducting prodigious volumes of correspondence and supervising the construction of the University of Virginia. In The Lost Symbol, the Jefferson Bible is mentioned as a controversial revisionist text. Thomas Jefferson spent 16 years preparing The Life and Morals of Jesus of Nazareth (known as the Jefferson Bible). He had come to believe that the teachings of Jesus had been corrupted by various interventions over the centuries, including those of medieval popes and corrupt priests. In his version of the Bible, Jefferson left out of the Gospels the miracles of Jesus and other parts he considered to be irrational. The text included the parables and teachings of Jesus and ended with his crucifixion and burial. Although Jefferson allowed some friends to see his work, it was never published in his lifetime. Outwardly Jefferson maintained the Anglican tradition, and when in Philadelphia he attended the Unitarian church. Writing to a Unitarian minister, Benjamin Waterhouse, he said, ‘I rejoice that in this blessed country of free enquiry and belief, which has surrendered its creed and conscience to neither kings nor priests, the genuine doctrine of only one God is reviving, and I trust there is not a young man now living who will not die a Unitarian.’ It was for Jefferson’s religious tolerance that Uriah P. Levy, a Jewish naval officer, gave to the nation a statue of Thomas Jefferson that was the first such artwork to be erected in the Rotunda of the Capitol Building. The statue, by Pierre-Jean David d’Angers, was presented in 1834 and is mentioned in The Lost Symbol. Levy also purchased Jefferson’s estate at Monticello in the same year and spent heavily to restore the property and open it to visitors. Another of Levy’s heroes was the Marquis de Lafayette. Thomas Jefferson had an abiding love of collecting books and acquired thousands of volumes on diverse topics, including science, the ancient world and philosophy. During his time in France, he collected extensively, supplementing his library at Monticello. After the Library of Congress was burned by the British in 1814, Jefferson offered to sell his collection, the largest private one in the United States, to Congress as a replacement. The transaction was arranged

the following year with 6,487 books involved. Jefferson said in a letter that ‘I do not know that it contains any branch of science which Congress would wish to exclude from this collection . . . there is in fact no subject to which a member of Congress may not have occasion to refer.’ When Jefferson’s old friend Lafayette visited America in 1824 he visited Monticello, and after thirty-five years the two men were reacquainted. Lafayette described Jefferson in his memoirs as ‘bearing marvelously well under his eighty-one years of age, in full possession of all the vigor of his mind and heart which he has consecrated to the building of a good and fine university’. This was the University of Virginia, which received its charter in 1819 and had been founded by Jefferson, who, as well as designing its buildings, including the famous Rotunda, arranged the curriculum. Among his many other achievements is something that Robert Langdon would no doubt know all about: Jefferson invented the wheel cipher, leading to his title ‘the Father of American Cryptography’. The wheel cipher comprised 26 wooden cylinders on a spindle, with the letters of the alphabet carved into the edge of each wheel. David Khan in The Codebreakers describes how ‘Jefferson’s wheel cipher was far and away the most advanced devised in its day. It seems to have come out of the blue rather than as a result of mature reflection upon cryptography.’ Thomas Jefferson died at his estate on (as befits the author of the Declaration of Independence) 4 July 1826. On the previous day, in his famous last recorded words, he had asked, ‘Is it the fourth?’ In recognition of his immense contribution to his country, Jefferson is one of the four presidents, along with George Washington, Theodore Roosevelt and Abraham Lincoln, to feature in the famous sculpture at Mount Rushmore. This colossal monument in South Dakota consists of 60-foot-high heads carved out of the granite mountain and symbolises elements of the first 150 years in the history of the United States. Jefferson takes his place among the great leaders of America for his role in enshrining the principles of democracy in the country and for the expansion westwards via the land purchase. The Jefferson Memorial was dedicated on 13 April 1943, 200 years after Jefferson’s birth. The design was based on the Rotunda at the University of Virginia, Jefferson’s own project, and the Pantheon in Rome. Three architects, John Russell Pope, Otto Eggers

and Daniel Higgins, were responsible for the design. The memorial sits due south of the White House and the Washington Monument, across the Potomac Tidal Basin. On the interior frieze of the dome is a quote from Jefferson: ‘I have sworn upon the altar of God eternal hostility against every kind of tyranny over the mind of man.’ On the dust jacket of the US edition of The Lost Symbol there is a sequence of numbers running around a circular design. For each number, if you turn to the corresponding chapter in the book (for example, if you select the number 22 then you should turn to Chapter 22) and identify the first letter of the alphabet that appears in that chapter (Chapter 22 begins with the word ‘pacing’, so take the letter ‘p’), the phrase spelled out by the sequence of numbers is ‘popes pantheon’, an allusion to the Jefferson Memorial and its architect John Russell Pope. Another prominent building in Washington DC designed by Pope was the House of the Temple, the Masonic temple that is the headquarters of Scottish Rite Freemasonry and the setting of a climactic showdown in The Lost Symbol. Continuing due north from the Jefferson Memorial, past the White House and up Sixteenth Street, you come to the House of the Temple. There has been speculation that, in common with many of the Founding Fathers, Jefferson may have been a Freemason. There seems to be no documentary evidence of his initiation into a lodge, although of course if this had happened in France during the Revolutionary period any records may have been lost. Though Thomas Jefferson may not have been a Freemason, it is undoubtedly true that many of his contemporaries, peers, friends and associates were indeed members of various lodges and societies. It is beyond doubt that Jefferson would have been exposed to these societies and that a man of his intellect and standing would have been intimately familiar with the rites, rituals and symbolism of many, if not all, of them. It is clear that Jefferson followed a path of deism, which suggests he might have been sympathetic towards and understanding of Freemasonic principles. SEE ALSO: House of the Temple

KRYPTOS Kryptos is a sculpture on display at CIA headquarters in Langley, Virginia, which hides an encrypted message. The sculpture comprises a number of components, including a large S-shaped metal scroll on which are stamped four blocks of text; granite slabs with copper Morse code messages; an engraved compass pointing to a lodestone; and a pool, amongst other features in the landscaped area. The materials used were polished red granite, quartz, copperplate, lodestone, mycanthus grasses, water and petrified wood. Kryptos means ‘hidden’ in Ancient Greek and indeed the sculpture contains a hidden message; in fact, there are several, though the artist has indicated that there is one overall solution to the sculpture, which is probably arrived at by unravelling all the disparate elements. The artist who created Kryptos is Jim Sanborn. Born in Washington DC in 1945, he was commissioned to create the work of art in 1988 and the piece was dedicated in 1990. He was paid $250,000 at its completion. Since then, code-breakers, including many CIA employees, have attempted to decipher the sculpture’s message. Sanborn had never designed such a complex piece before he worked on Kryptos; in fact, he knew hardly anything about cryptography. However, working closely with Ed Scheidt, a former head of Langley’s Cryptographic Center, he learned how to devise the complex code. Scheidt first schooled him in the art of code- making and code-breaking, teaching him all the techniques from the nineteenth century through to the Second World War. But it was Sanborn who came up with the final solution to the puzzle. Since the installation of the sculpture, three of the four panels on the main copper scroll, known as K1, K2 and K3, have been solved and the text revealed. K1 reads as follows (the spelling is said to be intentional): Between subtle shading and the absence of light lies the nuance of iqlusion K2 results in a longer message, in which ‘X’ indicates a line break:

It was totally invisible hows that possible? They used the earths magnetic field x the information was gathered and transmitted undergruund to an unknown location x does langley know about this? they should its buried out there somewhere x who knows the exact location? only ww this was his last message x thirty eight degrees fifty seven minutes six point five seconds north seventy seven degrees eight minutes forty four seconds west x layer two. K3 turns out to be a section of text from Howard Carter’s account of the moment when he and Lord Carnarvon first broke into the tomb of Tutankhamun in the Valley of the Kings in Egypt. The full text is: Slowly desparatly slowly the remains of passage debris that encumbered the lower part of the doorway was removed with trembling hands i made a tiny breach in the upper left hand corner and then widening the hole a little i inserted the candle and peered the hot air escaping from the chamber caused the flame to flicker but presently details of the room within emerged from the mist x can you see anything q (?) The final section of the text, K4, a sequence of 97 characters, has still not been solved, some 19 years after the artwork was installed. A group of determined code-breakers have assembled on the Internet to form a community devoted to solving the final K4 panel of Kryptos and it now numbers 1,300. They make concerted efforts to crack the code together and agree to make a joint announcement should any of the group find a solution. Some of the Morse code messages on other sections of the sculpture read: SOS, T is your position, shadow forces and virtually invisible. It is thought that the coordinates in the K2 section of Kryptos point to a location just south-east of the sculpture and seem to suggest that something is buried there. To paraphrase the solution of K2: ‘The information was gathered and transmitted underground to an

unknown location . . . Does Langley know about this . . . They should, it’s buried out there somewhere . . . Who knows the exact location? Only WW.’ This, together with the coordinates, makes it a very intriguing puzzle, almost as dramatic as a Dan Brown thriller. The truth is that the meaning ‘hidden’ within the sculpture does not just relate to the code. When we combine the tantalising clues from the decoded message with the extract detailing Howard Carter’s uncovering of the tomb, it becomes likely that the sculpture is pointing to a hidden artefact. However, until the fourth section of the copper screen is decoded we will have to wait to find out what exactly Kryptos leads to. We do know who ‘WW’ refers to, though. At the time Kryptos was installed, William Webster was the director of the CIA. Sanborn said he had been given the solution to the sculpture’s codes (although he has since claimed that Webster does not have the full solution). At the beginning of The Lost Symbol, Dan Brown tells us in one of his facts that there is a document locked in a safe in the CIA headquarters that relates to a hidden artefact. So we wait until someone manages to crack the mystery of Kryptos and solve the whole puzzle. However, we may be in for a long wait. In an interview in 2009 with Wired magazine, Scheidt, the cryptographer who tutored Sanborn, said, ‘There may be more to the puzzle than what you see. Just because you broke it doesn’t mean you have the answer.’ This suggests that there may be more layers to the puzzle that need to be solved, even when all four sections of the text have been deciphered. Before its publication there had been speculation that Kryptos would feature heavily in The Lost Symbol; however, it plays only a minor role in the finished book and is by no means central to the plot. The question of whether this was due to Jim Sanborn’s preference that the sculpture be omitted from the storyline is open to speculation. Snippets of the deciphered Kryptos code were actually featured on the US cover of Dan Brown’s previous novel featuring Robert Langdon, The Da Vinci Code. Due to the popularity of The Da Vinci Code clues and now The Lost Symbol, one thing is certain: there are now likely to be many more people wanting to get involved in solving the puzzle of Kryptos. And in answer to the question posed in the section of Kryptos known as K3 ...
Yes, it is wonderful. SEE ALSO: CIA – Office of Security

L’ENFANT, PIERRE An architect named Pierre Charles L’Enfant was originally responsible for the geometrical layout of the city of Washington, which was later adjusted by George Washington and Thomas Jefferson along with Andrew Ellicott. He was the planner who is credited by Dan Brown early in The Lost Symbol with adorning the capital city with Masonic symbolism. Shortly afterwards, Brown avers that poor Pierre’s ghost has been seen manifesting itself in the Capitol Building, trying to collect payment of his bill, now rather overdue, having awaited settlement for more than 200 years. Brown also speaks of L’Enfant, along with George Washington and Benjamin Franklin, as Master Freemasons. It is mentioned elsewhere in this book that many of Washington DC’s monumental buildings were dedicated by Freemasons in accordance with their ceremonies. So who was this man with the French name who is mentioned in such august company? Pierre Charles L’Enfant was born in Paris in 1754. His father taught at the French Royal Academy of Painting and Sculpture, and young Pierre studied there under him. In 1776, he enrolled as a volunteer in the American Revolutionary Army and travelled to America with the Marquis de Lafayette. Lafayette, despite his own aristocratic background, was committed to the cause of American independence and was commissioned by Congress as a major general, becoming a firm friend of George Washington. It is well attested that the Marquis de Lafayette was a Freemason. At the Masonic Temple in Philadelphia there is an apron given by Lafayette to Washington. It is replete with symbolism, including the pillars of Boaz and Jachin and the all-seeing eye. L’Enfant was wounded at the Siege of Savannah and subsequently served on George Washington’s staff as an engineer. The fledgling Congress appointed him a Major of Engineers in 1783 in tribute to his service. He was responsible for the design of a medal and diploma for a company of one-time officers in the Revolutionary Army who called themselves the Society of the Cincinnati in reference to Cincinnatus, a legendary Roman patriot of early republican times. Returning to France, L’Enfant assisted in forming a French branch of this society,

the purpose of which was, and still is, to keep alive the ideals of the officers who took part in the Revolutionary War. When designing the insignia for the medal and diploma mentioned above, L’Enfant suggested that a bald eagle should feature prominently, on the grounds that it ‘is peculiar to this continent, and is distinguished from those of other climates by its white head and tail [so it] appears to me to deserve attention’. L’Enfant went back to America in 1784, making a living as an architect and doing work for Congress. One odd project he undertook around this time was Morris House in Philadelphia, which was a flamboyant folly and never completed. Robert Morris had commissioned a substantial dwelling, but the architect was so ambitious that it became obvious that the whole concept was far too extravagant. In 1788, L’Enfant was employed to transform City Hall in New York into a building fit to house the infant federal government. To symbolise the newly independent 13 states, he used an eagle holding 13 arrows, as well as 13 stars and rays. Congress decided that a new capital city for a new seat of government should be constructed, and accordingly President Washington engaged L’Enfant to draw up plans for official approval. Pierre L’Enfant knew, of course, that the ideal city of the classical world had been one based on a grid system, and decided that the young United States, with its political principles drawn from the great civilisations of Greece and Rome, should have such a city. His streets were therefore arranged on a gridiron plan, forming irregular rectangular blocks. The centres of attraction were to be the President’s dwelling and the Capitol Building, and the squares in their vicinity would afford spaces in which to place monuments and water features. Thomas Jefferson, then Secretary of State, obtained maps of selected European cities to provide inspiration to L’Enfant. The works of outstanding designers such as Christopher Wren in England and André Le Nôtre in France were drawn upon. Unfortunately, L’Enfant allowed his understanding of the importance of his brief to develop into an overweening sense of his own importance. He would not accept as mandatory the instructions he received from the city commissioners, even when he was ordered to do so by the President. His schemes were considered impossibly grandiose and his ruthless action in having the house of an influential citizen demolished because he wanted to put an

avenue there was resented. It must have been difficult for George Washington, who was living in Philadelphia during his Presidency, to keep a restraining hand on his friend L’Enfant, who was displaying his volatile temperament in the future Washington DC. The President had, it must be recalled, been a brother in arms with him. Pierre L’Enfant threatened to resign and the President had, in the end, little alternative but to dismiss him. Andrew Ellicott was called in to take over the project, and it is largely his work that can be seen today. In 1812, the United States Military Academy offered L’Enfant the chair of Professor of Engineering, but for some reason he turned the job down. Two years later, he did a little work on the building of Fort Washington, situated on the Potomac River, but within a short time he was replaced. After a while, L’Enfant claimed more than $95,000 for work produced before his dismissal from the Washington job. Congress paid him just less than $4,000, telling him it was all his efforts had been worth. He lived on in Maryland, with friends, apparently without a penny to his name. Presumably it was the missing $91,000 that his ghost was searching for in the Capitol Building. In 1909, his remains were reinterred at Arlington National Cemetery in a monument granted rather belatedly to him by Congress. Perhaps he is now at peace. The argument that the layout of Washington DC was inspired by Freemasonic principles relies in large part on Pierre L’Enfant having been a Freemason. There seems to be no documentary proof that he was, and no Lodge claims him as a former member. On the other hand, two of his mentors, the Marquis de Lafayette and George Washington, were Freemasons, and growing up in the 1760s and 1770s in France, he would certainly have been familiar with Freemasonic principles. Pierre L’Enfant’s plans for the layout of the city are displayed on a grand scale on the pavement of Freedom Plaza, as described elsewhere in this book. Even as late as 1990, at the completion of the Washington National Cathedral, aspects of the original vision of Pierre L’Enfant were being realised, as it was he who first proposed a ‘great church for national purposes’. SEE ALSO: Freedom Plaza, Washington DC

LIBRARY OF CONGRESS Having escaped the clutches of the CIA, Robert Langdon and his rescuer, Warren Bellamy, arrive at the Library of Congress via a tunnel from the Capitol Building. Once inside, they pass through the Great Hall and into the Main Reading Room, which Bellamy promises will be safe. Despite his desperation at the turn of events, Langdon pauses to consider the room’s splendour, reflecting that it is possibly the most amazing room in the world. The Library of Congress dates back to 1800, when an act of Congress made $5,000 available for the provision of ‘such books as may be necessary for the use of Congress’. These were to be housed within the original Capitol Building in ‘a suitable apartment for containing them therein’. However, following the American defeat at the Battle of Bladensburg on 24 August 1814, British troops entered Washington, burning and looting many public buildings, including the Capitol, and in the process destroyed 3,000 volumes from the library’s collection. To alleviate the loss, former president Thomas Jefferson offered to sell his extensive personal collection of 6,487 books to Congress for whatever they wished to pay, writing, ‘I do not know that it contains any branch of science which Congress would wish to exclude from their collection.’ Eventually, Congress agreed to purchase Jefferson’s library for $23,950, thus forming the basis of the new collection. Unfortunately, another fire, on Christmas Eve 1851, destroyed 35,000 titles, including 4,324 from Jefferson’s original collection. Although more funds were forthcoming from Congress to enhance the collection once more, it was not until the library came under the auspices of Ainsworth Rand Spofford, librarian of Congress from 1864 to 1897, that the collection expanded considerably, aided by the 1870 copyright law, which stated that two copies of every copyrighted book or other printed material had to be sent to the Library of Congress. The resulting influx soon necessitated a move to a larger, purpose-built building, with work on its construction beginning in 1892. Built in the Renaissance style, the Thomas Jefferson Building has been called ‘the largest, the costliest, and the safest’ library building in the world. The library is the research facility for Congress, its official mission statement being to make its resources available and useful

to the Congress and the American people and to sustain and preserve a universal collection of knowledge and creativity for future generations. In terms of the size of its collection, the library is the largest in the world, having nearly 142 million items, with over 32 million books and 62 million manuscripts housed in more than 650 miles of bookshelves. Each day a staggering 10,000 items are added to the library’s collection, mainly due to the copyright requirement. To house all of the library’s departments and resources, the facility now spreads over three buildings on Capitol Hill – the Thomas Jefferson Building, the John Adams Building (built in 1938) and the James Madison Memorial Building (opened in 1981). As well as the library, other resources include the Office of the Librarian, the Congressional Research Service, the US Copyright Office and the Law Library of Congress, which alone holds over three million volumes. The original and most famous building of the Library of Congress – and the one in which Langdon finds himself – is the magnificent Thomas Jefferson Building. Its exterior is rectangular, inset with a T-shaped structure that forms the Great Hall and the Main Reading Room. The Great Hall’s interior is opulently finished in Italian marble, with a marble floor inlaid with brass to form a sun surrounded by the 12 signs of the zodiac. Above this the stucco ceiling is decorated with gold leaf, whilst the roof ‘s panelled beams are embellished with aluminium leaf and set between stained-glass windows. Looking down on the hall are eight statues of Minerva, the Roman goddess of learning and wisdom, in her guises as Minerva of War and Minerva of Peace. Minerva was the Roman version of the Greek goddess Athena, many images of whom are to be found in Washington DC. A large mosaic depicting Minerva stands in the Great Hall. This was executed by artist Elihu Vedder, who had strong Masonic and Rosicrucian connections. The Great Hall is decorated with many examples of the trades and hobbies of Americans in 1897, when the building was completed. The two grand staircases are decorated with cherub-like small children (putti) in various guises, among them a gardener complete with gardening tools and a physician with a vessel, mortar and the Asclepius serpent of medicine. A mechanic, entomologist, farmer and cook, to name but a few, are also in attendance.

The East Corridor pays particular homage to America’s important role in scientific discoveries and advancements, the arts, humanities, law and medicine. It is here that Langdon passes the bulletproof display cabinets containing the Gutenberg Bible, the first printed book, and the handwritten Giant Bible of Mainz, both of which were produced in Germany in the 1450s. Just below the ceiling are six paintings by John White Alexander entitled The Evolution of the Book, highlighting the stages of human development that led to the appearance of the printed word. Leading off from the Great Hall, the Main Reading Room provides access to the library’s general collection of 70,000 volumes and is a free resource open upon registration to anyone over the age of 16. This most striking room is octagonal in shape, reaching up 160 feet to its domed roof. Around the octagon, eight marble columns each support a plaster statue of a woman, symbolising art, commerce, history, law, philosophy, poetry, religion and science. The eight stained-glass windows in the archways beneath the dome represent the forty-eight state seals of the United States (Hawaii and Alaska were not part of the USA when the building was constructed). Around the galleries above are 16 bronze statues of men who exemplify the human endeavours represented by the eight female statues. Art is embodied by Michelangelo and Ludwig van Beethoven; commerce by Christopher Columbus and Robert Fulton; history by Herodotus and Edward Gibbon; law by Solon and James Kent; philosophy by Plato and Sir Francis Bacon; poetry by Homer and William Shakespeare; religion by Moses and St Paul; and science by Sir Isaac Newton and Joseph Henry. It is the statue of Moses, complete with horns, that leads Langdon to consider the mistranslation of the Bible (Exodus 34:29) by St Jerome. In error, the passage ‘his face was radiant’, meaning he was glorified/enlightened by being in the presence of God, was mistaken for ‘his face was horned’, hence the depictions of Moses ever since. The architectural and decorative grandeur continue through into the library’s other rooms and galleries set on the building’s two floors. They include the Members of Congress Room, the Jefferson Congressional Reading Room, the Asian Reading Room, the European Reading Room and the American Folklife Center, amongst many others. The Rare Books and Special Collections Reading Room has a collection of some 650,000 books and other printed materials,

including medieval manuscripts, 3,000 of which were bought by Congress from a personal collection that included the famous Gutenberg Bible, one of only three in existence. An important part of the rare book collection is on show in the Jefferson Collection exhibition. Since 1998, the library has replaced more than 4,000 of the titles lost in the destruction of 1814 by scouring the library’s records, Jefferson’s personal papers and correspondence, and other historical sources in order to collate a list of Jefferson’s original books so that the library can obtain the exact same editions that Jefferson had collected. SEE ALSO: Thomas Jefferson

MCTAGGART, LYNNE Lynne McTaggart is mentioned in The Lost Symbol because her book The Intention Experiment is cited as a work that inspired Katherine Solomon to continue pursuing her research within the field of Noetic science. A journalist and author, McTaggart has written five books to date, two of which are bestsellers, The Field and The Intention Experiment. She also runs the much-lauded What Doctors Don’t Tell You health journal, launched in 1989 on the premise of creating a truly independent journal, free from the influence of major pharmaceutical companies and government bodies. However, it is probably for the body of work known as the Intention Experiment that McTaggart is most well known. This represents not just the book by that name, but also an active Internet community of volunteers which McTaggart has put together with her husband, Bryan Hubbard, and a team of scientists. They often conduct Web- based experiments and pool the collective power of their minds to achieve specific aims. We discover in The Lost Symbol that Katherine Solomon’s research has already proven that focused thought can affect any living organisms, including the growth rate of plants. This chapter seems to have been based precisely on the work of McTaggart and her team and mirrors an experiment carried out by the Intention Experiment group. The series of experiments in question was known as the Water Germination Experiments and took place in June and July 2008. McTaggart asked an audience in Hamburg, Germany, to choose a bottle of water out of four samples, the aim being to add the chosen bottle to a selection of seeds that were to be germinated. With a bottle chosen, the audience was instructed to send out the following intention to the water: ‘My intention is that all the seeds given water from our target jar will sprout at least three inches by the fourth day of growing.’ The results after five days showed that the seeds that had been given the chosen water sample grew higher than the other samples that had received ordinary water. Also, in the test sample 100 per cent of the seeds had germinated, while in normal cases only 90 per cent would be expected to germinate. The experiment was deemed

a success. Since 2008, larger experiments have been conducted, involving much bigger groups of people sending out their intentions. The largest such experiment was the Peace Intention Experiment, with a significantly sized ‘group mind’ of participants connected via the Internet trying to focus on bringing lasting peace to the north section of Sri Lanka. Analysts believe the experiment worked, as there was a dramatic decrease in the amount of violence in the area in the weeks following the exercise. The description of McTaggart’s work in The Lost Symbol seems to be accurate and McTaggart has welcomed her surprise inclusion in the book, commenting: ‘Using the world’s bestselling book as a platform to introduce the idea of the power of thought to an entirely new audience will help to promote the work of consciousness research.’ She also made the following illuminating comments, highlighting some of the remarkable aspects of her ongoing work: Intention improves through practice of learned techniques. I interviewed dozens of ‘masters of intentions’ – Qigong masters, Buddhist monks, master healers – and they all discussed particular learned techniques they learned to use to focus their intention . . . To manifest an intention requires laser-like focus, a full sensory visualisation and a profound belief ... Particles are affected by the observer. This is a fundamental principle of quantum physics: observing a subatomic particle turns that potential something into something real. This is probably the most fascinating aspect of McTaggart’s work – that it is our interaction with the material realm, our consciousness itself, that affects the physical world around us. One of the puzzles thrown up by quantum physics is the behaviour of matter at the quantum level. If minute particles of matter can be in all places at once, what is it that actually forces them to appear in one location and act as solid matter? McTaggart’s science provides a tentative answer: it is our living consciousness, our role as observer, that influences those tiny pieces of matter,

somehow coalescing them into being. This throws up more questions than it answers. For example, does this perhaps prove the idea that we all create our own universe? If each of us influences the behaviour of quantum particles and literally brings them into being, then can we be sure we share the same universe with other observers? Perhaps we really do all create our own private universes that are unique to us. As Katherine hints in The Lost Symbol, maybe we really are all masters of our own universe.

MAGIC SQUARES For a symbologist like Robert Langdon, solving puzzles and cracking codes is second nature, and interestingly Dan Brown’s own father was a mathematician. Brown has described how he was often set codes to solve as a child. In much the same way that we relax now with crosswords or number puzzles, it appears that for centuries people have taken pleasure in manipulating numbers for fun. The creation of so-called magic squares has taken place in many civilizations and their ingenuity is appealing on many levels. In essence, in a magic square the rows, columns and diagonal lines of numbers all add up to the same figure. The complexity can be deepened by including a wraparound level or by considering the grid as a cube. The numbers used to create the square are usually sequential, for example in a 3x3 grid they will be the numbers one to nine. The Lo Shu square is thought to date from around 650 bc and is a 3x3 (‘order 3’) grid, where all the axes add up to the number 15. In Chinese literature, the legend of the Lo Shu square tells of a series of grids containing dots that were seen on the back of a tortoise that was observed near the River Lo. The Kubera Kolam is a variation on the Lo Shu square, in that 19 has been added to each number, so the digits are 20 to 29 and the magic total is 72. The Kubera Kolam, mentioned by Dan Brown in the novel, is a pattern, generally made of rice flour, that is commonly laid out each day on the floor of a house in India and thought to bring prosperity to the home. Magic squares are also found in Arab works from the tenth century AD. They were published in an encyclopedia in modern-day Iraq that has the first examples of grids of the orders 5 and 6. The

Rasa’il Ihkwan al’Safa, as this encyclopedia is known, was linked to a group known as the Brethren of Purity. The Masonic researcher Chris McClintock, in his Sun of God thesis, has recently suggested that these Brethren were a conduit between ancient teachings and modern-day Freemasonry. The first magic square that Langdon encounters in The Lost Symbol is the 4x4 grid depicted by Albrecht Dürer in his picture Melencolia I. In this square, there is the additional element that the date of the picture’s creation, 1514, is depicted in two adjacent squares on the bottom row. Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, a writer of Renaissance esoteric material, produced his De occulta philosophia between 1509 and 1510, and in the three books that make up the work he includes a series of magic squares. In contrast to modern opinions that the study of the occult, or magic, would be irreligious, Agrippa claimed that the best way for man to know God and nature was through the study of magic. In the third book of the De occulta philosophia, Agrippa reveals the name of Jesus to contain the power of the Tetragrammaton. Agrippa constructed a series of magic squares, each one relating to one of the planets and known as kameas. There is another layer of mystery added when a name or word is translated from letters to numbers and its shape traced around the position of the numbers in the kamea. The resulting pattern, when produced for magical purposes, is one example of a sigil, a symbol made up of different mystical elements, and we are told in The Lost Symbol that the character Mal’akh has a number of sigils tattooed on his body. Benjamin Franklin produced an 8x8 grid that forms a central puzzle in The Lost Symbol, enabling Langdon to solve the arrangement of 64 symbols that forms the map pointing to the location of the ‘lost’ symbol. The grid arranged by Franklin has the rows and columns adding up to 260. Unlike many other magic squares, the diagonal rows do not add up to 260; possibly more impressive, however, are the ‘bent rows’ of eight adjacent squares that equal the total. The realisation that it is Franklin’s mathematical square that is being referred to occurs after the clue ‘eight Franklin Square’ is first mistaken for an address, which would have pointed to the building of a Masonic group commonly called the Shriners, the Almas Shrine Temple, located facing Franklin Square in Washington DC.

Franklin wrote that he himself had been ‘induc’d to amuse myself with making magic squares, or circles’ when trying to relieve himself of boredom. Given his many other accomplishments, we may wonder where this spare time came from, though Franklin is also famous for producing a 16x16 magic square, a phenomenal undertaking. Franklin wrote in a letter: Being one day in the country at the house of our common friend, the late learned Mr Logan, he showed me a folio French book, filled with magic squares, wrote, if I forget not, by one M. Frenicle . . . he did not recollect that any one Englishman had distinguished themselves in the same way. Does this account for the fact that the UK cover of The Lost Symbol does not contain the magic square puzzle present on the back of the US edition? In a replica of the Dürer square that Brown has trained his readers to solve within the novel is the message: ‘Your Mind is the Key’. Considering the discussion towards the end of the novel between Langdon and Katherine Solomon on the power of human thought and the mind of man receiving enlightenment, this would seem to be a message close to Dan Brown’s heart. SEE ALSO: Albrecht Dürer, Benjamin Franklin, Melencolia I, Shriners

MELENCOLIA I In their search for a clue to the meaning of the puzzle they are trying to solve, the protagonists in The Lost Symbol are given a date, 1514, and what is described as a symbature. This is a symbol used in place of a signature, and the initials ‘A’ and ‘D’ are recognised as belonging to the artist Albrecht Dürer. Further intuition leads them to a famous engraving by Dürer, created in 1514, his Melencolia I. Although the engraving is in the National Gallery in Washington DC, the chase does not require Langdon to view the actual picture. Using an image on a computer screen, he finds the essential element of the design for their code-breaking purposes is revealed as a magic square containing 16 numbers. To admire the work in all its complexity, turn to the plate section in this book. Entire books and theses have been devoted to trying to explain the elements within the engraving and the concepts that Dürer was trying to express. One of his most enigmatic and studied works, Melencolia I is unusual in having the title presented on the plate – the archaic spelling of Melencolia is on a banner being held by a creature which is a rodent/bat/snake hybrid. Dürer has included elements of the science of alchemy and this painting is full of symbolic reference to that practice. For instance, the rainbow in the background of Melencolia I represents the colours that supposedly appeared during preparation of the Philosopher’s Stone, the instrument needed to transmute base metals, such as lead, into gold. It was also reputed to have the power to change people from their mortal to an immortal state. Other items of an alchemical nature and paraphernalia can be seen in the picture, including a crucible, a sphere, woodworking tools, scales and compasses. Dürer’s Melencolia I is in many ways a compendium of symbolism, and the faint image of a skull on the face of the polyhedron further compounds the mystery. Since the Roman numeral I follows the title of this picture, it seems likely that it was intended to be the first of a series. This series may have been planned to include four works, since melancholy is one of the four temperaments possessed by different types of people. The other three are choleric, phlegmatic and sanguine. The temperaments link to the four humours – black bile, yellow bile, phlegm and blood – and also to the four elements and

the planets. Physicians, scientists, philosophers and all those at that time interested in the human condition would have been familiar with, and influenced by, this accepted knowledge. The word melancholia actually means ‘black bile’ and it was believed that persons who had an imbalance of this in their bodies would be of a melancholic disposition as a result. Melancholy was linked to the earth and to the planet Saturn. Another suggestion has been made that a series of three Melencolias could have been planned, each depicting one of the three elements of the soul described by Aristotle: the imagination, the rational and the mental. In analysing the image, Frances Yates explains in The Occult Philosophy in the Elizabethan Age: Dürer’s Melancholy has a livid hue, the swarthy complexion, the ‘black face’ of the type, and she supports her pensive head on her hand in the characteristic pose. She holds compasses for measuring and numbering. Beside her is the purse, for counting money. Around her are tools, such as an artisan might use. Obviously she is melancholic, characterised by the physical type, pose, and occupations of the old, bad, melancholy, but she seems also to express some more lofty and intellectual type of endeavour. She is not actually doing anything, just sitting and thinking. What do those geometrical forms mean, and why does a ladder rise heavenward behind the polyhedron? So, is the image a metaphor for wasted genius? It seems that in every age great talent and ability is often linked to mental instability or torment. From the fragile genius of Mozart and the extravagant lifestyle of the poet Byron to the destructive behaviour of many rock stars, the idea of the tormented genius is one familiar to us all. This seems to be the suggestion of Klibansky, Panofsky and Saxl in Saturn and Melancholy: The humour melancholicus, when it takes fire and glows, generates the frenzy (furore) which leads us to wisdom and revelation, especially when it is

combined with a heavenly influence, above all with that of Saturn ... Therefore Aristotle says in the Problemata that through melancholy some men have become divine beings, foretelling the future like Sybils . . . while others have become poets . . . and he says further that all men who have been distinguished in any branch of knowledge have generally been melancholics. Dürer could be showing us the inside of his mind. Mary Heaton certainly speculated thus as long ago as 1870 in her book The History of the Life of Albrecht Dürer of Nürnberg: Perhaps his own soul’s wings had beaten in vain against the impassable wall that bounds our mental horizon, before he drew those wings that spring from her powerful shoulders, and seem a mere mockery in the cramped position in which she is placed. What are we to make of Dan Brown’s choice of the artist Dürer and this engraving in The Lost Symbol? Robert Langdon is certainly very learned and intelligent and shows great resourcefulness in tackling the predicaments that the author conjures up for him. Despite these qualities, Langdon remains a character who finds it difficult to believe. He says himself, ‘faith has never come easily to me’. This is the man who found the Holy Grail and saved Rome from certain destruction. Here is a depiction of someone waiting for the spark of inspiration to lighten the gloom, an echo of the tortured genius who resides in a melancholic inner world but who has incredible creativity and that ignition of brilliance when needed. Is it possible that Brown himself not only identifies with his lead character, Robert Langdon, but also with these melancholic, tortured geniuses that he features in his novels? SEE ALSO: Alchemy, Albrecht Dürer, Philosopher’s Stone

NEWTON, SIR ISAAC Isaac Newton was born in Lincolnshire on 25 December 1642 and received a knighthood from Queen Anne in 1705. He was an outstanding example of a polymath, possessing a deep understanding and skill across many fields of learning, any one of which would have been sufficient to satisfy an ordinary person. Newton, as we will see, was in no way ordinary. He studied physics, mathematics and astronomy, theology, aspects of philosophy and the arcane subject of alchemy. Readers of Dan Brown’s The Da Vinci Code will already be well acquainted with Newton, whose tomb in Westminster Abbey provided a clue on the quest for the Holy Grail. Now, in The Lost Symbol, we encounter several further references to Isaac Newton in connection with a scale-of-temperature measurement and his studies as an alchemist. In 1661, Newton was admitted to Trinity College, Cambridge, on a work-and-study basis. He much preferred to absorb the ideas of the more modern philosophers and astronomers than to dedicate his time, as was then the norm, to Aristotelian teachings. He graduated in 1665, the year of the Great Plague, and returned as a fellow of the college two years later. In popular legend, he discovered the nature of gravity while sitting under an apple tree when a piece of fruit dropped onto his head. In his words, he simply observed an apple falling. Whatever actually happened, he pondered the fact that objects fall towards the earth in our everyday experience and over the course of many years formulated his law of universal gravitation. In the last century, this was superseded by Einstein’s theory of general relativity, but it is still accepted as an approximation, except in the case of massive objects or where ultimate accuracy is required. Newton’s law appeared in his Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica, published in 1687, which triggered a tremendous argument with Robert Hooke, another brilliant scientist, who claimed that his own research had been hijacked. However, Newton gave credit to earlier scientists such as Copernicus, Brahe, Galileo and Kepler, saying, ‘If I have seen further, it is by standing on the shoulders of giants.’ Following Aristotle, it had always been taught that light was

white. Newton was the first to dare to contradict this received wisdom when he was bold enough to point out that in fact sunlight shining through a prism breaks up into a whole spectrum of colours. Since he wrongly assumed from this discovery that telescopes with refracting lenses would cause problems, he proceeded to invent the reflecting telescope.
