Towards the end of the seventeenth century, Newton turned his thoughts towards measuring temperature, when he devised a thermometer using the Newton scale, which had 33 degrees as its boiling point. Beginning by theorising about describing heat in terms degrees ranging from cold winter air to glowing coals, which was clearly not going very far in determining a scale, he then decided to heat linseed oil and compare its volume between that at the temperature of melting snow and that at water’s boiling point. The Swedish scientist Anders Celsius had probably heard about Newton’s invention and produced his own temperature scale, almost exactly three times larger. Both have zero degrees for freezing, but Newton’s 33-degree boiling point corresponds to 100 degrees Celsius. The Celsius scale is used today (sometimes called Centigrade), since it is more practical, while Newton’s will have been unfamiliar to most readers of The Lost Symbol. The immersion of a pyramid into boiling water to reveal a luminescent message moves the plot along and provides another link with the symbolism associated with the number 33. Newton had a great interest in religion, although he was an unorthodox Christian. His own father died before Isaac was born and his mother subsequently married a clergyman, with whom he was not on good terms. He admitted threatening to burn their house down at some point during his youth, and it is possible that his faith was coloured by his attitude towards his stepfather. It is said that Newton accepted the Arian heresy; Arian beliefs included that Jesus was not of the same substance as God the Father and that there had been a time when Jesus did not exist. Studying closely the texts in the Bible, looking in particular for scientific information, he wrote religious tracts, believing that he was one of those chosen by God to shine light on the meaning of the scriptures. He said, ‘I have a fundamental belief in the Bible as the word of God, written by those who were inspired.’ Unpublished documents written by him prophesy that the end of

the world will come in 2060, or alternatively that a new world will be created that will be blessed with divine peace. Six years after Newton’s death, Observations Upon the Prophesies of Daniel and the Apocalypse of St John, his important work on the Bible, was published. When the motto Jeova Sanctus Unus, i.e. one true God, is revealed in The Lost Symbol, Robert Langdon explains that this provided a pseudonym for Newton. In Latin (where the ‘i’ is substituted for a ‘j’ and the ‘u’ and ‘v’ are interchangeable), Isaacus Neutonuus is an anagram of Jeova Sanctus Unus. This signature was used by Newton when writing to friends about alchemical topics and exchanging documents so that he did not risk his identity being known. Dan Brown also makes an allusion to a legend regarding Isaac Newton’s dog, Diamond, who reputedly tipped over a candle and started a fire that destroyed important documents. In the novel, Peter Solomon’s dog, Hercules, eats a precious seventeenth-century illuminated vellum copy of the Bible belonging to Langdon. While there is no direct evidence that Sir Isaac Newton was a Freemason, there are suggestions that he may well have been a member of the craft. According to some, he was the Master of the mysterious Priory of Sion between 1691 and 1727. He was a member of the Spalding Gentlemen’s Society, a learned society that has included among its members Lord Tennyson, Sir Hans Sloane, Sir Joseph Banks and Alexander Pope. He was clearly interested in subjects such as the importance of Noah, which Masons also find significant, but despite Newton’s fame and prestige no Masonic lodge appears to claim him as a past member. It is known that Newton was interested in alchemy, which could have been highly dangerous during his lifetime. Penalties were very severe for someone dabbling in the subject – public execution being one. His papers suggest that the Philosopher’s Stone (a necessary tool) and the Elixir of Life (a supposed universal solvent) were two holy grails he might have sought. James Frazier in his book Contested Iconography explains the delay in publishing Newton’s alchemical work: In an effort designed to protect Newton’s image and standing, the deliberate suppression of his alchemical endeavors began almost immediately following his death . . . The alchemical and

theological manuscripts were bundled together and marked by Dr Pellet as being unsuitable for publication. This included texts and manuscripts on alchemy and theology totaling in excess of two million four hundred thousand words. Newton also claimed to have discovered differential calculus separately from Gottfried Liebniz, another polymath. A quarrelsome fellow, Newton claimed that the German had stolen his ideas. This dispute, and the ongoing arguments with Robert Hooke and others, show a side to his character that is not particularly attractive. Newton was also a poor teacher, apparently, since his students avoided his lectures. Humphrey Newton, a distant relative, wrote in a letter: ‘So few went to hear him, and fewer that understood him, that oft times he did in a manner, for want of hearers, read to the walls.’ Clearly students could not keep up with the capacity of his mind, and he would have preferred to be away from them, doing his own research. Newton had a great interest in the learning of ancient peoples, particularly the Egyptians. In The Chronology of Ancient Kingdoms, Amended, he reported that the study of astrology had begun in Egypt under the guidance of the priests. The measurements of the Egyptians, and the cubit especially, were subject to his analysis. Among his other activities, he held the posts of Warden and Master of the Royal Mint, beginning in 1696. With his typical vigour, he embarked upon a campaign against forgery, which was rife at the time, though another capital offence. He was Master of the Mint until the end of his life. He was also a member of the Royal Society, and its president from 1703 until his death, and a Member of Parliament from 1689 to 1690, and again in 1701. Sir Isaac Newton died on 20 March 1727. He is buried in Westminster Abbey in London; he was the first scientist to be interred there, a singular honour. The economist Maynard Keynes, who purchased a large part of Newton’s manuscript collection, said in a speech to the Royal Society in 1942, ‘Newton was not the first of the age of reason. He was the last of the magicians.’ SEE ALSO: Alchemy, Philosopher’s Stone

NUMBER SYMBOLISM Numbers feature prominently in The Lost Symbol, whether in the form of magic squares, the encoded location of rooms beneath the Capitol Building or dates from history that act as the key to secret codes. The number that plays the most significant role in Dan Brown’s novel is 33. The most obvious examples are the references to 33rd-degree Masons, the highest degree within Scottish Rite Freemasonry. The emblem of this degree comprises a double-headed eagle, the phrase ‘Ordo Ab Chao’ (order from chaos), which is referred to often in The Lost Symbol, and the number 33 within a pyramid. It is this that features on Peter Solomon’s ring. In Freemasonry, the number 33 is very special indeed and its significance in the brotherhood has long been debated and discussed. Manly P. Hall shed some light on the meaning of the 33 degrees or stages of Freemasonry in The Secret Teachings of All Ages. His conflation of the central Freemasonic figure of Hiram with concepts from Hindu mysticism is simply staggering: Sufficient similarity exists between the Masonic Hiram and the Kundalini of Hindu mysticism to warrant the assumption that Hiram may be considered a symbol also of the Spirit Fire moving through the sixth ventricle of the spinal column. The exact science of human regeneration is the Lost Key of Masonry, for when the Spirit Fire is lifted up through the thirty-three degrees, or segments of the spinal column, and enters into the domed chamber of the human skull, it finally passes into the pituitary body (Isis), where it invokes Ra (the pineal gland) and demands the Sacred Name. Operative Masonry, in the fullest meaning of that term, signifies the process by which the Eye of Horus is opened. The human spine contains 33 segments and Dan Brown seems to have been aware of this connection between the 33 degrees of Masonry and the spinal column, because Mal’akh has a tattoo of a

staircase on his back, with each stair resting on a vertebra as it ascends to the base of his skull. Katherine Solomon tells Robert Langdon at the end of The Lost Symbol that the spine is Jacob’s ladder and the skull is the true temple. Although there are 33 degrees of Scottish Rite Freemasonry, in effect, there are only 32 degrees to work through, the 33rd being an honorary degree. This is fascinating because there are 32 Paths of Wisdom in the Tree of Life of the Kabbalah, the mystical branch of Judaism. Thirty-two also equates with the number of mentions of God in Chapter One of the Book of Genesis in the Torah. When someone successfully completes all 32 Paths of Wisdom, they attain enlightenment, which could be thought of as the final 33rd Path. Langdon tells us that the worship of the number 33 had its origins long ago in Ancient Greece. The great mathematician Pythagoras described the number 33 as the most important of what he called the ‘master numbers’: 11, 22, 33 and 44. We will return to Pythagoras and his obsession with the symbolism of numbers later. Many believe Jesus was crucified at the age of 33. He began his ministry at the age of thirty and died three years later in ad 33 (if we believe that our calendar started precisely at the time of the birth of Jesus). Furthermore, and more importantly in the context of Freemasonry, Solomon’s Temple in Jerusalem, the First Temple of the Jews, stood for 33 years. King David was said to have ruled for 33 years in Jerusalem. Sir Francis Bacon, author of The New Atlantis, used a secret cipher number that also just happened to be 33, which was the numerical value of his name based on sacred numerology. The number has occurred again and again in religious, occultic and esoteric teachings throughout history. The House of the Temple in Washington, the location of the climactic scene between Mal’akh and his father, is the home of the Supreme Council, or, as it says on a plaque at its entrance: The Temple of the Supreme Council of the Thirty- third and last degree of the Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite of Freemasonry for the Southern Jurisdiction of the United States, Erected to God and Dedicated to the Service of humanity, Salve Frater! The building has 33 outer columns, each of which is 33 feet tall,

and in the Executive Chamber there are 33 ceremonial chairs because the Supreme Council has 33 members. The Capitol Building also has connections to the number 33. William Henry and Dr Mark Gray describe them in Freedom’s Gate: The Capitol Rotunda is a large, circular room located in the center of the Capitol Dome on the second floor. 96 feet in diameter, it is the symbolic and physical heart of the U.S. Capitol. It is the ceremonial center of the United States of America. After Barack Obama was sworn in on January 20, 2009 on the West Porch of the Capitol he ascended 33 steps into the Rotunda. In an early sketch by Constantino Brumidi of The Apotheosis of Washington, he placed 33 maidens around George Washington. In the second draft, he replaced the 33 maidens with the 13 we see in the final painting; in this second sketch, however, he painted 33 stars over the heads of the 13 maidens. Taking the search for symbolism a stage further, The Lost Symbol was released on 15 September 2009, or 15/09/09. If we take those numbers and add them together, we arrive at 33. Dan Brown is not the first to become obsessed with numbers and their meaning. Numerology is an ancient discipline with a history that goes back through the ages and is closely linked to divination. Pythagoras himself said that ‘the world is built upon the power of numbers’ and much of what we know of numerology comes from the teachings of the great Ancient Greek mathematician. Pythagoras assigned meanings to certain numbers and then applied this ‘code’ to the names of people and the gods in an attempt to divine something about their true nature. In trying to explain this complex combination of science and magic, he said, ‘All things of the universe have a numerical attribute that uniquely describes them.’ This is, essentially, the core of numerology. The Hebrews devised an incredibly complex numerological system known as gematria, which is built upon the work of Pythagoras. But they took it a stage further, applying values to whole phrases, prayers and sections of the Talmud. You could study gematria for years and not learn all its secrets. An example of how it works and of how layers of meaning can be

secreted within sacred texts is given in Manly P. Hall’s The Secret Teachings of All Ages: All higher numbers can be reduced to one of the original ten numerals, and the 10 itself to 1. Therefore, all groups of numbers resulting from the translation of names of deities into their numerical equivalents have a basis in one of the first ten numbers. By this system, in which the digits are added together, 666 becomes 6+6+6 or 18, and this, in turn, becomes 1+8 or 9. According to Revelation, 144,000 are to be saved. This number becomes 1+4+4+0+0+0, which equals 9, thus proving that both the Beast of Babylon and the number of the saved refer to man himself, whose symbol is the number 9. This system can be used successfully with both Greek and Hebrew letter values. While the numerological significance of numbers such as 33 has been lost to most of us, ripples from this encoded knowledge make themselves felt even in the modern world. For example, in the case of the belief that Jesus Christ was 33 at the time of his death, although it is very unlikely that this was his actual age, 33 has become a number encoded into the story of Jesus. Whoever devised the idea wanted this number to be passed down through the ages, wanted it to be remembered. And so it is with the rituals of the Freemasons. Not all of the participants understand the full meaning behind the symbolism of the numbers involved, but the process ensures that the degree of knowledge is kept alive and transmitted throughout the ages. SEE ALSO: Manly P. Hall, House of the Temple

ONE TRUE GOD This phrase is found on the granite pyramid that Robert Langdon locates in Room SBB13 deep beneath the Capitol Building. After Langdon has decoded the symbols found on the side of the pyramid, he ends up with the phrase ‘Jeova Sanctus Unus’. Langdon notes that the phrase is Latin and Katherine Solomon tells us that it is synonymous with the name of God found in the Jewish Torah: Jeova, Jehovah, Yahweh. ‘Jeova Sanctus Unus’ means literally ‘one true God’. According to the holy books of the Jews, Yahweh is indeed the one true God, the same God who guided Moses from Egypt and who then passed to mankind the Ten Commandments. We see this precise moment when God reveals himself in the Book of Exodus 20:1–3: ‘Then God spoke all these words. He said, “I am Yahweh your God who brought you out of Egypt, where you lived as slaves. You shall have no other gods to rival me.”‘ However, our modern name Yahweh is only the English form of the original Hebrew, which was made up of four letters: YHWH. The term is also known as the Tetragrammaton, literally ‘having four letters’ in Greek. This hints at just how sacred the name was. In fact, it was known as the Ineffable Name, or the Unutterable Name. Because Yahweh is the true and personal name of God, Orthodox Jews consider it too sacred to be spoken. If we remember the Ten Commandments, we find: ‘You shall not misuse the name of Yahweh your God, for Yahweh will not leave unpunished anyone who misuses his name.’ (Exodus 20:7) So Orthodox Jews never speak the word aloud. When Solomon’s Temple stood in Jerusalem, the name was spoken by the High Priest on the Jewish holiday Yom Kippur, but since the destruction of the Temple in Roman times, the term has not been vocalised by observant Jews. In fact it is said that the true and correct pronunciation of the name has been lost through the ages. In common usage, the word ‘Lord’ is used instead of YHWH. The concept of one true God is known as monotheism. The Abrahamic religions ( Judaism, Christianity and Islam) are monotheistic, but the roots of monotheism are found further back in time. Zoroastrianism, born in Persia sometime during the first millennium bc, has at its core the belief in one god known as Ahura

Mazda. Zoroastrianism was influential in the creation of Judaism, which in turn helped shape Christianity. The true age of Zoroastrianism is not known for certain, and it may have been predated by another monotheistic faith, that of Akhenaten in Ancient Egypt. Under the pharaoh Akhenaten, the Egyptians worshipped the Aten, the disc of the sun. Atenism was a short-lived religion and flourished only during the lifetime of the heretic ruler Amenhotep IV, who adopted the name Akhenaten. When he died sometime around 1355 bc, the religion died with him. However, we still have records of the beliefs of Atenism, and a text now known as ‘The Great Hymn to the Aten’ was found at Amarna, the city that Akhenaten built in honour of his god: How manifold it is, what thou hast made! They are hidden from the face [of man]. O sole god, like whom there is no other! Thou didst create the world according to thy desire . . . Although this hymn bears an uncanny resemblance to a passage found in the Book of Psalms in the Bible, Psalm 104, it is not clear if the ‘Hymn to the Aten’ influenced its writing. However, an intriguing aspect of Psalm 104 is that it starts by ascribing characteristics that could be considered those of the sun to God, reinforcing the idea that Psalm 104 could be based in some part on the ‘Hymn to the Aten’. It begins: Bless Yahweh, my soul, Yahweh, my God, how great you are! Clothed in majesty and splendour, wearing the light as a robe! You stretch out the heavens like a tent, build your palace on the waters above, making the clouds your chariot, gliding on the wings of the wind, appointing the winds your messengers, flames of fire your servants. Whether the ‘Hymn to the Aten’ really is the earliest reference to the worship of one true God is still debated by scholars, but one thing is clear: monotheism, belief in one god, is an ancient concept. In Masonic symbolic lore, the ‘one true God’ concept is represented by the title Great Architect of the Universe. In The Lost Symbol, it turns out that the phrase ‘one true god’ has another level of significance’. Langdon reveals that ‘Jeova Sanctus

Unus’ was also the pseudonym of the famous scientist Isaac Newton. Langdon explains that Newton’s name in Latin was Isaacus Neutonuus and that this was an anagram of the phrase ‘Jeova Sanctus Unus’ as the ‘I’ would have been transposed with a ‘J’. It is true that Newton signed all of his alchemical works ‘Jeova Sanctus Unus’. In his lifetime, Newton committed millions of words to paper and he seems to have spent much of his later life examining the Bible itself, believing that sacred knowledge was encoded within. John Maynard Keynes, who collected together much of Newton’s prolific output, claimed – after reading his full works – that Newton believed that ‘the universe is a cryptogram set by the Almighty’. SEE ALSO: Great Architect of the Universe, Isaac Newton

THE ORDER OF THE EASTERN STAR Unlike its more famous counterpart Freemasonry, the Order of the Eastern Star (OES) and its Masonic links are relatively unknown to the general public. Indeed, this point is made when Professor Robert Langdon is questioned by one of his Harvard students about the exclusion of women from Freemasonry. Langdon points out that the Order of the Eastern Star is the women’s branch of Masonry. While it is true that the majority of members are women, the OES is actually open to men and women and has both a Worthy Matron and Worthy Patron as its highest officers in each chapter and overall. Its international headquarters are in Washington DC in Dupont Circle, and there are some 10,000 chapters in 20 countries with 1 million members worldwide. To join the OES you must be either a Mason or a female relative of a Mason (a Mason’s wife, daughter, niece, stepmother, sister, sister-in-law or even mother-in-law, although interestingly aunt is not mentioned in the list of eligible affiliations). As well as these, members of the International Order of Job’s Daughters and International Order of the Rainbow for Girls, youth organisations for girls sponsored by the Masons, are also able to join once they have reached 18 years of age. The OES is a ‘social order’ for people of all faiths who believe in a Supreme Being (atheists are not allowed to join) and wish to advance the well-being of others. Its central tenets and lessons, taught through the degrees, are fidelity, constancy, loyalty, faith and love. In accordance with these principles, its members raise a great deal of money for their local community and international charities. As Langdon observes, it has been mooted that the OES was founded in France as early as 1703, although this is not certain. However, what is known is that by 1850 Dr Rob Morris, an American lawyer and Master Mason, had instigated the Eastern Star degrees in the present form to enable women to join a Masonic fraternity so that they too could answer the philanthropic impulse that inspired their male relations to become Masons. At this time, Dr Morris wrote the ritual for the order, published in 1865 under the title The Rosary of the Eastern Star, detailing the degrees of the order, names, signs, symbols, colours and principles. Why he chose

the specific symbols and emblems that he did, their deeper meanings and the character-building lessons associated with them are secrets closely guarded by the order, although the symbols are said to relate to the stories associated with the five biblical woman – Adah, Ruth, Esther, Martha and Electa – who are held up as the heroines OED members should seek to emulate. The five biblical heroines are symbolised by an inverted, five- pointed star and are each associated with a specific role, colour and symbol. Hence Adah is a daughter, her colour is blue for fidelity and her symbol is a sword and veil, signifying that she sacrificed her life to save her father’s honour. She represents the first degree in the Eastern Star ritual and is the top right point of the star. Going in a clockwise direction, the second degree is Ruth, the widow, represented by yellow (constancy) and a barley sheaf, the emblem of plenty, alluding to Ruth gleaning leftover barley stalks to provide for her in her widowhood. The heroine of the third degree of the star is Esther, the wife. Coloured white for loyalty, it is the downward point of the star, featuring the crown and sceptre representing both Esther’s standing as queen and her noble spirit in her willingness to sacrifice herself for her people. The fourth point is green (faith), representing Martha, the sister. It contains a depiction of a broken column, which indicates the uncertainties of life. The final, fifth degree is red (love) for Electa, the mother. She represents forbearance and acceptance of the will of God despite harsh treatment and persecution. Her symbol is the cup, signifying her charity and hospitality. In the middle of the five-pointed star is a pentagon in which sits an altar with an open book, symbolising obedience to the word of God. Around the pentagon is the word FATAL, which stands for ‘Fairest Among Thousands, Altogether Lovely’. While it is easy to see why a five-pointed star was chosen, given the five roles generally allotted to women, it is harder to understand why an inverted pentagram was decided on as their emblem, given the negative connotations usually associated with to this symbol today. The reason often given for this is that the inverted star represents the Star of Bethlehem, which pointed down from Heaven to Earth and showed the way to Christ and his teachings. Indeed, the Star of Bethlehem would appear to be alluded to in the order’s name, especially considering the OED motto: ‘We have seen his star in the east, and are come to worship

him.’ (Matthew 2:2) Dr Rob Morris made this connection in 1886, when he stated, as quoted in History of the Order of the Eastern Star by Willis D. Engle: The Eastern Star: The Star of Bethlehem once guided three wise men to the place where the infant Jesus lay. But the Eastern Star is this hour guiding fifty thousand wise women to the highest plane of earthly merit and usefulness. However, some commentators have noted that the emblem of the order cannot be the Star of Bethlehem as traditionally this is represented as a six-pointed star. Instead, they argue that according to Ancient Egyptian texts and iconography a five-pointed star specifically relates to Sirius, which in Ancient Egypt was represented by the goddess Sopdet, regarded as having given birth to the Morning Star. Others have noted that the inverted pentagram is closely associated with Baphomet, a figure that has been incorrectly identified with the Devil and Satanism. However, it has been shown by Dr Hugh Schonfield that by employing the sixth-century BC Atbash cipher, the term Baphomet (alleged to be a pagan idol, whose worship was one of the charges brought against the Knights Templar) becomes Sophia, the Greek for wisdom, closely linked to the Sacred Feminine. Famous members of the OED have included Eleanor Roosevelt, the wife of Franklin D. Roosevelt, the 32nd president of the United States, Laura Ingalls Wilder, author of the Little House series of children’s books, and the memoirist and poet Maya Angelou. SEE ALSO: Freemasonry

OUROBOROS Dan Brown writes in The Lost Symbol that the character Mal’akh has a tattoo on his head of a snake devouring its own tail, and names it as the Ouroboros. Is this something invented by the author or is it something real that most of us have probably never encountered? At the start of Chapter 128 in the novel we are supplied with important information, no less than a picture of the Ouroboros. There it is again, the snake swallowing its own tail. It is the seventh symbol in the sequence of images that Robert Langdon is trying to decipher and is introduced as a symbol for wholeness. The figure of the serpent biting its own tail seems to have first been designed by the Ancient Egyptians in about the middle of the second millennium BC. Only a few hundred years after that period, during the Zhou Dynasty in China, the dragon or snake swallowing its own tail was being illustrated. Is it coincidental that two great civilisations divided by a massive continent each developed the concept of this symbol entirely separately from each other? The Phoenicians took to the symbol of the Ouroboros and it became part of their culture. These people originally inhabited the present-day Syrian coastal area around the Mediterranean Sea. These enterprising folk became highly successful economic migrants, setting up colonies around the Mediterranean shores and on the islands. Being excellent sailors and having a talent for successful trading, they prospered as merchants. They are credited with having discovered how to make glass, a sought-after luxury commodity, and through their trading links their ideas were disseminated widely. The Ancient Greeks then adopted the Ouroboros and gave it the name by which we know it today, which

means ‘tail-eater’. Alternative spellings include Uroboros and Oureboros. The Ouroboros has come to symbolise the cycle of nature: life out of death, creation out of destruction. One theory proposed is that the Chinese yin and yang is an older symbol and that it was this that was transformed, probably in Egypt, into the Ouroboros, to which it has similarities. Yin and yang represent creation and the Ouroboros constantly recreates itself. Yin is symbolic of earth, female, dark and negative, whereas yang corresponds to heaven, male, light and positive. To create a balance, each half needs to feed off the other. So many and varied are the opinions concerning the origins of the Ouroboros that there is, perhaps appropriately considering the subject matter, an equal and opposite school of thought, which insists that the Ouroboros was the inspiration for the yin/yang device. In alchemy the Ouroboros is a snake, or sometimes a dragon, which in earlier times was often referred to as a worm. It forms a circle as it feeds upon itself, constantly self-recycling, a metaphor for the cycle of birth and death. Alchemists also regard the Ouroboros as symbolising the clash of opposites. Gnosticism, a form of spiritual teaching holding that its followers had special enlightenment, taught that the sun disc could be thought of as a huge dragon holding its own tail in its mouth. Most Gnostics referred to God as ‘Monad’ (One). An imperfect god had created an equally imperfect world, they believed, and this was inhabited by divine souls, namely people. Another form of mysticism, hermeticism is a compendium of beliefs based on the supposed writings of Hermes Trismegistus (Hermes the Thrice-Great), supposed to have been a brilliant Egyptian priest. He was believed to have been associated with the god of wisdom, Thoth. During the Renaissance, hermeticist beliefs greatly influenced those with leisure and the ability to dabble in magic and the occult. One of their symbols was the Ouroboros, symbolising the continuous cycle of life. In several degrees of Scottish Rite Freemasonry, the regalia, especially aprons, of those who have attained the degree is adorned with the image of the Ouroboros. Norse mythology contains its own version of the Ouroboros, the snake Jormundgand. It was one of the three children of the great god Loki, the Shape Changer, the Sly One. Long ago, Odin, the

greatest of the gods, realised that one day Jormundgand, a serpent, would bring great trouble, so he threw the snake into the deep ocean surrounding the world. However the creature was so huge that it could circle the world, biting its own tail. Gods and men are caught in its grip. It is said that Friedrich August Kekulé, a German chemist of the nineteenth century, dreamed of the tail-consuming snake. He was at the time researching the chemical benzene and was finding progress impossible. He woke, pondered the circle the snake had formed and realised that his dream was the solution; his snake was a closed carbon ring. He had solved his problem by falling asleep on the job. The Ouroboros has had significance for widely diverse peoples over a very long span of history. While at first glance it might be thought that these peoples have had little in common, in fact they have all been united by the symbol of the snake that eats itself. SEE ALSO: Alchemy, Hermeticism, Scottish Rite Freemasonry

PHILOSOPHER’S STONE The Philosopher’s Stone is one of the greatest secrets of alchemy, so great in fact that we don’t know precisely what it was. The true nature of what it really was has been veiled in so much secrecy over the centuries that it is hard to divine. In The Lost Symbol, Robert Langdon discovers an acronym written on the wall of a room deep below the Capitol Building: VITRIOL. We are told stands for ‘visita interiora terrae, rectificando invenies occultum lapidem’, which translates as ‘visit the interior of the earth, and by rectifying, you will find the hidden stone’. The most interesting part of that phrase is ‘occultum lapidem’, the ‘hidden stone’. We learn that this may relate to the Philosopher’s Stone of the alchemists, truly their Holy Grail. So, before we go any further, what exactly do we know about the Philosopher’s Stone? Well, this fabled object or substance was described as an elixir of immortality, the fountain of youth that appears in countless cultures in one form or another. In the Middle Ages in particular, the concept of an elixir that could confer eternal life was known as the Philosopher’s Stone and alchemists were obsessed with attempting to create it. Some of the greatest alchemists of Europe and the Middle East turned their hands and minds to the discovery of this elixir: Ostanes, Nicolas Flamel, Count St Germain, Fulcanelli and even Isaac Newton were among those who quested after this elusive substance. As well as the ability to grant immortality, the elixir was considered an agent by which transmutations such as lead to gold could be performed. It was the subject of many experiments and much debate over the centuries, and many doubted that it truly existed, believing rather it was a symbol for an ideal substance, perfection itself. Zosimus, the Byzantine historian who lived towards the end of the fifth century, wrote of the Philosopher’s Stone: ‘Receive this stone which is not a stone, a precious thing that has no value, a thing of many shapes which has no shapes, this unknown which is known to all.’ We know that alchemy had two paths, one that we could term exoteric, which was concerned with the pursuit of turning base

metals into higher states, such as gold, and one that could be called esoteric, which was more interested in the transformation of a mortal man’s soul into the divine. In this respect, it is interesting to note that many have equated the Philosopher’s Stone with the Holy Grail itself. In one of the earliest accounts of the Grail, Parzival, written by Wolfram von Eschenbach some time in the first part of the thirteenth century, we are told quite clearly that the Grail is in fact a stone: If you do not know it, it shall here be named to you. It is called lapsit excillis. By the power of that stone the phoenix burns to ashes, but the ashes give him life again. Thus does the phoenix moult and change its plumage, which afterwards is bright and shining and as lovely as before. There never was a human so ill but that, if he one day sees that stone, he cannot die within the week that follows. And in looks he will not fade. His appearance will stay the same, be it maid or man, as on the day he saw the stone, the same as when the best years of his life began, and though he should see the stone for two hundred years, it will never change, save that his hair might perhaps turn grey. Such power does the stone give a man that flesh and bones are at once made young again. The stone is also called the Grail. This is fascinating because here we find the same properties as the elixir known as the Philosopher’s Stone. In The Elixir and the Stone, Michael Baigent and Richard Leigh discuss the possible meaning of lapsit excillis: Scholars have suggested numerous interpretations of the phrase ‘lapsit excillis’, all of them more or less plausible. It might be a corruption of lapis ex caelis – ‘stone from the heavens’. It might be a truncation of lapis lapsus ex caelus – ‘a stone fallen from heaven’. Most obviously, of course, it might be lapis elixir, the Philosophers’ Stone and elixir of alchemy. [Wolfram’s Parzival] is laden with alchemical

symbolism. The phoenix, for example, is a familiar image in alchemical works, and Wolfram invokes it in a familiar alchemical context. There is another curious candidate and this is ‘lapis lapsus exiliens’, which seems to be a translation of the name of a legendary stone mentioned by the twelfth-century Arabic geographer Muhammad al-Idrisi, which he termed ‘the stone that rose and fell’ and which was connected with the rock found in the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem, the stone from which Mohammed ascended to heaven. This stone is known as the Eben Shetiyah by Jewish scholars, which translates as ‘the stone of foundation’. Another clue that leads us to consider whether the Holy Grail and the Philosopher’s Stone might be the same object is the story of the legendary Hermes Trismegistus, ‘thrice great Hermes’, whose writings are the foundation of hermeticism and alchemy. Hermes Trismegistus is credited with having written ‘The Emerald Tablet’, a treatise that is full of alchemical knowledge. Isaac Newton translated the text, which includes the following line describing the emerald tablet of the title: ‘It ascends from the Earth to Heaven and again it descends to the Earth and receives the force of things superior and inferior.’ Notice the curious similarity here between what Newton describes as an object that ‘ascends from the Earth to Heaven and again it descends to the Earth’ and the stone described by al-Idrisi, ‘the stone that rose and fell’. The question is, did the emerald tablet really exist in a physical form? Looking again at lapis ex caelis, ‘stone from the heavens’, leads us towards meteorites, which we know were highly prized in antiquity (see the entry on the Akedah in this book). There is a substance called moldavite that resembles green glass and is formed when meteorites strike the earth. This semi-precious stone is often used in jewellery and has gem-like qualities. Looking again at Isaac Newton’s translation of ‘The Emerald Tablet’ provides a tantalising clue: ‘Its force or power is entire if it be converted into earth.’ This describes moldavite exactly. It is created through fire when the ‘power’, or energy, of a meteor impacts with the earth, creating this new substance through the sheer force of the event – sacred chemistry of the gods, if you happen to be an alchemist. A recent translation by Nineveh Shadrach from the original Arabic of ‘The Emerald Tablet’ cites the line in question as ‘It is a

fire that became our earth’, which again describes the creation of moldavite precisely. This new translation also contains an intriguing variation on the line that we see in Newton’s version: ‘It extracts the lights from the heights and descends to the earth containing the power of the above and the below for it is with the light of the lights. Therefore the darkness flees from it.’ Is it possible that ‘the Emerald Tablet’ was a large piece of moldavite upon which the words of Hermes Trismegistus were engraved? This would be fascinating because the word from which ‘grail’ is taken is very likely to be the Persian word ghr, which means ‘pearl’ or ‘stone’. Furthermore, the Persian word ghr’al, which looks very much like the word ‘grail’, means ‘engraved stone’. The implications of all this are astounding, for it means that we don’t have to decide between lapis ex caelis, ‘stone from the heavens’, and lapis elixir, the Philosopher’s Stone, as a meaning for the Holy Grail. If ‘the Emerald Tablet’ was a graven piece of moldavite, then the Philosopher’s Stone is both of these at the same time: a sacred meteoritic stone from heaven with magical properties, engraved with the alchemical teachings of Hermes Trismegistus. If this is in essence what the Philosopher’s Stone was/is, then it would indeed be the most highly prized of artefacts from the ancient world. Meteorites have been worshipped in many cultures across Europe, the Middle East, the whole world, in fact. It is therefore not surprising to discover that one of the most sacred objects of myth and legend, the Philosopher’s Stone, could have its origins in the very heavens themselves. SEE ALSO: Alchemy, Hermetica, Sir Isaac Newton

PINEAL GLAND This tiny part of the brain is responsible for the efficient functioning of several metabolic systems within the body. It is also imbued by some with a symbolic link to the so-called ‘third eye’. The Lost Symbol contains a conversation between Robert Langdon and Katherine Solomon in which they discuss the human brain and the pineal gland in particular. It is described as being active in meditative states and producing a substance that can heal the body, likened to the biblical manna that sustained the followers of Moses in the wilderness. Katherine and Robert discuss the notion that the ‘Temple’ that is mentioned in the Bible refers to the human mind. Katherine quotes from Corinthians to support her argument. The sceptical Langdon raises the fact that the Temple is described as having an inner and an outer section, separated by a veil. He may have been thinking of the passage describing the construction of the Temple, worded in some translations of Exodus 26:33 thus: ‘and the veil shall divide unto you between the holy place and the most holy’. Once again Katherine has an answer for him, noting that the two parts of the brain are separated by a ‘veil of web-like tissue’. Whether or not the Bible is using a metaphor for the human brain, the pineal gland continues to attract interest from scientists and philosophers. The gland is approximately 7 mm long in humans and is located near the centre of the brain between the two hemispheres. It is responsible for the production of a hormone called melatonin, which regulates the body’s daily rhythms. When the retina of the eye is stimulated with light, impulses are sent down the optic nerve to a part of the brain called the hypothalamus. From here, sympathetic nerves link to the pineal gland and inhibit the production of melatonin. The result of this is that when no light reaches the eye, for example at night-time, these signals no longer inhibit melatonin production and this can then trigger the body to induce sleep. Melatonin was first isolated in 1958. It has become very popular as a supplement and has been suggested as a cure for jet lag and other sleep disorders, while conditions such as seasonal affective disorder may be related to its production.

As with so many other aspects of anatomy, the first description of the pineal gland came from Galen (ad 130–210), the Greek doctor and philosopher whose opinions were followed until the seventeenth century. It was Galen who explained that the gland takes its name from the pine cone – pinus pinea in Latin – due to a similarity in appearance. In Galen’s opinion, the gland’s function was to support blood vessels and he was dismissive of other suggestions that it regulated the flow of so-called psychic pneuma in the brain. René Descartes, the seventeenth-century French philosopher, believed that the pineal gland was the ‘seat of the soul’. He wrote in December 1640: Since it is the only solid part of the brain which is single, it must necessarily be the seat of the common sense, i.e. of thought, and consequently of the soul; for one cannot be separated from the other. He also explained: ‘My view is that this gland is the principal seat of the soul, and the place in which all our thoughts are formed.’ The pineal gland attracted the attention of Madame Helena Blavatsky, an esoteric writer and the founder of the Theosophical Society in 1875, who linked the ‘Eye of Shiva’, or the third eye, to it. She said that the pineal gland in modern man was a vestigial version of an ‘organ of spiritual vision’. In some animals, the pinealocytes, the cells from the pineal gland, closely resemble the photoreceptor cells of the eye, and early vertebrate fossils have been found with a pineal opening that further encourages the view of this gland as a third eye. The pineal gland is associated with the sixth chakra, or anja chakra, which is referred to as the third eye. In Indian teaching, it is known as the gyananakashu, the eye of knowledge, and many Hindus wear a mark known as a tilak between their eyebrows to acknowledge this. The positioning by the Ancient Egyptians of the ureus, or cobra headdress, in the centre of the forehead reveals their belief in something similar to the third eye.

ROSICRUCIANS An A to Z of the Occult, by Simon Cox and Mark Foster, explains that the Society of Rosicrucians was ‘an esoteric society formed with the intention of bringing about a change in European civilisation, of creating a more perfect society based on hermetic values and alchemical teachings’. As with the vast majority of esoteric societies, including the Freemasons, trying to ascertain its actual origins is difficult, if not impossible. Many writers long before Dan Brown have suggested that the Rosicrucians were the originators of Freemasonry. Robert Langdon explains in The Lost Symbol that the Rose Cross is a symbol of Freemasonry in honour of the early Rosicrucians and their contribution to Masonic philosophy. Freemasonry does indeed contain various rituals referring to the Brotherhood of the Rose and Cross. The 18th degree of the Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite is called the Rose Croix degree, and a Rosy Cross degree forms part of the ceremonies of the Royal Order of Scotland. There are also Rosicrucian societies with membership restricted to Freemasons alone. One such society, the Societas Rosicruciana in Anglia (SRIA), was founded in London in 1867. It should not be confused with the non-Masonic Societas Rosicruciana in America, founded in 1909. To confuse matters further, there is also an American Freemasonic equivalent known as the Societas Rosicruciana in Civitatibus Foederatis (SRICF). The Grade structure of these societies is: First Order Grade I – Zelator Grade II – Theoricus Grade III – Practicus Grade IV – Philosophus Second Order Grade V – Adeptus Minor Grade VI – Adeptus Major Grade VII – Adeptus Exemptus Third Order

Grade VIII – Magister Grade IX – Magus Each grade invites the member to study further the Rosicrucian mysteries. A number of members of the English SRIA were particularly mystically minded Masons and they founded the famous occult school known as the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn in 1888. One later member of the Golden Dawn was accused of practising black magic and creating his own religion – he was none other than the infamous magician Aleister Crowley. Crowley is also alleged to have been a 33rd-degree Mason, although this has been contested. Mal’akh, the villain of The Lost Symbol, studied Crowley in his quest for power and knowledge. The Christian mystic Arthur Edward Waite was a contemporary of Crowley’s. A Freemason and member of the Golden Dawn, he is most famous for the Rider-Waite Tarot deck, which is perhaps the most popular Tarot deck of all time. A prolific writer on all things esoteric, he wrote in A New Encyclopaedia of Freemasonry (1922) that we ‘have further to remember that the Rosicrucian Mystery was one of Divine Rebirth, such indeed as we meet with – though under many veils – in the ceremony of Freemasonry’. This ‘Divine Rebirth’ is one that takes place within the individual and it relates to the message in the climactic chapter of The Lost Symbol. At the Washington Monument, Peter Solomon reveals to Robert Langdon that the truth of the Ancient Mysteries is the realisation that people are not God’s subjects but in fact possess the capability to be gods themselves through the understanding of this truth. The American-based Rosicrucian order, the Ancient and Mystical Order Rosae Crucis (AMORC), mentioned by Robert Langdon, state that their purpose is ‘the study of the elusive mysteries of life and the universe’. This ‘ancient’ organisation was actually founded in New York in 1915. In their defence, however, they do claim that they are actually the inheritors of an ‘oral tradition’ that impressively stems back some 3,500 years to the reign of the Egyptian Pharaoh Tuthmosis III. AMORC further claim their influences include the ‘heretic’ Pharaoh Amenhotep IV. He became known as Akhenaten and was a revolutionary pharaoh who threw out the old gods of Egypt and replaced them with one god, the Aten. This is the first record of the

one true God concept in history – in other words, monotheism, which is what the great religions of the book are all based upon. Amongst many others, Rosicrucians claim as members the physicians Paracelsus and Michael Maier, the alchemist Robert Fludd, Sir Isaac Newton, Sir Francis Bacon, Benjamin Franklin, the mathematician John Dee, the Freemason and antiquarian Elias Ashmole and the mystic Jacob Boehme. This is referred to by Robert Langdon, who implies that many of those listed above were Rosicrucians. In terms of documentary proof, the first evidence or mention of the Rosicrucians appears in the collection of early seventeenth- century pamphlets known as the Rosicrucian Manifestos. Dan Brown’s character Katherine Solomon, the Noetic scientist and sister of Peter, explains to Langdon that she has studied these documents as part of her research. The Manifestos circulated in Germany before word of the mysterious and mystical brotherhood spread across Europe, eventually finding its way to the United States and the rest of the world. The first manifesto, Fama Fraternitatis, or a Discovery of the Fraternity of the Most Laudable Order of the Rosy Cross, was printed in Kassel, Germany, in 1614 (although earlier handwritten copies dating from 1610–11 have since come to light). In 1615, the second manifesto, entitled Confessio Fraternatatis, or Confession of the Laudable Fraternity of the Most Honorable Order of the Rosy Cross, Written to All the Learned of Europe, followed. It is not known who wrote these manifestos, and some academics have questioned whether the group actually existed, or if it was all just an elaborate hoax. What followed, however, was real, in that self-styled Rosicrucian groups began to appear and have done so ever since. In 1616, another Rosicrucian document, The Chymical Wedding of Christian Rosenkreutz, appeared. This was in a slightly different style and has been attributed to the Lutheran pastor Johannes Valentinus Andreae. The phrase ‘chemical wedding’ is worthy of note, as it is a reference to the alchemical process of spiritual transmutation whereby a marriage of opposites is sought in order to discover the Elixir of Life or Philosopher’s Stone, to achieve knowledge of God. Explanations as to why the society was called the Rosy or Rose Cross vary, but it is certainly connected to symbolism. In The Lost Symbol, Robert Langdon explains to Katherine that the Rose Cross is

a binary symbol or ‘two symbols fused to create one’. The idea is that the Egyptians used a cross to express the intersection of the celestial and human realms, or the famous concept ‘As above, so it is below’. This is also the meaning behind the Freemasons’ use of the square and compass configuration, representing transformation. The rose represents love, or spirit, and the equal-armed cross equates to matter. Thus spirit is crucified in matter and the work of the Rosicrucian mystic is to set the spirit free by exploring, understanding and balancing or marrying rational thinking with spirituality. The allusion to Christ and the promise of resurrection within the Christian tradition is obvious. The early documents state that what is being made public for the first time is an order founded by a mystic called Brother Christian Rosenkreutz. He was said to have been born in 1378 and as an adult was a wise and learned man who travelled abroad to study with Arab mystics, from whom he learned esoteric wisdom, such as the Kabbalah, hermeticism and alchemy. On his return to Europe, he was shunned by the academic community, so he instituted a society to do good works in secret. In Rosicrucianism, each brother is asked to blend into the culture he finds himself in and keep himself unknown, but he is asked to report once a year upon his progress. One further stipulation is that each member will choose a successor with whom to share the mysteries and pass on the secrets. When Christian Rosenkreutz died, he was placed in a secret vault of seven sides and three levels, which also contained books of learning and occult equipment. The tomb is described as having ever-burning lamps, which, it was claimed, were still glowing when it was apparently rediscovered around 1604, though its location was kept secret; the body of the founder was supposedly perfectly preserved. The earliest known printed version of the Fama Fraternitatis in English is the translation by the philosopher Thomas Vaughan in 1652. A very interesting footnote, however, in Frances Yates’s book The Rosicrucian Enlightenment, states that a handwritten copy dated 1633 was found preserved in the library of Sir David Lindsay, 1st Lord Lindsay of Balcarres, who is known to have had an interest in alchemy. It may just be a wonderful coincidence, but his granddaughter married the founder of the Royal Society, or ‘Invisible College’, who was arguably the first true ‘gentleman

Mason’ or ‘Freemason’, Sir Robert Moray. It cannot be coincidence, however, that in 1638 a Scotsman called Henry Adamson wrote a strange poem that includes the much-quoted lines: For we be brethren of the Rosie Crosse; We have the Mason Word and second sight, Things for to come we can foretell aright. SEE ALSO: Alchemy, Aleister Crowley, Freemasonry, Hermetica, One True God

ROYAL SOCIETY AND THE INVISIBLE COLLEGE The Royal Society, or, to give its full title, the Royal Society of London for the Improvement of Natural Knowledge, is an august body of the most respected scientists of our age. Current fellows include Stephen Hawking, Richard Dawkins and Sir Timothy Berners-Lee. Given its highly respectable pedigree, one wonders how such an institution could be mentioned in The Lost Symbol in connection with the arcane study of alchemy. Dan Brown in fact credits the Invisible College, a society of learned and brilliant minds, with being an elite within the Royal Society. Its members joined together to share their knowledge and advance their studies, and the present-day Royal Society has benefited from their understanding of the ancient knowledge passed down through the centuries from the mystery schools of Egypt. The character Peter Solomon in The Lost Symbol is said to have ancestors who were members of the Royal Society. A successor body to the Invisible College, the Royal Society emerged following the collaboration of a series of philosophers who respected and discussed the work of Sir Francis Bacon. In his book The New Atlantis, Bacon described an establishment called ‘Salomon’s House’, where investigations into the natural world were carried out. It is this concept of a group of sages seeking to widen the extent of human knowledge and the principles of experimental science, further outlined by Bacon in The Advancement of Learning, that inspired the founding of the Invisible College. Robert Boyle, one of those who followed the investigative principles of Bacon, referred to the Invisible College by name in 1646. Boyle was an alchemist, as well as the author of The Sceptical Chymist. In a letter to his former tutor, he wrote: The best of it is that the cornerstones of the Invisible (or as they term themselves the Philosophical) College, do now and then honour me with their company, which makes me sorry for those pressing occasions that urge my departure. The Royal Society was founded on 28 November 1660 at Gresham College after a lecture given by Sir Christopher Wren. The 12

founding members aimed to form a ‘Colledge for the Promoting of Physico-Mathematicall Experimentall Learning’. Wren, the renowned architect who designed among several other masterpieces St Paul’s Cathedral in London, like so many enlightened men of his time did not confine himself to one field of study and his scientific enquiries involved the fields of medicine, astronomy and microscopy. A key founder member of the Royal Society was Sir Robert Moray, a leading Freemason – and almost certainly the same Robert Moray whose Masonic initiation in 1641 was the first recorded example of a Speculative (i.e. non-working mason) becoming a member. Moray was a soldier who had fought in the French Army and had been in contact with Charles II during his exile. King Charles II was interested in science, as attested by his involvement with the Royal Observatory at Greenwich, and when Moray informed him of the society’s formation, he gave his approval. A second Royal Charter was granted in 1663 to what was by then known as ‘the Royal Society of London for Improving Natural Knowledge’. Another founder member of the Royal Society was Elias Ashmole, initiated as a Freemason in 1646, before the establishment of the Grand Lodge. Ashmole was a true Renaissance man, being interested in such diverse subjects as politics, history, the military and astrology, but most of all alchemy. During the English Civil War, Ashmole was a fervent supporter of the Royalists and when Charles II gained the throne Ashmole was rewarded with lucrative posts. His legacy can still be seen today in Oxford; he donated his vast collection of antiquities, books and research to the institution we now know as the Ashmolean Museum. Robert Hooke, who is known as the ‘father of microscopy’, was the society’s first curator of experiments; he was also employed as a surveyor after the Great Fire of London in 1666. His multiple talents and interests typify the pedigree of the society’s early members. There are tangible results of the scientific advances made by members of the Royal Society and they are easy to identify and understand, but this is not true of the Invisible College. Did an elite within the society’s ranks continue to base their philosophy on ancient mystical teachings? Certainly many members of the Royal Society over the years have been Freemasons, in some cases in high positions within the craft.

Masonic author Robert Lomas in The Invisible College comments on the career of John Theophilus Desaguilers as follows: Desaguilers had been introduced to Freemasonry while employed by the then President of the Royal Society, Isaac Newton, as an experimental demonstrator for the Society’s meetings. Desaguilers started out as an employee of the Royal Society. Under the patronage of Newton he became a Fellow of the Royal Society, and he also rose to the highest ranks in English Freemasonry. Desaguilers was in fact the Grand Master of the Premier Grand Lodge of England in 1719. The name Sir Isaac Newton appears frequently when hidden knowledge or esoteric involvement in science is discussed. Newton was the president of the Royal Society from 1703 to his death in 1727. The men who formed the Royal Society, learned across many disciplines and able to read Latin and Greek texts in their original language, would undoubtedly have been familiar with ancient teachings and philosophies, including those described as alchemical or hermetic. In The Advancement of Learning, Sir Francis Bacon wrote: ‘There should be a fraternity or brotherhood in learning, through which learned men might exchange knowledge and help one another . . . The brotherhood of learning should transcend national boundaries.’ Bacon’s ideal of an international brotherhood has been fulfilled within the Royal Society, which admits eligible members residing outside the United Kingdom, Ireland and the Commonwealth. That the brightest and most innovative scientific minds of the age have a forum in which to share and develop their ideas is indeed the dream of Sir Francis Bacon made reality and a true victory for enlightenment. SEE ALSO: Sir Francis Bacon, Sir Isaac Newton

SCOTTISH RITE FREEMASONRY A major element of the storyline of The Lost Symbol is Scottish Rite Freemasonry and especially its 33rd degree. In his writing, Dan Brown claims this is the highest degree in all of Freemasonry and that something special will be revealed to members of this ultra- elite group. Its symbol is an alchemical double-headed eagle. The home of the Scottish Rite is the House of the Temple in Washington DC. The novel explains that members know the House of the Temple as Heredom, named after a mythical mountain in Scotland. But what is the Scottish Rite? Does it have anything to do with Scotland? Is there a great secret that is only revealed to the elite 33rd-degree members? And, if so, what is its significance? There are so many references to Scotland, Scottish and Ecosse rites and degrees that many wonder why the home of Scottish Rite Freemasonry is actually the United States of America. According to the Masonic Encyclopaedia, written by Henry Wilson Coil, himself a 33rd-degree Mason, and edited by three other 33rddegree Masons: Scotch, Scots and Scottish are among the most troublesome words in Masonic writing. So long as they referred only to Scotland, all was well. But, about 1740, they began to be used to describe numerous degrees which were produced in Europe by authors who never saw Scotland. As discussed in the entry on the development of Freemasonry, when the first Grand Lodge of Freemasons was formed in 1717 there were no ‘high degrees’. It was a two-degree system, with a third degree only making an appearance in the 1730s. Collectively, these three degrees of ‘craft’ Masonry became known as Blue Masonry. In 1737, Chevalier Andrew Ramsey, an exiled Scotsman living in France who had at one time been tutor to Prince Charles Edward Stuart (Bonnie Prince Charlie), was the Grand Orator of the French Freemasons. That year he delivered a Masonic address that was to inextricably link Scottish references to Freemasonry in a way that would change it for ever. This all took place in the context of political and religious unrest across Europe. Historians and academics agree that Ramsey’s lecture was mostly

mythological in nature. The reason seems to have been that he wanted to give a noble and chivalric lineage to Freemasonry that was perhaps lacking in the merely ‘craft’ aspect of the British three degrees. The French loved the fact that the Hauts Grades, the Freemasonic ‘high degrees’ of chivalry that would include Templar and Rosicrucian degrees, began to appear. Ramsey’s boldest claim was the suggestion that Freemasonry was actually founded at the time of the Crusades, as the following extract from his oration, taken from The Quest for the Celtic Key by Karen Ralls-Macleod and Ian Robertson, explains: At the time of the Crusades in Palestine many princes, lords, and citizens associated themselves, and vowed to restore the Temple of the Christians in the Holy Land, and to employ themselves in bringing back their architecture to its first institution. They agreed upon several ancient signs and symbolic words drawn from the well of religion in order to recognise themselves amongst the heathen and Saracens. These signs and words were only communicated to those who promised solemnly, and even sometimes at the foot of the altar never to reveal them. This sacred promise was therefore not an execrable oath, as it has been called, but a respectable bond to unite Christians of all nationalities in one confraternity. Some time afterwards our Order formed an intimate union with the Knights of St John of Jerusalem. From that time our Lodges took the name of Lodges of St John. He went on to say: The kings, princes, and lords returned from Palestine to their own lands and there established divers Lodges. At the time of the last Crusades many Lodges were already erected in Germany, Italy, Spain, France, and from thence in Scotland, because of the close alliance between the French and the Scotch.

James, Lord Steward of Scotland, was Grand Master of a Lodge established at Kilwinning, in the West of Scotland, MCCLXXXVI (ad 1286), shortly after the death of Alexander III, King of Scotland, and one year before John Baliol [sic] mounted the throne. This lord received as Freemasons into his Lodge the Earls of Gloucester and Ulster, the one English, the other Irish. By degrees our Lodges and our rites were neglected in most places. This is why of so many historians only those of Great Britain speak of our Order. Nevertheless it preserved its splendor among those Scotsmen to whom the Kings of France confided during many centuries the safeguard of their royal persons. Ramsey did not suggest creating new rites, but this is exactly what his lecture produced, and very soon Scots Masonry was born. The term Scottish, Scots, Scotch or Ecosse became a brand name for what were seen as elite knightly and Templar-styled orders. In 1738, In Eminenti, the first papal bull attacking Freemasonry and prohibiting Catholics from becoming Freemasons, was issued. The first Lodge to be affected by the bull was, interestingly, a Lodge in Rome comprised of Jacobites, supporters of the exiled Scottish Stuart monarchy. Although most French Freemasons were Roman Catholics, and therefore subject to the authority of the Pope, the bull did nothing to dissuade them and they embraced the new craze. From France, Scots Masonry quickly spread across Europe and America, and more than 1,100 degrees appeared over the years that followed, forming more than 100 rites. Many of these rites had a short existence, but amongst these early developments we find the birth of the Royal Order of Scotland, the Rose Croix degree, the Rectified Scottish Rite, and the Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite. In 1761, Stephen Morin was given the authority to take a 25- degree system, known as the Rite of Perfection, to the western hemisphere. Starting from the West Indies, this form of Freemasonry spread to the American mainland. The newly emerging York Rite, containing Royal Arch Chapters, Cryptic Councils and the Commandery of Knight Templar, was also taking

root at the same time on the American continent. A change from the 25-degree Rite of Perfection to a new 33- degree system took place under the Constitution of 1786. The number of degrees in the new system was settled on as an allusion to the 33 years of the life of Christ. By 1802, the Supreme Council of the 33rd degree was the name adopted, but this changed to become the Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite in 1804, in agreement with the Supreme Council in France. Oddly enough, the Scottish Rite was not established in Scotland until as late as 1846. The full creation of what we know today as Scottish Rite came about when Albert Pike, Confederate general and Freemason, became the Sovereign Grand Commander of the Southern Jurisdiction in 1859, a position he held until his death in 1891. Famously, he rewrote and developed the rituals, producing a book that some refer to as the ‘bible’ of the Scottish Rite, The Morals and Dogma of the Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite of Freemasonry, published in 1871. Pike promoted the Rite as the supreme sanctuary for Freemasonry, containing within its degrees the wisdom of Kabbalah, hermeticism, alchemy and the philosophical teachings of the Rosicrucians. It is stated throughout Freemasonry that there are no degrees higher than the Blue degrees: Apprentice, Fellow Craft and Master Mason. That said, however, the exclusivity of the 33rd makes it one of the most highly prized degrees. The so-called higher degrees are meant to give more detail and instruction to help members reflect on the teachings of Blue Masonry. The symbolism is greatly added to and embellished throughout the Scottish Rite. The double-headed eagle, or phoenix, is the badge of the final degrees of the Scottish Rite and is said to be an alchemical interpretation similar to the ‘Chemical Marriage’ referred to in the Rosicrucian chapter. To quote Brother G. Peters, 32nd degree: As Scottish Rite Masons, may we each undertake the task of so analysing and purifying our natures, that we too may be as proud, noble, august and bold as the Eagle which is our symbol, showing our minds the direct path of the ascent into the Heavens, carrying our souls aloft to the very throne of All Creation.

The emblem is ancient in origin and is called by many the ‘Double- Headed Eagle of Lagash’, Lagash being an ancient Sumerian city. It has been used over the centuries by rulers such as Charlemagne, who adopted it around ad 802, when he became head of the German Empire, the two heads representing the union of Rome and Germany. Its use seems to have come into Freemasonry with the French Rite of Perfection around 1758, and it was the emblem of the Council of Emperors of the East and West in Paris. The successors of that council became the Supreme Councils of the 33rd Degree throughout the world. It has been said that the founder of the Scottish Rite was actually King Frederick II (the Great) of Prussia, whose heraldic arms bore the double-headed eagle, but although he was known to be a Freemason it is believed that this claim for the Rite is a fable propagated by the Masonic writers Albert Pike and Albert Mackey to give a splendid pedigree to their beloved Order. In The Lost Symbol, as Robert Langdon is dashing into the Temple Room of the House of the Temple he passes a bronze bust of Albert Pike, in a nod to the origins of the Scottish Rite that Dan Brown has chosen to include. Although the 33 degrees are often spoken of, there are actually technically only 29. The first three are the craft degrees, and four to thirty-two are the degrees proper. The final degree is an honour bestowed on members for outstanding service to Freemasonry. As members are informed: Sublime Princes of the Royal Secret of the Thirty- second Degree, not less than thirty-three years of age, at an annual session of the Supreme Council, may be elected Sovereign Grand Inspectors General of the Thirty-third and Last Degree, Honorary Members of the Supreme Council, by unanimous vote taken by secret ballot. This honour is conferred because of ‘outstanding service to the Fraternity or for service to others which reflects credit upon the Order’. Honorary Members have the right to be present at all sessions of the Supreme Council, except executive sessions, and to a voice therein, but no vote. Sovereign Grand Inspectors General of the Thirty-third and Last

Degree may be elected Active Members of the Supreme Council at the Annual Meetings thereof. The Mother Supreme Council of the World, as it is called, which is basically the Grand Lodge of the Rite, as mentioned in The Lost Symbol, is the House of the Temple in Washington DC. The degree structure that it operates (and it should be noted that there are slightly different names within the Northern Jurisdiction of the USA and other jurisdictions) is as follows: 4th degree Secret Master 5th degree Perfect Master 6th degree Intimate Secretary 7th degree Provost and Judge 8th degree Intendant of the Building 9th degree Elu of the Nine 10th degree Elu of the Fifteen 11th degree Elu of the Twelve 12th degree Master Architect 13th degree Royal Arch of Solomon 14th degree Perfect Elu 15th degree Knight of the East, or Knight of the Sword, or Knight of the Eagle 16th degree Prince of Jerusalem 17th degree Knight of the East and West 18th degree Knight Rose Croix 19th degree Grand Pontiff 20th degree Master of the Symbolic Lodge 21st degree Noachite, or Prussian Knight 22nd degree Knight of the Royal Axe, or Prince of Libanus 23rd degree Chief of the Tabernacle 24th degree Prince of the Tabernacle 25th degree Knight of the Brazen Serpent 26th degree Prince of Mercy, or Scottish Trinitarian 27th degree Knight of the Sun, or Prince Adept 28th degree Knight Commander of the Temple 29th degree Scottish Knight of Saint Andrew 30th degree Knight Kadosh, or Knight of the White and

Black Eagle 31st degree Inspector Inquisitor 32nd degree Master of the Royal Secret 33rd degree Inspector General Robert Langdon suggests that members of the Rite know the House of the Temple as Heredom. Heredom is also the title of the journal of the annual transactions of the Scottish Rite Research Society. However, the term is actually most famously linked to the Royal Order of Scotland, which is another order entirely. It dates to around the 1740s and still works its eighteenth-century ritual virtually intact. Its worldwide headquarters are in Scotland, at its Grand Lodge in Edinburgh. The Royal Order comprises two degrees, namely the Heredom of Kilwinning and the Knighthood of the Rosy Cross. In 1877, the Masonic authority Kenneth Mackenzie wrote: Heredom – a word of doubtful significance in Masonry. It has successively been associated with the Royal Order of Heredom in Scotland, with the word Heroden as a Scottish mountain, and from the Greek words for Holy and House; thus the title of the Rose Croix of Heredom would convey the meaning Rosy Cross of the Holy House. The House of the Rosy Cross (the House of the Temple), which Langdon states rivals Scotland’s Rosslyn Chapel architecturally, is a twentieth-century construction completed in 1915 to become the ‘spiritual’ home of the Rite. It is an amazing replica of one of the Seven Wonders of the World, the Mausoleum of King Mausolus at Halicarnassus. It is from this king that we get the word mausoleum, meaning ‘for dead remains’. As well as being a Grand Masonic temple, the House of the Temple is in fact also a mausoleum. In 1944, and later, in 1953, with the permission of the United States Congress, the remains of the past Sovereign Grand Commanders Albert Pike and John Henry Cowels were placed in vaults either side of the ‘light well’. On a final note regarding The Lost Symbol and High Grade Freemasonry, secret vaults and the Lost Word feature as an enduring allegory throughout Freemasonry. In the 2004 adventure

movie National Treasure, that which is hidden is a material treasure. In the film, the Declaration of Independence acts like a pirate map and the hidden message is no more esoteric than ‘X marks the spot’. In The Lost Symbol, Dan Brown at least seems to have grasped the message and indeed the mystery of the ancient traditions that Freemasonry claims as its own. The secret is that the great treasure is not lost, and is not material, but is hidden or sleeping within each of us, waiting to be recovered. SEE ALSO: Freemasonry, Heredom, House of the Temple

SEAL OF SOLOMON/ STAR OF DAVID In The Lost Symbol, having made the first, fundamental steps towards deciphering the pyramid and capstone, Katherine Solomon and Robert Langdon grab a cab and head north-west, away from the Jefferson Building. In an apparent eureka moment, Katherine Solomon states that the term Jeova Sanctus Unus, one true God, is summed up in the sacred symbol of the Hebrews, the Seal of Solomon, also known as the Star of David, which is also a highly significant Masonic symbol. By drawing the Star of David on the Great Seal of the United States, found on a Dollar Bill, Katherine reveals the term ‘MASON’, leading her to declare that they should immediately head for Freedom Plaza. The Seal of Solomon consists of two equilateral triangles, one pointing upward and the other downward, shown either as a solid shape or more usually in outline, with the two triangles intertwined to create a six-pointed star. This symbol is known variously as the Seal of Solomon, Star of David or Shield of David, the last term thought to derive from the metal structure used to strengthen King David’s battle shield. The origins of the symbol are obscure, but since 1897, when it was first used as a Zionist nationalist symbol, it has been widely regarded as a Jewish emblem and is closely identified with the state of Israel. However, despite its identification with Judaism, the Seal of Solomon/Star of David does not have any specific Jewish religious significance and indeed is not solely a Judaic symbol. Nevertheless, within Jewish tradition it appears that the Seal of Solomon’s earliest use was as an amulet against evil. Talmudic texts from the medieval period make reference to the Seal of Solomon engraved upon a magical ring, a divine gift to King Solomon that acted as both a protection against demons and a means of

commanding them. It would appear that some time after the eleventh century, the term Seal of Solomon was superceded by Star of David, although why this change should have taken place is uncertain. By the twelfth century, the Seal of Solomon/Star of David motif is mentioned in Jewish biblical commentaries, notably Eshkol ha-Kofer by Judah ben Elijah Hadassi, who notes that the ‘Shield of David’ sign acts as a form of protection in connection with the mezuzah, a piece of parchment placed outside Jewish homes that carries verses from the Torah. Bearing in mind the emblem’s shield connotations, it is not surprising that its early use appears to have been as an amulet and symbol of protection on doorways and entrances. The hexagram is used extensively in Islamic tradition, with the six-pointed star engraved on the bottom of cups, on various artefacts and as architectural decoration in mosques and other structures, as well as being mentioned in literature, where the symbol specifically linked to King Solomon and his magical seal ring. In fact, it is thought that the Judaic tradition of the Seal of Solomon/Star of David hexagram had an Arabic source. It is purported that Kabbalistic literature illustrated with Islamic decorative arts transmitted the symbol to Judaism. As evidence for this idea, the Jewish philosopher Professor Gershom Scholem cites thirteenth-century copies of Jewish religious books decorated with the symbol; these had been translated in Islamic countries and then had found their way to Spain and Germany. As in the Islamic tradition, the Seal of Solomon/Star of David was also used as a decorative motif in synagogues. Christopher Knight and Robert Lomas point out in The Hiram Key that Alfred Gotte, a nineteenth- century synagogue builder, stated that: As its geometrical shape lent itself easily to all structural and ornamental purposes, it has now been . . . an established fact, already hallowed by tradition, that the Megan David for the Jews is the same kind of holy symbol that the Cross and the Crescent are for the monotheistic faiths. Indeed, a stone from a late third-century synagogue in Galilee is engraved with the Shield of David, underlining its architectural use. The stone came from an entrance arch, further emphasising the

hexagram’s early use as a symbol of protection, as suggested by its association with the mezuzah. When Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent rebuilt most of the Temple Mount in Jerusalem in 1536, he decorated the walls around the city with Seals of Solomon as a means of protection. Whatever its origins, the Seal of Solomon has great significance in the Kabbalah, the Jewish mystical tradition, where the hexagram has a number of meanings. Primarily it symbolises the number seven: its six points represent the directions up, down, north, south, east and west, illustrating the universal and omnipotent dominion of God, and the central hexagon, containing the Tree of Life, represents harmony and grace. The two triangles embody good and evil, God and mankind, heaven and earth. The upward triangle also represents fire and is symbolic of mankind’s desire to return to God. The downward-pointing triangle represents water and the descent of the divine into the physical. Additionally, the Kabbalistic hexagram can be used to illustrate the ten Sephiroth (the attributes/ emanations of God), with the Tree of Life in the centre and the nine remaining Sephiroth at the points and outer angles of the hexagram. The twelve signs of the zodiac are also incorporated into the Kabbalistic hexagram within the six points. As in the Kabbalah, the hexagram is used in alchemy to represent fire and water. In addition, when a horizontal line is drawn across the upward fire triangle and across the downward water triangle, earth and air are also represented, thus illustrating the four elements. In alchemy the hexagram is therefore the sign of transmutation, with Herbert Silberer’s book Hidden Symbolism of Alchemy and the Occult Arts calling the Seal of Solomon the Philosopher’s Stone that would bring about a spiritual metamorphosis.
