In The Continuum Encyclopedia of Symbols, Udo Becker notes that the hexagram is ‘often a symbol of the interpenetration of the visible and invisible worlds’ and is the ‘symbol of the union of all opposites since it is composed of the basic shapes and signs of the elements’. The hexagram is highly significant in Buddhism, being the symbol for Anahata, the heart chakra in tantric yoga, while in Hindu religious practices and tradition the symbol has enormous importance and meaning, being revered as the sign of the sacred union between Shiva and Shakti. As such, the two interlocking triangles symbolise the male and female aspects that together

represent Creation itself. The concept of the male ‘blade’ and female ‘chalice’ appears to be an ancient one, suggesting the male procreative power and the female reproductive power. This theme featured heavily – and controversially – in Dan Brown’s previous novel The Da Vinci Code. In Magdalene’s Lost Legacy, Margaret Starbird states that united these symbols are ‘in sacred harmony renewing the cycles of life on the planet. And in their intimate intertwining the symbol of the hexagram – – the archetypal image of the sacred marriage.’ The ‘intimate’ partnership suggested by the sacred union of the two triangles in the form of the hexagram might be the reason the Great Seal of the United States has the thirteen stars, representative of the original colonies, displayed in the shape of the Star of David. Within Freemasonry, the Seal of Solomon/Star of David is symbolic of the union of male and female, active and passive and other opposite forces such as dark and light, good and evil, and it is widely used as insignia for badges of office, often being placed within a circle, or as a decorative element in Masonic temples. The hexagram in Paganism is symbolic of harmony and knowledge and represents the concept of ‘As above, so it is below’, the balance between the macrocosm and the microcosm, while in Satanism the symbol has taken on a more sinister meaning, often associated with curses (note the phrase ‘to put a hex on someone’) or used to invoke dark forces. The seventeenth-century magical text The Lesser Key of Solomon, which lists demons and spirits and their attributes, states that the hexagram is ‘shown unto the Spirits when they do appear, so that they be compelled to take human shape upon them and be obedient’. Indeed, Aleister Crowley used the ‘Hexagram of Solomon’ in the Ritual of the Beast, no doubt because the symbol is thought to represent 666, the number of the devil, having as it does six points, a six-sided hexagon and six small triangles. SEE ALSO: Alchemy, Aleister Crowley, Freemasonry, Great Seal of the United States

SHRINERS In The Lost Symbol, Dan Brown’s character Inoue Sato explains that the Ancient Arabic Order of the Nobles of the Mystic Shrine are generally known as the Shriners and that they are attached to the Masons. Turner Simkins, another character from the novel, identifies the Shriners as ‘guys who build hospitals for kids’ and recalls the distinctive red fezzes that its members wear. All very mysterious. Two things can immediately be confirmed. Sato is correct – the Ancient Arabic Order of the Nobles of the Mystic Shrine are normally called the Shriners, but their longer name is abbreviated to A.A.O.N.M.S. What is more, the organisation really does exist and builds those children’s hospitals. The Shriners started out in 1870 in Manhattan, where Freemasons regularly met for lunch. It was during these meetings that the idea of a new fraternity dedicated to fellowship and fun was conceived. One of this group, William Florence, a famous actor, was later invited to a gathering in Marseilles by an Arab diplomat, during which there was comedy with music and the evening finished with the assembly all agreeing to become members of a secret society. William made sketches and notes of this gathering, and that of two other meetings in Cairo and Algiers. Returning to New York in the summer of 1871, Florence and a friend, Walter Fleming, agreed on a ritual, costumes and insignia and initiated 11 other members into their fraternity. In keeping with their full title, there was an Arabic theme to their gatherings. Their membership grew and today there are around half a million Shriners. In Washington DC, the Almas Shrine Temple, located on Franklin Park, is a five-storey edifice built in 1929 in a distinctive Middle Eastern style. In The Lost Symbol, the clues ‘The Order’ and ‘Eight Franklin Square’ are initially assumed to refer to the Shriners and a location. Although the Arab theme is still part of the Shriners’ modus operandi, their rituals have no Islamic element. There is, in fact, no particularly religious aspect to their ceremony. However, since all Shriners have to be Masons, members must profess a belief in the Supreme Being. It would be impossible to join as an atheist or even

an agnostic. From its origins as an organisation intended to serve a social function, the Shriners acquired a place as essentially a Masonic drinking club. As John Greer explains in The Element Encyclopedia of Secret Societies and Hidden History: For the first half of its existence, if not more, the Shrine existed primarily as an excuse for partying and drinking on a heroic scale. By the early 1880s the annual convention of the Imperial Council, the international governing body of the Shrine, had already earned a reputation as the wildest party in American fraternalism. Eventually, a more public-spirited purpose was developed with fund-raising activities including provision for victims of the 1888 yellow fever epidemic in Florida. From 1930, the plan to build and maintain children’s hospitals, with which their name has now become closely associated, was launched. It is in this context that Turner Simkins mentions the organisation in The Lost Symbol. The Shriners Hospitals for Children has its headquarters in Tampa, Florida. Their admissions policy requires that patients must be under 18 years of age and capable of receiving treatment. There are now more than 20 of these not-for-profit free hospitals in North America. Each of these hospitals has some sort of specialism. For example, four of them treat burns victims, while three are particularly concerned with spinal-cord injuries. Sometimes patients with ongoing needs can receive both inpatient and outpatient care until they reach 21 years of age. In addition to the hospitals, the Shriners finance free screening clinics for children under 17. The specialists involved are generally expert in identifying and treating abnormal muscular and skeletal conditions. The distinctive headwear worn by Shriners – the fez – was chosen as part of their regalia because of its association with the Arab world. Though the hat is declining in popularity in North Africa, the Shriners have stuck to their tradition of wearing the black-tasselled red fez to maintain their connection with the past. Shrine circuses are among the most successful and enjoyable

attractions staged to raise contributions to their charities. Featuring acrobats, performing horses and dogs, jugglers and all the colourful and exciting aspects of a family circus, they attract huge audiences. Although the Shriners is a male organisation, it should be mentioned that female members of Shriner families can join an affiliated women’s group. Almost inevitably the women, whose organisation was formed in 1913, call themselves Daughters of the Nile. One of the most famous Shriners was Harold Lloyd (1893– 1971), comedian, film producer and silent screen actor. His face, with his trademark horn-rimmed circular glasses, is instantly recognisable to the older generation even today. He was not just a member, though. He was active enough to become Imperial Potentate of North America in 1949, and in 1963 Lloyd became president of the Shriners Hospital Corporation and chairman of the Board of Trustees. In 2000, the membership requirements for the Shriners were changed, removing the necessity for Shriners to hold high degrees within the Scottish Rite or the Knight Templar degree of the York Rite of Freemasonry. This was designed to increase the number of those joining the organisation; however, it has been reported that the move may have decreased Scottish Rite membership in some areas. Shriners derive a great deal of satisfaction from organising colourful, noisy and very spectacular parades. When Shriners take to the streets for one of these famous events, including their traditional small clown-style cars, they have drum corps, bagpipers and clowns contributing to the cacophonous excitement. While there are complaints from time to time about the inconvenience in the various towns where these processions take place, it seems fairly obvious that most citizens welcome the enjoyment generated. The Shriners were first formed to give an opportunity for its founding members to have fun – today that fun is taken into the wider community. These public activities seem likely to continue for many years to come. SEE ALSO: Freemasonry, Scottish Rite Freemasonry

SMITH, JOSEPH, AND THE BOOK OF MORMON One of the religious practices given as an example of ‘frightening if taken out of context’ in The Lost Symbol is the Mormon practice of baptism of the dead. This posthumous ceremony is possible for those who died before having a valid baptism and enables passage into God’s kingdom for those in the spirit world who accept the gospel. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints – sometimes referred to as the Mormon Church – was founded by Joseph Smith, its prophet, born in Sharon, Vermont, in 1805. The family eventually moved to New York State, since Smith’s parents’ farm proved unsuccessful, and because of their poverty the children had to work, as a result of which they did not receive much schooling. Joseph had a vision in 1827 of an angel called Moroni who had taken him to a hill where digging had revealed gold plates on which were inscribed the Book of Mormon in ‘reformed Egyptian’. The title is taken from the ‘prophet-historian’ Mormon, who is said to have compiled the writings on the plates. In addition, there were two stones, Urim and Thummin. In The Lost Symbol, Robert Langdon suggests that Joseph used these stones as ‘magic eyeglasses’ to translate the plates; it seems that the two stones are synonymous with the two lenses of a pair of spectacles. The method of transcription is explained by Richard van Wagoner and Steven Walker in Joseph Smith: The Gift of Seeing, where they quote Michael Morse, Smith’s brother-in-law, describing how ‘the mode of procedure consisted in Joseph’s placing the Seer Stone in the crown of a hat, then putting his face into the hat, so as to entirely cover his face’. Joseph Smith told of Jewish families who went to America in Old Testament times from Jerusalem. One group that Smith called the Lamanites were said to be among the ancestors of Native Americans. His translation of the gold plates also indicated that Jesus Christ had visited America after the Resurrection before ascending into heaven. A small group of believers began to lend their support to his ideas. By 1830, his translation of the Book of Mormon was complete. He found people who were willing to testify that they had seen the gold plates and their testimony is included in the

publication. Eventually, the plates, along with Urim and Thummin, were returned to the angel Moroni, who took them away. Publication of the Book of Mormon provoked a storm of protest from more orthodox churchgoers. Others, however, were attracted by its revelations and came along to be baptised as members of the infant Mormon Church. Joseph became an eloquent, humorous and persuasive speaker and attracted many new followers. Unlike so much of the hellfire and damnation preaching at the time, this new form of religion not only promised a very comfortable afterlife to those who had lived decent, honest lives but also that sinners would not face eternal cruel punishment. Unbelievers, referred to by the Mormons as ‘gentiles’, were frequently extremely hostile towards Joseph and his followers. As violent opposition grew, many of the faithful followed Joseph westwards to seek a more peaceful home in which to practise their faith. In 1839, they established a town in Illinois called Nauvoo, with their leader as mayor. A few years later, he had become ambitious enough to seek to become president of the United States. Not everything in his life was successful, though. Many of his closest friends and colleagues had bitter quarrels with him and left, or were thrown out of, the Church. Joseph’s most controversial piece of behaviour was to propose ‘celestial marriage’ to a number of women, many of them already married, some to his closest colleagues. These celestial marriages would apparently last for eternity and be superior to earthly marriages. The Mormons have for generations been strongly criticised for supporting polygamy. It should be noted that the Church officially gave up the practice as long ago as 1890 and excommunicates any members who disobey the proscription. There are, however, some so-called Mormon fundamentalists, mainly in the United States, Canada and Mexico, who claim that to be admitted to the highest degree of Mormon heaven it is an essential requirement. In 1844, a printing press was set up by several of Smith’s detractors, and in June the first and only edition of the Nauvoo Expositor was published. The newspaper was devoted to criticising Smith, so, along with the city council, he ordered the press to be destroyed. Following this, the governor of the state of Illinois ordered his arrest on the grounds that he had contravened the First Amendment, which guarantees free speech and freedom of the

press. The militia escorted him and some followers, including his older brother, Hyrum, to jail in Carthage, Illinois, which they guarded for fear that a mob of gentiles, or alternatively a troop of loyal Mormons, might attack. However, when an infiltration of the building by disguised ex-militiamen with blackened faces did occur, the defenders did not act. Joseph had been allowed to keep a gun and wounded some of his attackers as they approached him on the second floor of the jail. Out of ammunition, he ran towards the window but was shot by the insurgents. At the same time, attackers still outside saw him at the window and fired at him. He fell to the ground, where more shots were fired. His earthly life was over at 38. The Church of Latter-day Saints survived Joseph Smith’s death and is a powerful force even in countries distant from America. From 1847 until he died 30 years later, the ‘American Moses’ Brigham Young was president of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. He was instrumental in the founding of Salt Lake City and was the first governor of the territory of Utah. The famous university bearing his name is owned by the Mormon Church. The Encyclopaedia Britannica, in its summary of Mormon doctrine, gives the following explanation: ‘Mormon doctrine diverges from the orthodoxy of established Christianity . . . in affirming that God has evolved from man and that men might evolve into gods.’ No better description could be applied to the concept that Dan Brown is exploring within the pages of The Lost Symbol.

SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION In The Lost Symbol, the Smithsonian Institution plays a crucial role in events: Peter Solomon is its secretary, but more importantly Mal’akh, posing as Solomon’s assistant, deceives Langdon into travelling to Washington DC, ostensibly to give a talk at a Smithsonian gala dinner. The Smithsonian Institution is an educational and research institute administered by the US government. It is also part-funded by public money, in addition to private endowments, donations and the profits from its media and retail outlets. The Smithsonian Institution exists to preserve, study, exhibit and interpret collections of art, natural specimens and archival and library materials with an unrivalled ‘scope, depth, and quality’, whilst its research aims to increase and spread knowledge and support original research in science, art, history and culture. With its nineteen museums, nine research centres and national zoo, the Smithsonian Institution is the world’s largest museum complex; its diverse collections contain a staggering 136 million objects. In addition to this, there are also 156 affiliate museums worldwide, which are able to share the Smithsonian’s vast resources. Of the 19 museums, 17 are to be found in Washington DC, including the American Indian museum, American History museum, Natural History museum, the Air and Space Museum, the American Art Museum, the Portrait Gallery and the Smithsonian Institution Building. The other two Smithsonian museums are located in New York, and the Air and Space Museum’s Udvar-Hazy Center is based in Chantilly, Virginia. All of the Smithsonian’s facilities in Washington DC are free to the public. It was thanks to a bequest by James Smithson that the Smithsonian Institution was founded. Smithson was a celebrated British scientist and mineralogist who was born in 1765 in Paris, France, the illegitimate son of Sir Hugh Smithson, Duke of Northumberland, and Elizabeth Hungerford Keate Macie, a wealthy widow and reputed descendent of Henry VII of England. In 1782, James Macie, as he was known until a few years after his mother’s death in 1800, entered Pembroke College, Oxford, to read chemistry and mineralogy, obtaining a Master of Arts degree in 1786. A year later, aged 22, he became the youngest fellow to be elected to the

Royal Society, an academy of science established in London in 1660. James Smithson travelled all over Europe searching for and classifying minerals and crystals, publishing around 27 scientific papers. By the time of his death in Genoa, Italy, in 1829, Smithson had amassed a large personal fortune through his mother’s inheritance and shrewd investments, which he bequeathed to his nephew and sole heir, Henry James Hungerford. In his will, written in 1826, James Smithson stated that should his nephew die without issue, legitimate or otherwise, his estate was to go to ‘the United States of America, to found at Washington, under the name of the Smithsonian Institution, an establishment for the increase and diffusion of knowledge among men’. Bearing in mind that James Smithson had never visited the United States nor had he apparently made contact with anyone living there, his bequest is highly unusual. Some commentators believe his decision stems from an admiration for the United States’ spirit of enlightenment, or a wish to snub the stringent social code and strictures prevalent in Britain at the time – a code that denied him social status and title due to the stigma of illegitimacy. Interestingly, he appears to have been a detractor of the monarchy, writing in 1792: ‘May other nations, at the time of their reforms, be wise enough to cast off, at first, the contemptible encumbrance.’ He also later wrote that he wished for his name to ‘live in the memory of man, when the titles of the Northumberlands and the Percys are extinct and forgotten’, suggesting that he was unable to forgive the British class and social system for the penalties imposed upon him. With Henry Hungerford’s death in 1835, Smithson’s assets passed to the United States. Surprisingly, there was much debate over whether the bequest should be accepted or not, with John C. Calhoun, a South Carolina senator, stating that it was ‘beneath the dignity of the United States to receive presents of this kind’. By 1836, Congress had accepted the bequest; however, because of a lawsuit in London contesting the will, it was not until 1838 that the matter was finally settled and 11 boxes containing 104,960 gold sovereigns were loaded on to the USS Mediator and shipped to the United States, where the gold was melted down and minted into coin totalling $508,318. Eight years of further debate followed, focusing on what form the

Institution should take, where it should be sited, its administration and the building’s design, until the matter was finally settled and the Smithsonian Institution was established on 10 August 1846. In order to fulfil the Smithsonian’s multiple roles and functions, a new building was required. Designed by James Renwick Jr, the Smithsonian Institution Building on Jefferson Drive was completed in 1855 and included a library, chemical laboratory, natural history laboratory, lecture halls, museum and art gallery. Built of red sandstone, the building is now more generally known as ‘the Castle’ because of its nine towers and battlements. Whilst most delighted in its architecture, not everyone was happy with the end result. Dorothea Dix, a social reformer and crusader, called it a ‘monstrous pile of misshapen towers, arches, columns’. Today, the Smithsonian Institutional Building houses the administrative offices and information centre. As an organisation, the Smithsonian Institution is divided into four areas: science; history, art and culture; finance and administration; and Smithsonian enterprises. The Act of Congress establishing the Smithsonian Institution stated that it was to be administered by a Board of Regents who were responsible for overseeing and managing the Institution on behalf of the federal government and carrying out ‘the responsibilities of the United States as trustee of the Smithson trust’. The board’s role is taken very seriously, with special mention given in the statement of values that ‘the Smithsonian must be mindful that it is a public trust operating on behalf of the American public and the United States government to carry out its mission to increase and diffuse knowledge’. The high-profile Board of Regents is made up of seventeen members, meeting four times a year, consisting of the Chief Justice of the United States, the vice president of the United States, three members of the House of Representatives, three members of the Senate and nine citizens. The chief executive officer of the Smithsonian is the secretary, who is appointed by the Board of Regents. It was thanks to the vision and tenacity of the Institution’s first secretary, Joseph Henry, a distinguished physicist, that the Smithsonian grew and developed into the scientific and research organisation we know today. SEE ALSO: Royal Society and the Invisible College

SMSC – SMITHSONIAN MUSEUM SUPPORT CENTER One of the major locations for the action in The Lost Symbol is a secret laboratory hidden within a large support complex for the Smithsonian museums. The Smithsonian has what is arguably the world’s largest museum collection and it is certainly one of the most important in the world. Due to its vast size and the relatively small public display facilities, only a tiny portion of the collection can be displayed at any given time. Also, many of the artefacts are invaluable to scientific research and so the Smithsonian allows researchers access to elements of the collection while ensuring their survival for future generations. To address these concerns, the Smithsonian Museum Support Center (SMSC) was created, the vision of Vince Wilcox, director of the massive structure since 1981. Wilcox spent several years planning this state-of-the-art storage facility for one of the nation’s most valuable historical collections. Dedicated in May 1983, after two years in the making, the SMSC was built using the latest in museum technology, creating the perfect storage area for the Smithsonian’s vast collection. The facility is located in Suitland, Maryland, just outside Washington DC, approximately six miles from the famous Mall at the heart of the city. It covers four and a half acres and provides a total of 435,000 square feet of storage space for the collection. SMSC is made up of ample office and laboratory space and five ‘pods’ that house the actual collection. These pods are designed to ensure that the Smithsonian’s collection will survive for many generations to come by employing the latest in climate control and pest-management systems. Each of the pods is the size of a football field and approximately 28 feet in height. They have insulated outside walls that are over a foot and a half thick and are positioned in a zigzag pattern, making future pod additions to the existing building relatively easy. The office and laboratory space and the storage pods are separated by a 20-foot-wide corridor, known as the Street. It is currently estimated that the Smithsonian requires another 3.5 million square feet of storage; plans are in the works to address these needs over the next two to three decades by adding to the SMSC.

There are tens of thousands of storage cabinets housing the more than 54 million items in the collection. Everything from 44-foot- long totem poles to microscopic plants and animals is stored there. Because the facility is home to such a valuable collection, it is protected by a top-notch security system, which combines sophisticated monitoring and detection equipment with security staff. When you enter the facility, you are required to allow staff to search through any personal belongings brought into the SMSC at the first security checkpoint, then credentials for building access are issued. Employees are issued pass cards that open doors and record access to specific areas of the facility. February 2010 will see the completion of renovations to pod three, also known as the ‘wet pod’. Millions of biological specimens that have been preserved in fluids such as formalin and ethanol are stored in this pod. It is equipped with several special features, including explosion-proof electrical devices and special floor drains, all designed to give extra protection to the plethora of specimens stored within. Pod three is the setting for the murder of Trish Dunne in The Lost Symbol. Mal’akh drowns her in a tank filled with ethanol preserving a giant squid. Pods one, two, four and five are for the storage of other museum collections of both human and natural origin. Pod four has a section referred to as the ‘high bay’, which was created specifically to house the largest items in the collection, such as totem poles, large mammal skeletons and boats. In The Lost Symbol, pod five is where Katherine Solomon conducts her work in Noetic sciences. It should be noted that there is no reason to believe that such a facility exists in pod five, or in any part of the SMSC, for that matter. The laboratory facilities all feature the latest in available technology. The SMSC is also home to the Smithsonian’s Conservation Analytical Laboratory (CAL). Occupying 24,000 square feet of the laboratory, this area is used in the technical study of, research into and training in conservation techniques. There is also a ‘clean room’, which was specifically constructed for the department of mineral sciences. Their collection of Antarctic meteorites is stored in nitrogen gas, ensuring that the items are kept free from contaminants. The only other similar facility is at the Johnson Space Center in Houston. It is important to note that the SMSC was not created with public

displays of any kind in mind. By limiting the number of people who visit the facility, the random factor of human body heat is minimised. This factor has played havoc in other collections around the world. Similarly, many of the tombs open to the public in Egypt have been severely damaged by the erosion caused over decades of playing host to thousands of daily visitors. The principal goal of the SMSC is research into and preservation and conservation of the Smithsonian’s collection. A museum, by its very nature, is a contradiction in terms: by displaying the items for public viewing, you are exposing them to possible damage or contamination. The SMSC exists to minimise the potential dangers to the collection and to allow the public at large to benefit from the wonders included there. SEE ALSO: Institute of Noetic Sciences, Smithsonian Institution

SOLOMON’S TEMPLE ‘Is there no help for the widow’s son?’ These words were encoded on the dust jacket of the US edition of The Da Vinci Code back in 2003. It was from this dust jacket that many people first gleaned clues as to the content of what was to become The Lost Symbol. The phrase itself is Masonic in origin and points to an allegorical story that plays a prominent role in Freemasonic rites and rituals. It involves Hiram Abiff, Master Mason and chief architect of the legendary Solomon’s Temple in Jerusalem. In The Lost Symbol, the story of Hiram Abiff ‘s murder is vividly recreated during a Freemasonic initiation ceremony that has been clandestinely filmed by Mal’akh. Hiram Abiff, it seems, is the same Hiram referenced in the Bible, who was a master bronzeworker and craftsman employed by King Solomon on the construction of the Temple. The Hiram described in I Kings 7:13–14 is ‘the son of a widow’, coming from Tyre. He is not to be confused with Hiram, King of Tyre, who is mentioned as having sent materials for the construction of the Temple. Solomon’s Temple holds special significance for Freemasons, not only because of their association with Hiram Abiff but also because of some of the symbolic and mysterious elements displayed in the Temple. In 1801, the Masonic scholar the Reverend Dr George Oliver explained the significance of the Temple to Masons in Revelations of a Square: The Society adopted the Temple of Solomon for its symbol, because it was the most stable and the most magnificent structure that ever existed, whether we consider its foundation or superstructure; so that of all the societies men have invented, no one was ever more firmly united, or better planned, than the Masons . . . The edifices which Freemasons build are nothing more than virtues or vices to be erected or destroyed; and in this case heaven only occupies their minds, which soars above the corrupted world. The Temple of Solomon denotes reason and intelligence.

King Solomon was the son of the legendary leader of the Jews King David. King David himself had offered to build the First Temple to God, even going so far as to purchase and prepare the land for the site on Mount Moriah, but God refused him the honour and the duty fell to his son, Solomon. The main accounts of the building of the Temple are to be found in the Old Testament books of Joshua, Judges, I–II Samuel and I–II Kings. The dimensions and size of the original Temple are constantly debated and argued over, with many of the measurements being of some symbolic importance. At the eastern entrance to the Temple stood the two pillars Boaz and Jachin; today in every lodge room in the Masonic world, two pillars also called Boaz and Jachin stand to remind the initiate of the connection to the Temple of Solomon. We are told in the story of Hiram Abiff that he is murdered by three assassins who try to extract from him the secret password of the Master Mason. Hiram refuses to divulge the sacred word and is therefore killed. For Masons, this allegorical story teaches the initiate that one’s word is one’s bond and that the brevity of life should be understood. According to Masonic author Chris McClintock, the ritual in which an initiate is received into Freemasonry incorporates in a symbolic way the method by which Hiram Abiff was murdered. In the ritual, the candidate is first symbolically cut across the throat with a Masonic rule, echoing the first blow Hiram received. Next, the initiate is struck on the left breast with a heavy Masonic square, which is supposedly how the second assailant attacked Hiram. The final and fatal blow (metaphorically) is performed with a mallet, which is aimed at the head, again in imitation of the original story. It is during this ritual that Hiram is referred to as ‘the widow’s son’. In McClintock’s soon-to-be-published Sun of God, several astounding revelations are brought to light regarding not only the symbolic and mysterious origins of such rituals but also the deeper hidden identity of Hiram Abiff, as well as other characters involved in Masonic ritual. Within the Holy of Holies of Solomon’s Temple was placed the legendary Ark of the Covenant. This supernatural vessel was said to contain the two tablets that Moses brought down from Mount Sinai etched with the Ten Commandments of God. Interestingly, some Freemasonic lodges also include a replica of the Holy of Holies in which is placed a copy of the Ark of the Covenant. A fine example

of this is to be found in the Royal Arch Chapter Room of lodge (number 22) of Alexandria within the George Washington Masonic Memorial. It is claimed to be the most beautiful reproduction ever created for Masonic purposes. Today, the site of Solomon’s Temple is a centre of political machinations on a global scale. The Temple Mount, as it is now known, is under the control of a Muslim council, with Orthodox Jews forbidden to set foot on the site by order of many rabbinical authorities. To some fundamental Christians, it is on the Temple Mount that the Second Coming of the Messiah will be heralded and the mythical Third Temple will be built. To fundamentalists on all sides in the debate, the Temple Mount represents a rallying call for dogmatic belief and religious intolerance. Freemasonry sees Solomon’s Temple as a moveable feast: a temple to the Great Architect of the Universe that can be recreated in multiple locations, an example of the ‘As above, so it is below’ hermetic principle, a recreation of God’s house on earth. Solomon’s Temple was the First Temple to God – intended to be a microcosm of the greater universe. SEE ALSO: Boaz and Jachin, Freemasonry

WASHINGTON, GEORGE The image of George Washington wearing Freemasonic regalia and laying the cornerstone of the Capitol Building is not perhaps the one that first springs to mind when considering this great American. It is, however, significant within the pages of The Lost Symbol, where the links between the layout and architecture of the capital city of the USA and its first president are investigated. In February 1732, George Washington was born into a wealthy Virginia planter family whose forebears had their origins in England. Since his father died when he was only 11 years of age, much of his formative life was spent with relatives, although the Fairfax family, who were neighbours, also played a part. Lord Fairfax, the only British peer resident in colonial America, sent him with a group of men to survey his lands in the Shenandoah Valley, which young George clearly enjoyed; in 1749, at the age of 17, he was appointed Culpeper County surveyor. Washington leased then inherited a fine estate called Mount Vernon from his older half-brother Lawrence, who suffered from tuberculosis and died in 1752. Washington’s only trip outside America was a visit in 1751 to Barbados with Lawrence to try to improve his health. Washington was not, however, to have the luxury of enjoying his inheritance without interruption. He became an officer in the Virginia Militia in 1752, aged 20, and played a part in the French and Indian War (Seven Years’ War) of 1754–63, during which the Governor of Virginia, Robert Dinwiddie, twice gave him commissions to counter French ambitions in Ohio in support of the British interest. In 1755, he was with General Edward Braddock as an aide-de-camp on his march to Fort Duquesne. Despite holding the courtesy title of colonel, Washington was resentful of the British treatment of colonial officers such as himself, who were automatically subordinate to an officer of the same rank who held the King’s commission. The general was killed by the French when the British forces reached the Monongahela River, so Washington was forced to take charge. He retrieved the situation courageously and was noted for outstanding bravery. In recognition of his success, he was appointed the commander of all Virginia troops. He later led a force under Brigadier General John Forbes and recaptured Fort Duquesne,

which, after rebuilding, was renamed Fort Pitt after the British Prime Minister William Pitt the Elder. Having seen off the French, and with the honorary rank of brigadier general, Washington left the army in 1758. In addition to caring for his growing estates, Washington sat in the House of Burgesses in Williamsburg and for many years he did not show any opposition to the way his country was being run. Then, in 1765, the British Parliament passed the Stamp Act. Its aim was to help cover the cost of having British troops in North America to defend the colonists. With no representation in Parliament, the colonists were understandably outraged by the new tax. Violent protests broke out and it became apparent that the Act was not enforceable. By this time, Washington’s attitude towards the British interests in North America had begun to harden. He remarked that the British Parliament had ‘no more right to put their hands into my pocket, without my consent, than I have to put my hands into yours for money’. In 1774, he signed the Fairfax Resolves in Virginia, which called for the establishment of the Continental Congress. This would allow the colonies to collectively resist the actions of the British Parliament. Washington was elected one of the Virginia representatives to the First Continental Congress. Then, 15 years after his previous military command, he was again called upon, this time as commander in chief of the colonial army around Boston after the battles of Lexington and Concord. His assiduous enforcement of a siege ensured that the British were made to surrender the city and evacuate it in March 1776. During the following five years, despite some setbacks, his forces of American patriots achieved success over the British and their loyalist colonist allies. It was Washington’s energy and common sense, and the confidence that the army had in him, that contributed to the victory. The war effectively ended when General Cornwallis was forced to surrender Yorktown in October 1781. Two years later, Washington resigned his commission and returned to his estate at Mount Vernon, where he spent the next four years. As the political process moved towards a federal government, Washington went to Philadelphia to participate in plans to produce a constitution suitable for the union. George Washington was unanimously welcomed as president of the Constitutional

Convention in Philadelphia in 1787. The representatives widened the scope of its original brief, which was to revise the Articles of Confederation that were then in force. The result was that the Constitution of the United States was born and, two years later, in 1789, Washington was elected the first president of the United States of America in another unanimous vote. His inauguration took place in New York, then the seat of government. In 1792, he had the honour of being re-elected as president, and indeed could have run for a third time, but stepped down at the end of his second term, establishing a practice that has now been enshrined in law. In his farewell address to the people of the United States, he offered the following advice: ‘I hold the maxim no less applicable to public than to private affairs, that honesty is the best policy.’ The capital city of America was not fixed for the first few years of the republic’s history and Congress sat in various places, including Philadelphia and then New York. The location of the capital was a contentious one, with these two great cities rival claimants. Furthermore, the southern states did not want the capital to be in the north of the country. So it was decided to settle on a compromise location, on the Potomac River. In his diary entry of 12 July 1790, Washington wrote: ‘Had two bills presented to me by the joint committee of Congress. The one, an act for establishing the temporary and permanent seat of the Government of the United States.’ This became the Residence Act. The size of the new territory was fixed at 100 square miles and the Act specified that Congress would meet by 1800 in the new city. The president was given the authority to choose the exact site and appoint a surveyor. George Washington appointed Andrew Ellicott as his surveyor and by 1791 had selected the site of the District of Columbia. Pierre L’Enfant, a French architect, began designing the city plan, with the collaboration of Washington and Thomas Jefferson. In honour of Washington, the new city was named ‘the City of Washington in the Territory of Columbia’. George Washington is sometimes given the appellation ‘Father of His Country’. This was also the case for most Ancient Roman Emperors, who were voted thus by the Senate. The initials PP, standing for Pater Patriae, were proudly inscribed on their coins. There is a painting of Washington in the Senate by the artist

Rembrandt Peale called Patriae Pater; surrounding the image of Washington is a garland of oak leaves and the head of the god Jupiter. Rome referred to itself as a republic, but the republic of the United States prides itself on being a true democracy, governed as it is not by oppression but by agreement. Some disaffected Americans, many of them officers who claimed they had not been properly paid for their efforts in the war, seeing the great popularity of Washington, sought to change his position to that of king. Colonel Lewis Nicola wrote the Newburgh letter to Washington proposing that he become king and received a categorical reply: ‘Be assured Sir, no occurrence in the course of the War, has given me more painful sensations than your information of there being such ideas existing in the Army as you have expressed, and I must view with abhorrence, and reprehend with severity.’ In 1759, Washington had married Martha Dandridge (1732– 1802). She was the widow of Colonel Daniel Custis, with two small children still living. It is an endearing feature of Washington’s personality that he treated these children very much as if they were his own flesh and blood and adopted both of them. Washington showed himself as a simple human being and many stories about him indicate his willingness to perform manual labour when necessary. His wealth and position did not make him too proud, and he liked to play cards, billiards and other sports that gentlemen of his status at that time enjoyed. He was a man of his time and place, however, in that he owned slaves who worked on his land. Washington did ensure that they received the services of a doctor when it was required and is reputed to have been assiduous in ensuring that these fellow humans were well fed and adequately clothed (for his own clothes, he wore the best available and placed orders with London tailors). He refused to sell his slaves, explaining that he was against trading in human beings. During his presidency, he lived with his wife and their grandchildren in Philadelphia before returning to Mount Vernon two years before he died, on 12 December 1799. There had been plans to bury Washington in the crypt of the Capitol Building, but in his will he instructed that he be buried at Mount Vernon. On either side of the entrance to the tomb stand Egyptian-style obelisks.

As with many of the Founding Fathers of America, there is speculation over what Washington’s religious views were. He said in a letter to Sir Edward Newenham in 1792: ‘Of all the animosities which have existed among mankind those which are caused by a difference of sentiments in religion appear to be the most inveterate and distressing, and ought most to be deprecated.’ Washington attended services in Anglican and Episcopalian churches, such as that of Christ Church in Alexandria, Virginia; however, this has not prevented some speculation that in private his views may have been more inclined towards deism, a system that balances a belief in God with the laws of nature. Its adherents tend not to participate in some of the sacraments of organised religion and consequently attention has been focused on whether or not he took Holy Communion. Discussing this question in The Faiths of the Founding Fathers, David Holmes quotes the Episcopalian Bishop William White, who said, ‘General Washington never received the communion, in the churches of which I am parochial minister.’ On the other hand, it was the opinion of Washington’s granddaughter that prior to the Revolution he had taken Communion with his wife, Martha. It is possible, of course, that both accounts are correct, and that his beliefs and religious observance changed throughout his life, but because of the central role Washington plays in the history of America the subject of his faith remains hotly debated. The landmark memorial erected in Washington DC commemorating this great man is built of granite, faced with Maryland marble. It stands 555 feet high, echoing the dimensions of the monuments erected for the mightiest pharaohs of Ancient Egypt. The Washington Monument takes the form of an obelisk, a symbol of pride, reaching into the sky. Masonic ceremonies accompanied the laying of its cornerstone in 1848, as described in the entry on it in this book. Washington was also associated with Freemasonry, having been initiated at the Fredericksburg Lodge in Virginia as an Entered Apprentice on 4 November 1752. He became a Master Mason on 4 August 1753, at the age of 21. Washington was also a member of Alexandria Lodge No. 22 and was the Master of this Lodge at the time of his presidential inauguration. His entry into Freemasonry as a young man through to his participation in ceremonial Masonic regalia at events such as the cornerstone laying of the Capitol

Building clearly show that Freemasonry was an important and enduring part of his life. Evidence suggests that many of the great men associated with the American Revolution, including Washington, Benjamin Franklin, John Paul Jones and Paul Revere, were Freemasons, as were the Marquis de Lafayette and many of Washington’s generals and senior military commanders. Of the signatories to the Declaration of Independence, nine were members and seven others were at least closely associated with Masonry. Of the forty signatories of the Constitution, nine were Masons, thirteen may well have been and six others later joined the craft. It says a great deal about the character and integrity of Washington that even his defeated adversary, the stolid British King George III, appreciated his character and sacrifice for his country. The King is said to have remarked that if the commander in chief surrendered his position and returned to private life, he would be ‘the greatest man in the world’. SEE ALSO: Washington Masonic Memorial, Washington Monument

WASHINGTON DC Washington DC sits on the banks of the Potomac River like a shining diamond amidst the rolling hills of Virginia and Maryland. Indeed, the District of Columbia was originally laid out in a diamond shape some 100 miles square, with its corners facing the four cardinal compass points. The history of Washington DC reflects the history of the United States of America, rising majestically from the fire and turmoil of revolution. It was President George Washington himself who laid out the plan of the area that was to become the new city of Washington and eventually the District of Columbia. The streets and monuments of Washington are the main locations within the pages of The Lost Symbol. The city is the backdrop for the 12-hour drama that unfolds. In 1790, the Residence Act was passed, settling the question of where the new seat of government would be located. The new capital was planned on the banks of the Potomac River. Washington dispatched the surveyor Andrew Ellicott to the site, along with a team of surveyors and a very interesting character by the name of Benjamin Banneker. Banneker was the son of a freed slave and had a deep interest in and knowledge of astronomy. Banneker and Ellicott would go on to become important players in the birth of the fledgling city. The 100-mile-square area that they surveyed was marked with posts every mile, some of which survive to this day. By 1791, the new city was ready to be born. George Washington employed the services of architect and surveyor Pierre Charles L’Enfant, who was asked to produce a design for the layout of what was to become the city of Washington; however, as has been detailed elsewhere in this book, L’Enfant’s tenure was short and the city we see today is only partly his work – the rest is Ellicott’s. He stepped in to finish the layout and design of the city when L’Enfant was relieved of his post. In The Lost Symbol, symbologist Robert Langdon mentions to his students that Washington DC has inherent within its design star charts, astrological signs and zodiacs. Indeed, Langdon claims that Washington DC has more of these symbolic elements than any other city in the world. So what is the truth behind this, and the other

theories and ideas that Washington DC is laid out in a sacred and symbolic manner? According to author David Ovason, there are some 20 complete zodiacs to be found within Washington DC. Ovason goes on to explain in his groundbreaking book The Secret Architecture of Our Nation’s Capital that not only do these zodiacs exist within the fabric and architecture of the city but also that certain buildings and cornerstone-laying ceremonies were inaugurated on auspicious astrological dates. Ovason specifically claims that the constellation of Virgo, the Virgin, played an important role in the foundation of Washington DC. It is Ovason’s theory that these astrological alignments were planned and executed by important Freemasons who were responsible for the layout and planning of the city as it grew. Other researchers and conspiracy theorists claim that the street layout of Washington DC hides deeper symbolic meanings. Again, it is Freemasons who, according to these arguments, are responsible for this. One so-called ‘satanic’ feature is the appearance on a map or satellite image to the north of the White House of what looks like an inverted pentagram, or five-pointed star, with the main point converging on the White House itself. However, there is a slight problem with this theory: where Rhode Island Avenue intersects with Connecticut Avenue, it fails to continue onwards, meaning that the pentagram is missing this extension to its western point. Some claim a configuration indicative of a Masonic compass exists within the street layout, with Pennsylvania Avenue stretching out in a north-westerly direction from the Capitol Building and in a south-westerly direction Maryland Avenue. However, like the inverted pentagram to the north of the White House, one of the streets in question, Maryland Avenue, does not extend as far to the south-west and therefore the so-called compass is longer on one axis than the other. At the fringes of conspiracy theory, some researchers even see the outline of an owl within the gardens and grounds of the Capitol. Some claim this owl is a representation of Moloch, the fearsome fallen angel of Paradise Lost, in turn a biblical reference. The owl, it is claimed, also features on the One Dollar Bill. (See the entry One Dollar Bill for more information.) David Ovason notes that the area of the Federal Triangle, as it has come to be known, formed by 15th Street, Constitution Avenue and

Pennsylvania Avenue, is highly symbolic: It is almost as though L’Enfant laid upon his virgin parchment the Masonic square as symbol of the spirit of George Washington, and dedicated its three points to the founder of the nation. In the early map of the city, these three points formed a right-angled triangle, with the 90 degree angle on the monument, and the hypotenuse running down Pennsylvania Avenue, joining the White House with the Capitol. The longest edge of the triangle runs down the centre of the Mall. Ovason continues: ‘The L’Enfant triangle is imprinted into the earth, in much the same way as the three Masons draw a triangle with their shoes when they combine to make the Royal Arch.’ It is Ovason’s theory that this Federal Triangle is an earthly representation of the heavenly triangle of major stars that enclose the constellation of Virgo, the stars being Arcturus, Regulus and Spica. He explains: The undeniable fact is that this triangle of stars seems to reflect the central triangle in the plan of Washington, D.C. The stars of the Virgoan Triangle correspond with the L’Enfant triad as follows: * Arcturus falls on the White House * Regulus falls on the Capitol * Spica falls on the Washington Monument. As mentioned earlier, Benjamin Banneker was included in Andrew Ellicott’s surveying team. Since Banneker went on to write almanacs and papers on astronomy, he is the natural choice when looking to pinpoint the person responsible for influencing the city’s layout in this manner. It would seem that Washington DC is both a sacred and a symbolic city. The original layout envisioned by Pierre L’Enfant had deep esoteric meaning. L’Enfant was no doubt inspired by the design of his native Paris, with its boulevards and central sacred axis. In The Sacred Geometry of Washington, D.C., Nicholas R. Mann notes:

The challenge is to find the will and imagination to restore and expand the pattern of the original vision. Yet who today has anything like the vision that Pierre L’Enfant experienced in the spring of 1791, when he imagined Washington in relation to the ‘celestial axis’, and began to imprint upon the American landscape a geometric pattern that could perfectly represent the revolutionary principle of a new nation? The city L’Enfant dreamt, designed and passionately believed in was to surpass anything that anyone else could imagine at the time – even the vision of George Washington. SEE ALSO: Pierre L’Enfant, George Washington

WASHINGTON MASONIC MEMORIAL When Robert Langdon and Katherine Solomon need to throw the CIA off their scent in The Lost Symbol, they give the impression that they are visiting the Washington Masonic Memorial. This important Masonic edifice is located in Alexandria, south of Washington DC, providing an excuse for them to escape into the Metro transport system, although they ultimately head off elsewhere. Like many important buildings in the city, its design was inspired by the architecture of the classical world. The George Washington Masonic Memorial is based on the lighthouse at Alexandria in Egypt, known as the Pharos – in its day one of the Seven Wonders of the World. At the summit of the tower is an Egyptian pyramid and a representation of a flame in reference to the function of the lighthouse. Of course, the city that once housed the famous lighthouse and the location of the Masonic Memorial also share the same name: Alexandria. George Washington held the office of Master of Alexandria Lodge when he was inaugurated as the first president of the United States in 1789. After his death, the Lodge was renamed Alexandria- Washington Lodge No. 22. Unlike most Masonic buildings, his memorial was supported by donations from all 52 Grand Lodges in the United States. In 1910, Joseph Eggleston, the Grand Master of Virginia, invited every Grand Master in the United States to attend a meeting with the intention of planning and building a memorial to George Washington. Items of Washington’s Masonic regalia and important documents were housed in the Alexandria-Washington Lodge, but there were concerns about whether they were sufficiently safe, there having been a fire at their previous home. The location in Alexandria chosen for the memorial had once been suggested as a possible site for the Capitol Building by Thomas Jefferson. It was also close to landmarks familiar to George Washington, such as Christ Church, where he used to worship. The architect was Harvey W. Corbett, and in addition to the Egyptian influences in the building, he included an entrance inspired by the Parthenon in Athens and adorned the building with a mixture of ancient styles. The memorial had its cornerstone laid on 1 November 1923 in a Masonic ceremony attended by President Calvin Coolidge and former president William Taft, himself a

Freemason. In 1932, 200 years after George Washington’s birth, the memorial was dedicated, again with presidential support; this time Herbert Hoover participated. Internal work continued until final completion in 1970, although as recently as 1999 the well-known Masonic symbol of the square and compasses was installed on the lawn. On the first floor are the Shrine rooms used by the Ancient Arabic Order of the Nobles of the Mystic Shrine, known as Shriners, who are referred to in The Lost Symbol. In the museum dedicated to George Washington on the fourth floor of the tower are displayed various items of his Masonic regalia. These include the apron he had worn in the ceremony of laying the cornerstone of the Capitol Building. In the Royal Arch Chapter Room there are wall paintings of Hebrew and Egyptian design and a depiction of the ruins of Solomon’s Temple, a key theme in Masonry. There is also a replica of the Ark of the Covenant, which was, according to the Old Testament, housed in the Temple of Solomon. The murals are all the work of the artist Allyn Cox, who was also commissioned to complete the frieze in the Capitol Building Rotunda that was left unfinished at the death of Constantino Brumidi. SEE ALSO: Constantino Brumidi, Freemasonry, Shriners, George Washington

WASHINGTON MONUMENT Standing a magnificent 555 feet tall, this imposing monument is the tallest building within the city of Washington DC. Indeed, it is the tallest free-standing masonry-built structure in the world and the tallest obelisk. On completion, it became the tallest structure in the world and remained so until the building of the Eiffel Tower in 1889. On the spine of the jacket of the US version of The Lost Symbol, the Washington Monument is visible through a keyhole. This hints at revelations within the book: that it is below this lofty tower that the lost symbol itself is to be found. Designed by architect Robert Mills, construction of this incredible edifice began in 1848, with the ceremonial laying of the cornerstone taking place on 4 July 1848. Masonic president James K. Polk, the 11th president of the United States, undertook the honours, with some 20,000 people coming to witness the spectacle. Polk had also officiated at the cornerstone-laying ceremony for the Smithsonian in 1847. The monument was completed in 1884; however, for almost 25 years it had stood untouched while the American Civil War raged, left in an incomplete state – at an approximate height of 150 feet – while the grounds around the stump were used as a drill field for the Union Army. Mark Twain remarked that the monument at this time ‘looked like a hollow, oversized chimney’. In 1876, the responsibility for the survey of the entire monument site was handed over to the US Army Corps of Engineers, with Lieutenant Colonel Thomas L. Casey the officer in charge. Casey went on to perform an amazing job at the site. The fact that the monument not only still stands on the sodden and waterlogged ground but also has not been affected by it in the years since his survey and construction is great testament to his skills as an engineer. The marble used to construct the monument was initially quarried in Maryland, but this source dried up after the civil war and marble from Massachusetts was used instead. A subtle change in the shading of the masonry reveals where work stopped and then continued after the war’s end. Congress had originally voted in 1783 to build a statue of George

Washington on horseback and a site was agreed upon, but by 1800 these plans had been shelved and a mausoleum modelled on one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World – the mausoleum of King Mausolus at Halicarnassus in modern-day Turkey – had been proposed, the suggested materials being American granite and marble. This plan got as far as the foundation stone being laid by President Jefferson in 1804, when the stone sank into the soggy, waterlogged marsh that made up the ground at this spot. Funds for the monument then dried up for a significant period of time. Though the idea of the mausoleum was not taken up for the Washington Monument, it was to resurface many years later in the design and construction of the House of the Temple, the headquarters of the Scottish Rite of Freemasonry, Southern Jurisdiction, in Washington DC. The Washington National Monument Society, formed in 1833, reinitiated the plan for a memorial and launched a competition to choose the ultimate design. Robert Mills, the designer of a previous monument to Washington in Baltimore, was the successful architect. His original design was a neoclassical column some 600 feet high, with a colonnade around its base that would have supported statues of a chariot and horses. When work recommenced on the monument in 1876, this design was dropped in favour of the Egyptian-style obelisk we see today. Mills’s initial design was modified further by George Perkins Marsh, better known as America’s first environmentalist and the US representative in Italy from 1861 until his death in 1882. Whilst in Italy, Marsh embarked on a study of the many Egyptian obelisks in Rome (there are more standing obelisks in Rome than in Egypt) and even went so far as to travel to Egypt to undertake further research. He was able to determine that the Egyptian obelisks were constructed to certain set proportions. He calculated that the height of the Egyptian obelisk was ten times that of its baseline; that the obelisk walls would converge at a height some twenty times its baseline; that the angle of the pyramidion on top of the obelisk rarely deviated from 73 degrees; that the height of the pyramidion was equal to the baseline; and that the obelisk tapered at about a quarter of an inch per foot. As a result of this research, Marsh declared that the monument’s design should be reduced in height from 600 feet to 555 feet. ‘Throw out all the gingerbread of the Mills design,’ was the

advice that Marsh gave, and it is his influence that is responsible for the elegant edifice we see today in Washington. Originally intended to stand directly south of the White House and directly west of the Capitol, the monument was moved to its present location because of the unsuitability of the damp and uneven soil at the first construction point. Today, a small granite marker sits at the original site, commemorating the Jefferson Pier, which marked the second prime meridian of the United States. This marker sits some 390 feet WNW of the monument. One of the interesting facts about the monument is that individual blocks, most with inscriptions, were donated to the construction effort from within the United States and around the world. Casey managed to include most of these stones on the interior of the tower, and one of the stones in particular was to cause quite an upset. In the early 1850s, the Pope, Pius IX, donated a piece of marble to the project; however, this was stolen in 1854 by the anti-Catholic nativist American Party, sometimes known at the time as the ‘Know-Nothings’, who destroyed the marble by hurling it into the nearby Potomac River. On 22 February 1885, up to 1,000 people attended the formal dedication ceremony – this date being auspicious as it is the birthday of George Washington. Thomas L. Casey, the US Army engineer responsible for the safe construction of the monument, was one the speakers in attendance that day, along with then president Chester Arthur. When the monument was first opened to the public in 1888, the central elevator was considered unsafe for women to use, meaning that ladies and children had to take the 897 steps to the top of the monument in order to admire the view. This original elevator was a steam-powered device that took upwards of 20 minutes to reach the top level. In The Lost Symbol, the Washington Monument is given Masonic symbolic meaning and the denouement of the story takes place at the site. So, what Masonic connections does the monument have? We know for certain that Robert Mills was a Freemason, as were most of the members of the Washington National Monument Society. As is mentioned earlier, President Polk, who laid the cornerstone, was a Freemason and the ceremony was presided over by Benjamin B. French, Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of the District of Columbia, who wore the apron and sash that had

belonged to George Washington himself and had been worn at the laying of the cornerstone of the Capitol Building. At the cornerstone-laying ceremony of the Washington Monument, a considerable deposit of interesting items was buried in the foundations. Dan Brown alludes to one of these items in The Lost Symbol, namely the copy of the Holy Bible that is indeed part of this collection. Among the numerous other items there are a copy of the Constitution of the United States, a copy of the Declaration of Independence, various plans and sketches of the monument’s design, a catalogue of the Library of Congress, a collection of coins of the United States from the half dime to an eagle, an American flag and a coat of arms of the Washington family. According to author and researcher David Ovason, ‘In the original design, near the top of the obelisk, there was to have been an enormous five-pointed star.’ It has been claimed that this five- pointed star, like the stars included on the American flag, is a Masonic symbol, representing the star Sirius. The capstone on the pyramidion, a piece of pure aluminium weighing 100 ounces, was fixed in place and dedicated in a Masonic ceremony on 6 December 1884. The pyramidion itself has 13 courses, mimicking the unfinished pyramid of the Great Seal that is seen every day on the One Dollar Bill. However, there is a problem with the idea that the Washington Monument was completely Masonic in its execution. Although Mills was a Freemason, his original design was replaced by the revised plan of George Perkins Marsh and Thomas L. Casey, neither of whom have been proven to be members of any lodge. Ovason does claim Casey as a member of the craft, but gives no evidence of this affiliation. Interestingly, though, when we study the height and proportions of the Washington Monument, it becomes plain that number symbolism does play a significant role at the site. In The Sacred Geometry of Washington, D.C., Nicholas R. Mann states: It seems very likely that the decision to make the monument 555 feet 5+ inches high was influenced by one or a number of the branches of Freemasonry that existed in the city at that time. These men would have had specific symbolism and meanings in mind that related to the number 5. Why the

precise angle of the five-pointed pentacle or the pentalpha, 72 degrees, was not used for the crowning pyramidion seem therefore to pose us with something of a mystery. Yet by considering the dimensions of the monument in inches we can solve the mystery. The obelisk’s total height in inches is 6665.125+, which can be justifiably rounded up to 6666. The height of its pyramidion in inches is 660. The sides of its base in inches are 661.5. Then it is necessary to consider the angle of slope from the four corners of the base to the tip of the pyramidion. This is exactly 66 degrees 6 seconds, revealing the hidden number 666. The number symbolism inherent within the monument seems to point to 5 and 6 being the prevalent digits – both numbers of great significance in Freemasonic lore and in the ancient world. In The Lost Symbol, it is revealed that on the eastern face of the aluminium capstone there is the Latin phrase Laus Deo, meaning praise be to God. This is indeed true, with the four sides of the cap having inscriptions thus: NORTH FACE Joint Commission at Setting of Capstone Chester A. Arthur W.W. Corcoran, Chairman M.E. McLaughlin EAST FACE Laus Deo There has been controversy recently concerning the National Park Service’s decision to display a replica of the aluminium capstone of the monument at the visitor’s centre. With the original capstone 555 feet off the ground, it was previously inaccessible. But the replica was displayed so that the side with Laus Deo carved into it was set against a wall and therefore not visible to visitors. In the written material next to the display, the reference for the east side of the capstone was also missing in 2007, whereas previously it had contained the line: ‘The casting was inscribed with the phrase Laus Deo (Praise be to God).’ A lobby of those who saw the deliberate elimination of God from this national monument was mobilised to contact the National Park Service and the campaign was reported in the national news. In the face of protests, the capstone was rotated so that the Laus Deo inscription could be read and the associated notice adjusted to include details of the inscription. The Washington Monument stands today as a permanent and lasting symbol of endurance through adversity. Its message, like a lightning bolt from the heavens, is indelibly marked upon the fabric of Washington DC and it towers over the city as a fitting tribute to the first leader of the fledgling nation. It has stood through turbulent and tumultuous times, and led President Herbert Hoover to say of it, whilst in the midst of the stock market crash of 1929, ‘This apparently is the only stable thing in my administration.’ SEE ALSO: Dollar Bill Symbolism, Freemasonry, House of the Temple

WASHINGTON NATIONAL CATHEDRAL Having evaded the CIA, Robert Langdon and Katherine Solomon dash to the Washington National Cathedral, where they have been sent by the enigmatic old man, following his instruction to go to a refuge containing ten stones from Mount Sinai, including ‘one from heaven itself ‘ and ‘one with the visage of Luke’s dark father’. Set in a 57-acre site, the magnificent Washington National Cathedral took 83 years to complete after the foundation stone was laid in 1907 by Freemasonic president Theodore Roosevelt. The stone itself came from Bethlehem. The $65 million cost of the cathedral’s construction was raised solely by public donation, as is the money for its maintenance and upkeep today. Based on a design by the English architect George Frederick Bodley, a famed proponent of the neo-Gothic revival, the Episcopalian cathedral is dedicated to St Peter and St Paul. When Bodley died in 1907, followed ten years later by Henry Vaughan, his supervising architect, the design of the cathedral came under the auspices of American architect Philip Frohman. He continued in the spirit of Bodley’s master plan, making additions and changes where required. Today, the Washington National Cathedral is the sixth-largest cathedral in the world and is able to seat 4,000 people. Its east-to-west central aisle is 517 feet long and spans 104 feet, its two enormous front-facing towers are 232 feet tall and its central tower stands 30 storeys high. When the elevated position of the site is taken into account, this tower reaches a total of 676 feet above sea level, making its tip the highest point in Washington DC. The two symmetrical towers of the west-facing facade are decorated with no less than 288 angels, while rising out of the mid- nave, the enormous central bell tower, the Gloria in Excelsis Tower, houses 53 carillon bells and 10 peal bells, the only complete set of both types of bell in the United States. Built in a Gothic-inspired style, the Washington National Cathedral has all the conventional Gothic elements of flying buttresses, soaring arches, vaulted ceilings, carved stones and large stained-glass and rose windows. Gargoyles and grotesques are an important architectural element of any Gothic cathedral, and the Washington National Cathedral is no exception, boasting 112.

Gargoyles are carved stone waterspouts, usually in the form of unusual or evil-looking humans or animals, designed to direct rainwater away from the structure. Grotesques, on the other hand, while having the same purpose, do not incorporate waterspouts; rainwater simply bounces off them. Examples of gargoyles and grotesques can be found on the front and sides of the cathedral and include a curly-haired man reading a book, a cat clinging to the top of a tree, a dragon, a coiled snake, a three-eyed man with a millstone around his neck, the Greek god Pan with his pipes, a devil holding a pitchfork and a basket of fruit, a snake twisting around the skeleton of a winged creature, and a fat, warty toad. Its most famous and unique gargoyle, however, features the face of Darth Vader – this is the face of ‘Luke’s dark father’ that is mentioned in The Lost Symbol. Situated high up on the St Peter tower, it was the third-prize-winner in a competition held in the 1980s to design a new gargoyle. Built mainly of Indiana limestone, the cathedral also contains many architectural materials from sites around the world. The Canterbury Pulpit, which depicts the translation of the Bible from Latin into English, was carved from stone from Canterbury Cathedral, and the bishop’s seat, the Glastonbury Cathedra, is made from stone from Glastonbury, England. The stone for the Jerusalem Altar came from a quarry close to Jerusalem, and the ten stones in front of the altar, representing the Ten Commandments, came from Mount Sinai. It is these stones that are mentioned in the clue in The Lost Symbol. The front of the cathedral has a creation-themed frieze carved above the three doors: the creation of day is depicted above the left door, the creation of humans above the middle door and the creation of night above the right door. Portraying the concept of redemption through faith, there are statues depicting St Peter with his fishing net, representing the moment he was called to Christ’s ministry; Adam emerging from a stone; and St Paul blinded by God, representing the moment of his conversion to Christianity. Inside the cathedral, the 16 bays on each side of the wide nave hold statues, carvings and stained-glass windows detailing diverse aspects of the United States’ heritage, such as the search for freedom; the 1803 Lewis and Clark exploratory expedition; aspects of law; Woodrow Wilson, the 28th president; an image of Martin Luther King, who preached his last sermon in the cathedral just

days before he was assassinated; images of world peace; the roles of Christian women; a depiction of the 23rd Psalm (‘The Lord is my Shepherd’); and a bronze statue of Abraham Lincoln. There is also a window dedicated to the civil-war generals Robert E. Lee and Thomas ‘Stonewall’ Jackson, and the Space Window, containing a piece of moon rock, which commemorates the Apollo 11 mission. In all, the cathedral has two hundred and fifteen stained-glass windows, including three rose windows, all of which feature brightly coloured glass. In the middle of the nave, the west rose window details the creation story; the north rose window relates to the Last Judgement; the south rose window celebrates the Church Triumphant. The 18 windows of the nave clerestory show the preparation for the Messiah. At the east end of the cathedral is the high altar, separated from the main nave by an ornately carved rood-screen. Behind the high altar is the magnificent Ter Sanctus reredos, featuring 110 carved figures surrounding the central figure of Jesus. As well as the high altar, the cathedral has nine chapels: the War Memorial Chapel; the Children’s Chapel (built to the scale of a six year old); St John’s Chapel and St Mary’s Chapel, in the far nave; and the Good Shepherd Chapel, Bethlehem Chapel, Chapel of St Joseph of Arimathea and Resurrection Chapel, all situated in the crypt. The four crypt chapels are of a Romanesque design, imitating the tradition of building Gothic cathedrals over earlier Norman churches. Once a month, a large canvas labyrinth is placed on the floor of the central nave to enable the public to walk in prayer using the pattern of the famous labyrinth at Chartres Cathedral in France. The Washington National Cathedral has become the site of national prayer and was used for the service of thanksgiving at the end of the First World War. The state funerals of four presidents have been conducted in the cathedral, as have presidential inaugural prayer services. There are 220 people interred there, including President Woodrow Wilson, Helen Keller, her teacher Anne Sullivan and the cathedral’s architects Philip Frohman and Henry Vaughan. THE ZOHAR The notion that twentieth-century discoveries in physics, such as string theory, could have been predicted by ancient texts seems impossible; however, Peter Solomon suggests this to his sister Katherine in The Lost Symbol. He claims that the remarkable text that contains such prophecies is the Zohar. This book of Jewish mystical lore is one of the most important works in the Kabbalah. Its name translates as ‘splendour’ or ‘radiance’. Most likely developed in western Europe sometime in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, the Zohar is a collection of texts that are seen as some of the highest expressions of Jewish literary and mystical imagination ever written. Arthur Green in A Guide to the Zohar has this to say about the sacred text: The Zohar is a work of sacred fantasy. To say this about it is by no means to impugn the truth of its insights or to diminish the religious profundity of its teachings. The Middle Ages were filled with fantasy. Angels and demons, heavenly principalities, chambers of heaven and rungs within the soul, secret treasures of the spirit that could be seen only by the elect, esoteric domains without end – all of these were found in the writings of Jewish, Christian, and Islamic authors throughout medieval times. It should be noted that the Zohar is not a single entity but a series of books. In some modern translations, there are 23 volumes in the set. Debate rages over the ultimate origins of the Zohar, and today there are two camps: one, as noted above, which believes that the text was set down in medieval times; the second, with scholars such as Gershom Scholem, which suggests that the text originated around the first or second century AD. What impresses Katherine about the Zohar is its depictions of the ten Sephiroth. Peter Solomon notes that these can be interpreted as the ten dimensions of the quantum universe – in effect, string theory.

The concept of the Sephiroth is described in the Zohar. It means ‘enumerations’, of which there are ten, through which God reveals himself. These ten emanations are seen as different spiritual aspects of the godhead and when laid out on paper form the traditional Kabbalah Tree of Life. God, as a concept within the Zohar, is seen as embodying both the male and the female aspect and even has a female ‘counterpart’ called the Shekinah. This idea of an ancient Sacred Feminine is something Dan Brown explored in The Da Vinci Code. Robert Langdon and the dean of Washington National Cathedral discuss the circumpunct symbol in The Lost Symbol. In a link with the Zohar, the Kether, the highest Sephiroth, is said to have been represented by Kabbalists using the circumpunct. The Zohar is a complex and detailed text that demands a lifetime’s in-depth study. Its secrets and mysteries are only now beginning to come to light, as more and more people in the twenty- first century begin to look for a greater spiritual dimension to their lives.
